*Proof.* Multiply the polynomials and compare coefficients; the factorials in (7.3) cancel the binomial coefficients. The product norm inequality follows termwise from Lemma 7.1, and the discarded terms of degree >2 have nonnegative majorants. ∎

Thus an additive first-order mark at a merger always has a second-order cross row when its generating densities are multiplied. It cannot be discarded as a contact unless its precise support and the chosen subtraction justify that operation. These lemmas do not lose a factorial at each merger and do not assume that child history measures are independent.

### 7.2 Undivided coefficients: exact downstream cancellation through replacement kernels (P)

The following proves a complete cancellation statement for a specified class of replacements. It does not turn a rare upper majorant into a lower bound for another denominator.

Let v denote all retained variables, **including retained history labels**, x the variables being removed, and y the replacement variables. Let `n(v,x)≥0` be the actual incoming unnormalized density, with arbitrary selectors and source-independent normalizers included. Let `s(v,y)≥0` be the selected reference density, and assume only

`0<D(v):=∫s(v,y)dy<∞`

on the v-support of n. Define the source-independent replacement operator on signed/complex integrable coefficients by

`(Rη)(v,y) := [s(v,y)/D(v)] ∫η(v,x)dx`.   (7.5)

Measures and discrete sums can replace the displayed densities. A deterministic retained-variable map or a further positive probability kernel can be composed with R.

**Theorem 7.3 (mass, total variation, and all finite source coefficients).** Let `η_m(v,x)=n(v,x)F_m(v,x)` with `∫|η_m|<∞`, for `0≤m≤M`, and `F₀=1`. Then

`∫ Rη_m = ∫η_m`, `‖Rη_m‖TV≤‖η_m‖TV`.   (7.6)

For any finite composition of such source-independent replacements, both conclusions hold with constant one, independently of the number of replacements and how small D becomes. If `n_J=n exp(Σ_i J_iF_i)` and derivatives can be passed under the finite integral, every multi-index coefficient is carried as

`η_α=n ∏_i F_i^{α_i}`, `Rη_α=∂_J^α(Rn_J)|₀`.   (7.7)

The outgoing mark is the Radon–Nikodym derivative `Rη_α/Rn`; it is generally **not** `∏_i(F_i evaluated on y)^{α_i}`. For every p≥1,

`∫ |Rη_1/Rn|^p Rn ≤ ∫ |F_1|^p n`.   (7.8)

Zero-mass fibers are omitted. The same statements hold for coefficient arrays with the norm (7.1), using the integrated norm and fixed anchors.

*Proof.* Integrating (7.5) over y gives `D(v)/D(v)=1` pointwise in v. Fubini proves the first identity in (7.6), and the triangle inequality proves the second. Apply induction for any composition. Linearity and dominated differentiation prove (7.7). On each v-fiber the outgoing first mark is `∫nF_1 dx/∫n dx`, independent of y. Jensen's inequality for this **incoming** conditional probability proves (7.8); a general Markov kernel gives the same inequality by disintegration of the joint incoming/outgoing measure. For arrays use (7.2) and the convexity of the norm to the power p. ∎

The significance for B/Z is precise. A raw moment bound `∫n|F|²≤B` passes through every replacement with the same B. No local quotient `B/D(v)` or `B/(∫n dx)` is estimated, because its compensating outgoing density remains beside it until integration. This is a downstream cancellation, not an assumed comparison of B with either denominator. At the end normalization is by the **one original total mass** `Z=∫n`; a normalized estimate still reads `B/Z`. It is cutoff-uniform only if this final ratio is controlled (for example by a complete common-scalar stability estimate, or by estimates directly under the actual normalized Wilson law). Neither a lower bound for Z nor that ratio follows from a rare upper bound alone.

The source-free operator can be frozen at J=0 even if a hypothetical sourced algorithm would change it: mass preservation holds for every input coefficient, so it supplies an exact sourced representation without a source-dependent denominator. This is useful only while the resulting coefficients can be estimated on the admitted domains. It does not prove the required local graded norm.

**Corollary 7.4 (what can be carried through the schematic R-operation).** In LFR I, printed p.176, (0.3), fix a term with `v=V|_{Λ\Z′}`, `x=V|_{Z′}` and reference density `s=ρ(Z″,v,y)`. Then (7.5) is exactly that term of (0.3), with the inserted coefficient in its numerator. Thus (0.4) holds coefficientwise for every finite source jet, without any lower bound on D apart from positivity. Summing the terms before applying (7.6) includes the entire positive history measure. **Scope:** the author states on printed p.177 that the actual localized construction uses integrals of *parts* of densities near Z′. To apply Theorem 7.3 to that construction one must match the corresponding extracted outside factors and integration domains exactly, or use its actual mass-preserving kernel. The schematic (0.3) alone does not verify that matching for all localized/differentiated terms.

The same source's (0.5) then localizes and exponentiates these quotients. Those signed localized coefficients are no longer positive Markov kernels; a weighted absolute coefficient estimate must be proved before applying their connected expansion. Theorem 7.3 deliberately stops at this exact boundary.

### 7.3 Exact second-order transport, including retained-history means (P)

At a fixed cutoff normalize the original positive joint Wilson/history measure once. Let `X₀,…,X_K` be the successive retained states under source-independent probability kernels; include every retained history coordinate in each state. These variables form a Markov chain. Original observables F,G are functions of X₀ with finite second moments. Define

`f_k=E(F|X_k)`, `g_k=E(G|X_k)`,

`c_k=E(FG|X_k)−f_kg_k`.   (7.9)

For complex observables the displayed covariance is bilinear; the variance bounds below use real observables or the usual Hermitian covariance.

**Theorem 7.5 (source and contact tower).** For every k<K,

`f_{k+1}=E(f_k|X_{k+1})`,

`c_{k+1}=E(c_k|X_{k+1})+Cov(f_k,g_k|X_{k+1})`,   (7.10)

and

`Cov(F,G)=E c_K+Cov(f_K,g_K)`.   (7.11)

For F=G the exact nonnegative decomposition is

`Var(F)=Var(f_K)+Σ_{k=0}^{K−1} E Var(f_k|X_{k+1})`.   (7.12)

Here `c₀=0`. If X₀ already omits coordinates used by F, add `E Var(F|X₀)` to (7.12).

*Proof.* The Markov property implies `E(F|X_k,X_{k+1})=E(F|X_k)` and the same statement for FG. The tower property gives the first line of (7.10) and

`E(FG|X_{k+1})=E(c_k+f_kg_k|X_{k+1})`.

Subtract the product of the first moments to get the second line. Taking expectations and adding the final covariance proves (7.11). For F=G, iterate the second line and use c₀=0. ∎

This is the exact second source-derivative recursion for a sourced density: `∂_t log E(e^{tF}|X_k)|₀=f_k` and `∂_t² log E(e^{tF}|X_k)|₀=c_k`. These identities are formal finite-order identities at zero; they do not presume a cutoff-independent logarithmic disc. Mixed derivatives give (7.9). All cross terms from mergers are present by (7.4).

Disintegrating a stage further as `X_k=(H,Y)` gives an additional conditional-mean covariance when H is later removed. A function depending only on H can have zero conditional Y-gradient and nonzero variance. Equation (7.12) locates its contribution at the step which forgets H; no internal Poincaré estimate removes it. In particular a source readout frozen during live retention has no new integration cost at each waiting step: its measure coefficient is carried unchanged. Costs of the *history weight* and changed radii still require the reserve ledger in §7.4. Adding one copy of the frozen mark per live step would count a different observable.

Theorem 7.5 is compatible with the undivided construction in §7.2: the two raw coefficient measures `nF` and `nF²` are transported linearly, and the logarithmic second coefficient is formed only after conditioning on the outgoing state. It supplies a complete algebraic continuation through live retention, mergers and final integration. It does **not** estimate the resulting conditional covariance in the MT36 anchor norm, does not generate the factor g_k, and does not assert local counterterm support. Those are analytic estimates for the actual kernels.

### 7.4 Joint reserve payments, mergers, and the uncompensated old-age debt (P/C)

Use the actual source-free positive body `μ=Σ_ω μ_ω` on one completed component. Do not normalize its fibers. Write x=`g_e⁻²≥1`, E≥0 for its one allocated energy, T≥0 for its number of genuinely charged live-step records, and d(X) for the carrier distance. The hypothesis for this section is the **one combined reserve estimate**

`∫ exp(θE+λT)dμ ≤ C₀ exp[−c(log x)^p−κd(X)] =: B_c(X,x)`,   (7.13)

with θ,c,κ>0, p>1 and λ≥0. It must hold after all unmarked costs, entropy, independent normalizers and reference factors have been included. Neither I-0c nor scalar admission I-2 alone implies (7.13). Balaban's actual rare coefficient is logarithmic: LFR II (1.89), (1.100), not generally `exp(−c/g²)`. This section deliberately works with the weaker logarithmic reserve.

For each of finitely many *owned* rows ℓ assume the actual envelope

`Q_ℓ ≤ C_ℓ x^{a_ℓ} exp(d_ℓT)(1+E)^{b_ℓ}`, with `a_ℓ,d_ℓ,b_ℓ≥0`.   (7.14)

**Theorem 7.6 (one joint reserve for an arbitrary fixed packet).** For fixed powers q_ℓ≥0 put `A=Σ a_ℓq_ℓ`, `D=Σ d_ℓq_ℓ`, `B=Σ b_ℓq_ℓ`. If D≤λ and 0<δ<c, then

`∫ ∏_ℓ Q_ℓ^{q_ℓ} dμ ≤ (∏ C_ℓ^{q_ℓ}) M_B(θ) C_{A,δ,p} B_{c−δ}(X,x)`,   (7.15)

where `M_B(θ)=sup_{u≥0}(1+u)^B exp(−θu)` and

`C_{A,δ,p}=exp[((p−1)/p) A (A/(δp))^{1/(p−1)}]`

for A>0, and `C_{0,δ,p}=1`. Explicitly `M_B=1` if B≤θ and `M_B=(B/θ)^B exp(−B+θ)` otherwise. There is **one** B on the right, regardless of how many rows are multiplied.

*Proof.* Multiply (7.14). The energy polynomial times `exp(−θE)` is bounded by M_B, and `exp(DT)≤exp(λT)`. Equation (7.13) then bounds the integral by `(∏C_ℓ^{q_ℓ})M_B x^A B_c`. Maximizing `At−δt^p` over t=`log x≥0` gives the stated C and (7.15). All powers were added before either reserve was spent. No independence or repeated use of the same rare coefficient occurs. ∎

For the saved packet `|F|≤A_jρ²[r^sQ²+ur^bQ³+u²r²Q⁴]`, Minkowski yields

`‖F‖_{L²(μ)} ≤ A_jρ²[r^s(μQ⁴)^{1/2}+ur^b(μQ⁶)^{1/2}+u²r²(μQ⁸)^{1/2}]`.   (7.16)

Applying (7.15) once with the largest needed joint exponents controls all three rows while retaining their displayed age/coupling factors. For two different packets, expand their product and use (7.15) with their **sum** of exponents, not separate component masses. If curvature/current native depth costs have d=2 log L and d=3 log L, degree eight requires λ≥24 log L for a single all-current envelope. Additional differentiated scores or other rows add to D; they are not free. Extra current factors `g_e⁻q=x^{q/2}` can be paid by the same δ after they have been included in A. Constants depend on the finite packet orders and reserves, and not on a,K,history count or e once (7.13)–(7.14) hold uniformly.

**Lemma 7.7 (merger ledger telescoping).** On a finite rooted ancestry tree assign nonnegative credit c_v, expense e_v and surviving bank b_v to each node, with

`b_v+e_v ≤ c_v+Σ_{w child of v} b_w`.   (7.17)

Then `b_root+Σ_v e_v≤Σ_v c_v`. A credit attached to a leaf, renewal or merger surplus can therefore pay at most once; any source cost must occur among the e_v. Inserting a cost `λ` at each charged live node requires the corresponding enlarged inequalities (7.17), not just their unmarked versions.

*Proof.* Sum (7.17). Each non-root bank occurs once on each side and cancels. ∎

This elementary statement is the exact algebra needed at a merger. Lemma 7.2 supplies its marked cross rows and Theorem 7.6 supplies their joint polynomial payment **after** the actual scalar recurrence supplies (7.13). Reconstructing that enlarged recurrence for all actual gauge histories is not replaced by this algebra. The primary source's source-free merger induction is LFR II, printed pp.384–387, (1.80)–(1.88).

**Lemma 7.8 (what waiting can and cannot pay).** If a native record was born at scale ℓ, became continuously live at scale a_R≥ℓ, and remains live to scale e, with `e−a_R≤T`, then

`L^{D₀(e−ℓ)} ≤ exp(D₀ log L·T) L^{D₀(a_R−ℓ)}`.   (7.18)

Only the first factor is a live-reserve cost. If an independent saved clean estimate supplies `L^{−s(a_R−ℓ)}`, the product retains `L^{−(s−D₀)(a_R−ℓ)}`. It decays only when s>D₀; it is constant when s=D₀ and grows when s<D₀. A waiting factor cannot retroactively charge clean age, and an old radius cannot be reset by renaming its birth scale.

*Proof.* Split `e−ℓ=(e−a_R)+(a_R−ℓ)` and use the assumed live count. ∎

Finally, if `Q≤H(v)+Q_owned` with v still external, (7.16) retains `H(v)^4 μ1` in the quadratic-row square and `H(v)^8 μ1` in the quartic-row square. If v is eventually integrated, the necessary quantity is its **actual joint** integral `∫H(v)^8 μ_v1 dν(v)`; if v stays external, the corresponding uniform bound is needed. (7.13) for an internal energy cannot create that estimate. This precise residual survives the joint-reserve improvement.

### 7.5 Why finite packets do not give an analytic pressure, and a valid replacement criterion (P)

**Proposition 7.9 (rare-source countermodel).** Fix c,p,a>0 with p>1. For x sufficiently large let a probability law put mass `b_x=exp[−c(log x)^p]` at the value `F_x=x^a`, and mass `1−b_x` at zero. Every fixed positive moment is uniformly bounded as x→∞, and in fact

`E|F_x|^m=x^{am} exp[−c(log x)^p]→0` for each fixed m.

Nevertheless the moment generating function

`Z_x(t)=1−b_x+b_x exp(tx^a)`

has a zero

`t_x=x^{−a}[log((1−b_x)/b_x)+iπ]→0`.   (7.19)

Hence there is no cutoff-uniform zero-free disc. Multiplying Z_x by `exp(−L_x(t))` for any entire local counterterm does not remove these zeros.

*Proof.* Put y=log x. The moment logarithm is `amy−cy^p→−∞`. Substitution of t_x gives `exp(t_xx^a)=−(1−b_x)/b_x`, so Z_x(t_x)=0. Its modulus is `O(x^{−a}(log x)^p)→0`. The exponential of an entire function never vanishes. ∎

This is a counterexample to deriving a common source disc from fixed-order moment/reserve estimates, not a counterexample for Wilson histories. It applies even when every finite-order raw carrying estimate of the form (7.15) is available. The once-owned rare reserve can pay any *fixed* inverse coupling power; it cannot automatically pay the exponential of that power at fixed source amplitude. Thus proving all fixed source jets separately and then declaring their power series uniformly analytic would be invalid.

**Proposition 7.10 (near-one criterion for the true logarithm).** Let ν_a be the actual normalized terminal positive measure on T*. Suppose `H_a(z,ω)` is holomorphic on a fixed finite polydisc P, `H_a(0,ω)=0`, and there is a common integrable majorant permitting holomorphic integration such that

`sup_{a,z∈P} ∫ [exp(|H_a(z,ω)|)−1]dν_a(ω) ≤ η<1`.   (7.20)

Then `Z_a(z)=∫exp(H_a(z,ω))dν_a(ω)` is holomorphic and nonzero on P, the branch `G_a=log Z_a` with G_a(0)=0 exists on P, and

`|G_a(z)|≤−log(1−η)`.   (7.21)

Consequently, on smaller closed polydiscs, every source derivative obeys the usual Cauchy bound `|∂^αG_a(0)|≤α! [−log(1−η)]∏ r_i^{−α_i}`. A sufficient deterministic bound is `sup|H_a|≤h<log 2`, giving η=`e^h−1`.

*Proof.* Holomorphic integration gives analyticity. Since `|e^w−1|≤e^{|w|}−1`, (7.20) implies `|Z_a−1|≤η`. Define the logarithm by its convergent series about 1; summing its absolute values yields (7.21). Apply the multivariable Cauchy formula. ∎

For an exact representation `Z_full(J)/Z_full(0)=exp(L_a(J)) E_{ν_a} exp(H_a(J))`, (7.20) gives the analytic and bounded **subtracted** pressure with bound `Vol(T*)⁻¹[−log(1−η)]`. A small terminal source radius may depend on N,L,M,ℓ₀,t* and a prescribed finite family of tests; it must not depend on a or K. This criterion also states where large-field and history sums belong: inside ν_a and the expectation, before taking the logarithm.

That (3.11) needs only source degrees ≤4 is not proved. For a dimension-four operator in four dimensions, the source has engineering dimension zero; power counting permits local functions of every source degree. An all-order holomorphic contact functional, or a separately justified restriction to finitely many source derivatives, is needed. The quadratic contact localization proposed by T3 is not assumed in this theorem.

For susceptibility the stronger source class of §1.5, item 7, still requires its own zero-free estimate. Bounded physical C⁵ sources do not include uniformly all lattice plane waves. Proposition 7.10 may be applied to that class only after its hypotheses have been established for those sources.

### 7.6 A concrete live/R transition: compact marks on the original T′-integration variables (P with checked native scope)

This restricted result applies directly to the actual operator `T′_k(X)` in LFR II (1.71), printed pp.378–380, before the subsequent signed localization. Its proof does not assume that a healed old readout is a compact variable.

Fix the native real outer configuration U of that operator. The full integration/history sum in (1.71), including its selectors, Gaussian and Wilson factors, gauge constraints, inherited V(X⁻), vacuum terms and independent normalizers, defines a finite positive measure `μ_U`; write `M_U=μ_U1>0`. On the original native complex outer domain, the argument on printed pp.379–380 represents the same operator as

`T_z F=∫exp(σ_z) F dμ_U`, `σ_0=0`, `sup|σ_z|≤ε`.   (7.22)

Here z denotes the native complex outer coordinates (not a new preparation wall). We restrict to a smaller domain on which `ε<log 2`. Such restriction is legitimate for the stated native holomorphic bounds; it is not an admission of the independent old source domain. These formulas and the same-operator bounds (1.73)–(1.75) are used as printed. Printed p.378 explicitly permits two classes of component, including those retained as large-field components.

Insert a finite compact plaquette mark on the **original integrated group variables** of this operation:

`F_ω(V)=Σ_{p∈P_ω} J_p [1−Re Tr V_p/N]`, `Σ_{p∈P_ω}|J_p|≤A`,   (7.23)

where each complete plaquette stencil is in those group variables. History dependence of the finite set P_ω is permitted if it is part of the original retained record. A common gauge transformation or a relabeling leaves these plaquette words unchanged. The mark is not evaluated on a reconstructed complex old minimum. Since each normalized plaquette excess lies in [0,2], `|F_ω|≤2A=:M_F` on the whole actual positive body, independently of the depth of its live retention.

**Proposition 7.11 (finite compact-mark transition).** On the above original native domain:

(a) If the variables of (7.23) are retained in a live step, F is carried unchanged; its first and second raw source coefficients are F and F². No factor equal to the number of waiting steps is produced.

(b) At their integration by T′, the exact raw coefficients satisfy, for m=0,1,2 (indeed for every fixed m),

`|∂_t^m T_z(e^{tF})|_{t=0}| ≤ exp(ε) M_F^m M_U`.   (7.24)

They therefore retain any valid rare bound for M_U **once**. If a saved deterministic scalar a_{j,e} multiplies F, the right side has `|a_{j,e}|^m`, with its old age/radius/coupling data unchanged.

(c) Let `rM_F+ε<log 2`. Then `T_z(e^{tF})` is nonzero for |t|≤r, and

`log[T_z(e^{tF})/T_z1]`

is holomorphic in t,z there. With `C_ε=exp(ε)/(2−exp(ε))`, its first derivative at zero has modulus at most `C_ε M_F`, and its second at most `(C_ε+C_ε²)M_F²`. At the real native point this second derivative is the full variance under `μ_U/M_U`, including history means, and is ≤M_F².

*Proof.* Part (a) is the identity map on the retained variables; differentiate its source exponential. For (b), dominated differentiation in a bounded mark gives `T_zF^m`; apply positivity of μ_U. For (c),

`|T_z(e^{tF})−M_U|≤[exp(ε+rM_F)−1]M_U<M_U`.

The near-one logarithm therefore exists. The denominator `|T_z1|≥(2−exp ε)M_U`; divide the first two raw coefficients and use

`∂_t² log T_z(e^{tF})|₀ = T_zF²/T_z1 − (T_zF/T_z1)²`.

At the real point the probability variance is at most `E|F|²≤M_F²`. In a disintegration by retained history, both the conditional variance and the variance of the conditional mean are nonnegative and sum to this quantity by Theorem 7.5, so the latter is genuinely controlled here. ∎

This settles a real restricted R-2/R-3 transition, not just an abstract criterion: the mark uses literal compact variables in the original T′ body, the history sum is inside that body, the source normalizer is exactly T′1, and no absolute denominator lower bound is needed. The local source radius is independent of a,K when A is fixed. If the number or total weight of plaquettes grows, r retains the factor A⁻¹. A full physical source can have A diverging like the number of fine plaquettes; this proposition does not remove that dependence.

A further restricted interaction attachment is available. Suppose the **same actual body** retains `∫e^{τG}dμ_U≤B_c` after all original costs and the full inherited scalar obeys `|V_z|≤C_V G`, with τ>0. The raw connected coefficient is

`C_z(F,V)=T_z(FV)−(T_zF)(T_zV)/T_z1`.

Cauchy–Schwarz and the previous denominator estimate give

`|C_z(F,V)|≤[e^ε+e^{2ε}/(2−e^ε)] ‖F‖_{L²(μ_U)}‖V_z‖_{L²(μ_U)}`

`≤C(ε,τ,C_V) M_F B_c`.   (7.25)

If `B_c=C₀ exp[−c(log x)^p−κd(X)]`, x=`g_k⁻²`, then for any 0<δ<c, (7.15) with A=1/2 gives

`|C_z(F,V)|≤C_δ g_k M_F B_{c−δ}`.   (7.26)

The g_k is paid once from the surviving rare coefficient; it is not a clean O(g_k) bound on the full inherited V. Equation (7.25) includes the between-history contribution because the Cauchy–Schwarz norms are over the whole positive body. The extra reserve hypothesis must be verified by the enlarged original scalar recurrence; (1.73)–(1.75) alone gives no such reserve. Even when (7.26) holds, dividing it by T_z1 would again require a comparison with that mass. Keeping it as an undivided coefficient is the option supplied by §7.2.

**Boundary of this concrete result.** An inherited `R_j(P_old q_old Γ^R,J_phys)` is not of the compact form (7.23). Its saved current derivatives, weighted anchors, and pre-entry clean age still require I-2's actual packet plus the estimates in §7.4. Reopening a healed field as a fresh compact variable would change the observable and is not used here.

### 7.7 An alternate route to bounded marginal transport: a proportional complex coupling domain (P/C)

The logarithmic upper bound for z_K in (3.7) arose from the crude per-step estimate O(g_k²). The following stronger conclusion is possible without assuming I-3, provided the **coupling map itself**, with all its inherited dependence, has the specified complex control. This is an additional hypothesis on I-0c/T4, not a consequence of its real flow bound.

**Hypothesis CF.** Let b>0, 0<θ<1 and C<∞ be fixed. The exact scalar restriction of the source-free flow is given by nonautonomous holomorphic maps

`f_j(z)=z−b+r_j(z)`, `x_{j+1}=f_j(x_j)`,

with real x_j≥h, and for each j<K the remainder is holomorphic on `|z−x_j|<θx_j` and obeys

`|r_j(z)|≤C/x_j` throughout that disc.   (7.27)

The map includes any dependence of other running coordinates on this family; a real formula for one trajectory is not a holomorphic scalar family. Its discs have radius proportional to x_j, not a fixed absolute radius.

**Proposition 7.12 (bounded marginal Jacobian and common perturbation disc).** Put `D=2C/θ` and take h so large that `C/h≤b/2` and `D/h²≤1/2`. Let

`A_* = D[h⁻²+2/(bh)]`, `R_*=(θh/4)exp(−A_*)`.   (7.28)

Then, uniformly in K and k≤K, the scalar marginal Jacobian

`z_k=∂x_k/∂x₀=∏_{j<k}(1+r'_j(x_j))`

is positive and satisfies

`exp(−2A_*)≤z_k≤exp(A_*)`.   (7.29)

Every perturbation `|ζ|<R_*` of x₀ has a holomorphic trajectory under the same maps, with

`|x_j(ζ)−x_j|≤exp(A_*)|ζ|≤θx_j/4`.   (7.30)

In particular all fixed derivatives of `x_k(ζ)−x_k` at zero are uniformly bounded; for every `0<R<R_*`,

`|∂_ζ^m x_k(0)|≤m! exp(A_*) R^{1−m}`.   (7.31)

*Proof.* The real recurrence gives `x_j−x_{j+1}≥b/2`, hence `x_j≥x_k+(b/2)(k−j)`. Comparing the decreasing reciprocal-square series to its integral yields `Σ_{j<k}x_j⁻²≤h⁻²+2/(bh)`. Cauchy's estimate on (7.27) gives `|r'_j(z)|≤D/x_j²` for `|z−x_j|≤θx_j/2` (take limiting slightly smaller Cauchy circles). At the real centers `1+r'_j(x_j)>0`. The inequalities `log(1+u)≤|u|` and `log(1+u)≥−2|u|` for real |u|≤1/2 give (7.29).

For the perturbed trajectory, assume its previous points lie in the half-discs. Integrating f′ along the segment from x_j to x_j(ζ) gives

`|x_{j+1}(ζ)−x_{j+1}|≤(1+D/x_j²)|x_j(ζ)−x_j|`.

The product is bounded by exp(A_*); the definition of R_* closes the induction with a quarter-disc margin. Composition gives holomorphy. Apply Cauchy to `x_k(ζ)−x_k`, bounded by exp(A_*)R on each circle |ζ|=R, to obtain (7.31). ∎

For the constant Tr F² source of Remark 3.5, ζ=`−t/(2N²)`. Thus CF supplies a common complex constant-source perturbation disc `|t|<2N²R_*` and a uniformly bounded marginal coefficient, replacing the log-growth loss of (3.7). It does not bound the scalar vacuum response, the effective polymer response, position-dependent coupling derivatives, or the logarithm of the sourced partition function. Those require their own source norms and Proposition 7.10 or an appropriate connected expansion.

A fixed absolute remainder disc would only yield `|r'_j|=O(x_j⁻¹)`, whose sum can grow logarithmically; the proportional radius is exactly what converts that loss into the summable `O(x_j⁻²)` derivative. The next constructive test is to establish (7.27) for the actual effective coupling map after fixing its extraction convention, rather than to assume bounded z_K from the real asymptotic flow.

### 7.8 A genuine complex weak-coupling block estimate for the compact Wilson law (P)

This section continues the alternate route beyond hypothesis CF. It proves the required proportional complex-domain mechanism for an **actual fixed contractible Wilson block**, including its compact large-field complement. It is not an assertion about a growing block or the full periodic reference torus.

**Lemma 7.13 (determinant plus frozen-cutoff error).** Let H be a positive real n×n matrix, and K a real symmetric matrix with `‖H⁻¹/²KH⁻¹/²‖≤c`. For complex z,t with `|z−1|+c|t|≤θ<1`, set `B=zH−tK`. Then

`G(z,t)=∫_{Rⁿ}exp(−bᵀBb/2)db=(2π)^{n/2}(det H)⁻¹/² det(zI−tH⁻¹/²KH⁻¹/²)⁻¹/²`   (7.32)

is holomorphic and nonzero, with the branch continued from (z,t)=(1,0). Let `C_p={|b_i|≤p for every i}` and `v=max_i(H⁻¹)_{ii}`. Its relative cutoff error is at most

`|G−G_p|/|G| ≤ R_{n,θ}·2n exp[−(1−θ)p²/(2v)]`,

`R_{n,θ}=((1+θ)/(1−θ))^{n/2}`.   (7.33)

A holomorphic additional exponent E(z,t,b), bounded by ε on C_p, changes the cutoff integral by at most `R_{n,θ}(e^ε−1)|G|`. Consequently the full perturbed cutoff integral is zero-free whenever the sum of these two relative errors is <1.

*Proof.* The real part of B dominates `(1−θ)H`. Diagonalize the real symmetric matrix `H⁻¹/²KH⁻¹/²`; every determinant eigenvalue z−tλ lies in the disc of radius θ about 1. This proves (7.32) and `|G|≥(2π)^{n/2}(det H)⁻¹/²(1+θ)⁻n/2`. Bound the absolute tail by the Gaussian with precision `(1−θ)H` and use the union bound and the scalar Gaussian tail for its n coordinates. Dividing by the preceding lower bound gives (7.33). The perturbation estimate follows from `|e^E−1|≤e^ε−1` and the same absolute Gaussian integral. ∎

The factor R_{n,θ} is explicit and cannot be declared uniform as n grows. For independent fixed-size blocks the integrals factor, so nonvanishing holds block by block and the logarithmic bound adds. Correlated blocks need a connected estimate; replacing them by independent ones changes the law.

We now apply the mechanism directly, with no Gaussian-reference substitution. Let C be a **fixed finite contractible cubical cell complex** in four dimensions, with all its nearest-neighbor bonds E and plaquettes P. Give G=SU(N) its normalized Haar measure and fix generators with `−Tr(T_AT_B)=τδ_AB`, τ>0. Let `S_C=Σ_{p∈P}(N−Re Tr U_p)`. For the three original plane matchings define their restricted actions S_i, forces `F_{b,i}=(X_b^AS_i)_A` and

`H_f(U)=Σ_{b∈E} f_b[Σ_i|F_{b,i}|²−(1/3)|Σ_iF_{b,i}|²]`,

`h_f=βH_f`, `|f_b|≤1`, f real.   (7.34)

The scalar H_f is gauge invariant. If marks are placed on bonds whose full ambient plaquette stencils lie in C, (7.34) is literally the ambient frustration source restricted to those bonds. Boundary bonds otherwise have the cell action's force, which is a different observable and is not identified with a full-torus boundary force.

**Theorem 7.14 (uniform complex local Wilson integral).** Fix nonnegative θ₁,r with `θ:=θ₁+16τr<1`. There are β₀,C₁<∞ depending only on the fixed cell C, N, τ and θ, such that, for every β≥β₀, every real mark |f_b|≤1, and

`|z−1|≤θ₁`, `|t|≤r`,

the actual compact integral

`I_{β,f}(z,t)=∫ exp[−βz S_C(U)+t h_f(U)] dHaar(U)`   (7.35)

is nonzero. After exact spanning-tree gauge fixing, put `n=(|E|−|V|+1) dim G`. There are real symmetric matrices H>0 and K_f with

`S_C(exp A)=½AᵀHA+O(|A|³)`, `H_f(exp A)=½AᵀK_fA+O(|A|³)`,

`‖H⁻¹/²K_fH⁻¹/²‖≤16τ`,   (7.36)

and a constant c_C>0 independent of β,f,z,t, for which

`I_{β,f}(z,t)=c_C β⁻n/2 det(zI−tH⁻¹/²K_fH⁻¹/²)⁻¹/² [1+e_{β,f}(z,t)]`,

`sup|e_{β,f}|≤C₁/β`.   (7.37)

The remainder is holomorphic on the interior of any slightly larger fixed polydisc satisfying the same strict inequality θ<1. Thus the normalized frustration generating function `I_{β,f}(1,t)/I_{β,f}(1,0)` has a cutoff-independent zero-free disc and a uniform logarithmic bound on this fixed block. One convenient bound, after increasing β₀ so C₁/β≤1/2, is

`|log[I_{β,f}(1,t)/I_{β,f}(1,0)]|≤(n/2)[−log(1−16τr)]+2log 2`.   (7.38)

*Proof.* We give the compact comparison and the O(β⁻¹) remainder, not just a formal Laplace series.

**Global action control.** For one plaquette and one of its links, the vector of left derivatives obeys

`Σ_A|X_b^A s_p|²≤τ‖U_p−I‖²_HS=2τs_p`.

To see this, transport the derivative to a based plaquette word. The real linear functionals against `T_A/√τ` are an orthonormal subfamily for the real Hilbert–Schmidt product; subtract I, whose derivative trace vanishes, and apply the projection inequality. Orientation changes and conjugations preserve the estimate. A given matching has at most two plaquettes through b, hence `|F_{b,i}|²≤4τΣ_{p in that matching,p∋b}s_p`. Each plaquette has four edges. Since the bracket in (7.34) is nonnegative and bounded by `Σ_i|F_{b,i}|²`,

`|H_f(U)|≤16τ S_C(U)` on the **whole compact configuration space**.   (7.39)

Therefore `Re[zS_C−tH_f]≥(1−θ)S_C`, with no small-field assumption.

**Gauge quotient and isolated minimum.** Fix a spanning tree in the connected one-skeleton, set its bonds to I by gauge transformations, and keep the root gauge fixed. The change of variables preserves product Haar measure by its left/right invariance; successively eliminate the tree bond variables. Gauge-invariant integrals are exactly integrals over the remaining |E|−|V|+1 group variables. If S_C=0, every plaquette word is I. Contractibility implies path independence of transport, so the configuration is pure gauge; in tree gauge every remaining bond is I. Thus the compact quotient has a unique zero-action point. Its quadratic action is a positive constant times the squared linearized plaquette curl. If the curl vanishes, the linearized one-cochain is exact on C; its values vanish on the spanning tree, forcing its vertex potential to be constant and the one-cochain to vanish. This proves H>0. Expanding (7.39) at this point proves the relative quadratic inequality in (7.36). All constants here depend on the fixed cell; no claim of a cell-independent spectral gap is made.

**Uniform local expansion.** Use exponential coordinates A for the non-tree bonds in a small Euclidean ball around zero. The Haar density J(A) is analytic, positive at zero, and even under simultaneous A↦−A, so `J(A)/J(0)=1+O(|A|²)`. Finite Wilson words and their invariant derivatives are analytic in these coordinates. Since f ranges over a finite compact cube, uniformly in the stated z,t,f,

`zS_C(A)−tH_f(A)=½Aᵀ(zH−tK_f)A+P_{3,z,t,f}(A)+O(|A|⁴)`,   (7.40)

where P₃ is a homogeneous cubic with bounded coefficients. The constants and a fixed coordinate ball are independent of β. Shrink the ball so `S_C(A)≥c|A|²` there. On its compact complement the continuous action has a strictly positive minimum m_C.

Set `A=β⁻¹/²b` and take the symmetric box `|b_i|≤p_β:=log β`, contained in the coordinate ball for large β. The exponent correction there is

`q(b)=−β⁻¹/²P₃(b)+O(β⁻¹|b|⁴)`,

whose supremum tends to zero. Using `|e^q−1−q|≤½|q|²e^{|q|}` gives, on this box,

`e^{q(b)}J(β⁻¹/²b)/J(0)=1−β⁻¹/²P₃(b)+R_β(b)`,

`|R_β(b)|≤Cβ⁻¹(|b|²+|b|⁴+|b|⁶+|b|⁸)`   (7.41)

for β sufficiently large. The extra degree-eight term is harmless; β⁻²≤β⁻¹ was used. The cubic term integrates to zero exactly against the even complex Gaussian on this symmetric box. The Gaussian's real part dominates `(1−θ)H`, so every displayed polynomial moment is bounded uniformly in z,t,f and β. Hence the integral error on the box is at most `Cβ⁻¹` times the fixed reference Gaussian normalization; Lemma 7.13 bounds the ratio to the complex Gaussian normalization uniformly for this fixed n.

The Gaussian tail outside the box is `O(exp[−c(log β)²])`. The actual integral inside the coordinate ball but outside that box has the same bound after scaling, by (7.39) and `S_C(A)≥c|A|²`. The actual compact complement has modulus at most `exp[−(1−θ)βm_C]`; relative to β⁻n/2 it is exponentially small. For fixed n, these three tails are O(β⁻¹). Adding the pieces proves (7.37), with `c_C=J(0)(2π)^{n/2}(det H)⁻¹/²` in the chosen Haar-coordinate convention.

The compact integral is entire in z,t; the determinant branch is nonzero on the specified domain. Their ratio defines e holomorphically, and the estimates hold also on a slightly larger polydisc whenever the chosen one has strict margin. With |e|≤1/2, (7.37) proves nonvanishing. Finally diagonalize `H⁻¹/²K_fH⁻¹/²`; each eigenvalue has modulus ≤16τ. The determinant logarithm is bounded by `(n/2)[−log(1−16τr)]`, and each of the two error logarithms is bounded by log 2. This proves (7.38). ∎

**What this accomplishes for CF.** With t=0, (7.37) proves for the actual fixed-block partition integral a holomorphic residual

`R_C(w):=log I_C(w)+(n/2)log w−log c_C = O(β⁻¹)` on `|w−β|≤θ₁β`.

Cauchy on any smaller proportional disc gives `R'_C(β)=O(β⁻²)` and higher derivatives with their corresponding powers. Thus the proportional-disc mechanism of Proposition 7.12 is realized by a compact Wilson integral, including its large-field complement. It is the residual of a **block partition scalar**, not yet the extracted running-coupling remainder r_j. Proving CF for that coefficient requires uniformly controlled external/background derivatives of the actual renormalized block transformation.

**Unresolved extension.** On a periodic torus the flat set has toron moduli; on general inherited backgrounds the Hessian, saddle and determining rows vary; on increasing native blocks the dimension and spectral constants above need not stay fixed. The proof does not replace the actual correlated measure by a product of fixed-block laws. Uniform assembly of these local holomorphic estimates through the native covariance/localization and large-field R-operation is therefore a new quantitative step, not a consequence of this theorem. Nevertheless (7.35)–(7.38) are estimates for an actual compact non-Gaussian Wilson law and not a Gaussian surrogate.

**Theorem 7.15 (fixed-block retained boundary and a full local source polydisc).** Let C be a fixed contractible cubical block with connected boundary. Fix all boundary links to `exp(b_e)`, where b is a finite vector of Lie-algebra coordinates near zero, and integrate its interior links. Gauge transformations are fixed to I on the boundary. Choose a rooted forest connecting every interior vertex to the boundary and gauge its bonds to I. Let m be the number of remaining real integration coordinates. Put `H_e=D_e−|Σ_iF_{e,i}|²/3≥0`, and mark only links whose complete requested stencils are included in C. For independent complex source coefficients η_e define

`Φ(A;b,z,η)=zS_C(A;b)−Σ_e η_e H_e(A;b)`.   (7.42)

Fix small positive θ₁,r with `θ₁+16τr<1/4`. There exists δ>0, depending on C,N,τ,θ₁,r, such that uniformly on

`‖b‖<δ`, `|z−1|<θ₁`, `sup_e|η_e|<r`,

the phase has a unique critical point A_*(b,z,η) in a fixed neighborhood of zero. This point is holomorphic, `A_*(0,z,η)=0`, and `‖A_*‖≤C‖b‖`. Its Hessian `B_*=D_A²Φ(A_*;b,z,η)` has uniformly positive real part. For every sufficiently large β the **original compact conditional integral** satisfies

`I_β(b,z,η)=(2π/β)^{m/2} e^{−βΦ_*} J(A_*) (det B_*)⁻¹/² [1+E_β(b,z,η)]`,

`sup|E_β|≤C/β`, `Φ_*=Φ(A_*;b,z,η)`.   (7.43)

The integral and error are holomorphic on this domain (and on any closed smaller polydisc); `J(A_*)≠0`. In particular I_β has no zeros there. The normalized source logarithm becomes uniformly bounded **after the actual analytic critical-value difference is subtracted**. For fixed physical b its unsusbtracted critical-value contribution can be O(β‖b‖²); no uniform bound for that raw contribution is asserted.

*Proof.* At boundary identity, a zero-action field is pure gauge on the contractible cell. Its gauge on the connected boundary is constant, and the interior rooted-forest gauge removes its remaining freedom. Thus zero is the unique minimum in the compact forest-gauge quotient. The corresponding linearized argument proves positive definiteness of its interior Hessian H.

For the independent sources, let K_e be the Hessian of H_e at zero. Each K_e is positive semidefinite, because H_e≥0 and H_e(0)=0. Equation (7.39) implies `Σ_eK_e≤16τH`. Set `C_e=H⁻¹/²K_eH⁻¹/²` and define `Vv=(C_e^{1/2}v)_e`. Then `V*V=Σ_eC_e≤16τI`, so

`‖Σ_eη_e C_e‖=‖V* diag(η_e I)V‖≤16τ sup_e|η_e|`   (7.44)

also for complex η. Thus the source/coupling Hessian at b=0 is uniformly invertible and accretive on the chosen polydisc. The finite-dimensional holomorphic implicit-function theorem, applied uniformly over a slightly larger closed source/coupling polydisc, gives A_*, its O(‖b‖) bound, and a uniform accretive Hessian for sufficiently small complex b. This is a theorem on the original fixed interior variables and retained boundary parameters; no boundary variable is integrated out or reset.

For completeness the necessary contour step is as follows. Choose a small real coordinate cube Q about zero in the forest-gauge variables, with closure in their common holomorphic chart. At b=0 the compact complement of Q has a positive action gap. The global bound (7.39) and `θ₁+16τr<1/4` preserve a positive real-part phase gap there. Holomorphic dependence on the finitely many boundary coordinates and compactness preserve it for sufficiently small complex b. The critical value is O(‖b‖²), so decrease δ until the complement's gap exceeds `Re Φ_*` by a fixed γ>0.

Translate the local integration cube from Q to `A_*+Q` through the chain `Q+sA_*`, 0≤s≤1. On every swept face, the base real coordinates have a fixed nonzero distance from zero. Uniform continuity, the source margin, and the smallness of A_* and b ensure `Re(Φ−Φ_*)≥γ′>0` there. The holomorphic top-degree form `exp(−βΦ(A))J(A)dA₁…dA_m` is closed. Stokes' theorem on this chain equates the two cube integrals up to the swept-face integrals, each bounded by `C exp[−β(Re Φ_*+γ′)]`. This justifies the translation without treating an oscillatory integral as a positive one.

On `A_*+Q`, write `A=A_*+y` with y real. Taylor expansion gives

`Φ=Φ_*+½yᵀB_*y+P_{3,*}(y)+O(|y|⁴)`,

with uniform analytic constants. Shrink Q so the real part of the quadratic term dominates the higher terms for real y. Set `y=β⁻¹/²v`. The Gaussian has an accretive complex Hessian; its normalization is nonzero uniformly in the fixed parameter domain. Its odd cubic correction and the odd linear correction from `J(A_*+y)/J(A_*)` integrate to zero over a symmetric truncation. The same polynomial remainder estimate as (7.41) then gives a relative O(β⁻¹) error. Gaussian, local-chart, swept-face and compact-complement tails are exponentially small relative to `β⁻m/2 exp(−βΦ_*)`. This proves (7.43). Holomorphy follows from the original compact integral and the analytic nonzero factors in (7.43), not from a merely formal saddle expansion. ∎

The boundary reaction is retained explicitly. Differentiating the critical value gives

`D_bΦ_*=(∂_bΦ)(A_*;b,z,η)`, `‖D_bΦ_*‖≤C‖b‖`, `‖D_b²Φ_*‖≤C`.   (7.45)

The first equality follows because `D_AΦ(A_*)=0`; the bounds follow from the common analytic domain and the absence of a linear jet at b=0. For the full exponent the reaction is β times (7.45). These are fixed-block physical-boundary bounds, not a bound for arbitrary old joined constraint multipliers. Exact identifying row maps, gauge frames and adjoint supports would still have to match before using them in LM42.

The theorem proves zero-freeness and an analytic scalar extraction on a real retained-boundary neighborhood with a genuine complex extension. Its constants require a fixed block, fixed forest/constraints, common original stencils, a positive constrained Hessian at the flat boundary, and a sufficiently small boundary neighborhood. Uniformity as these geometric data change is not contained in the fixed-dimensional implicit-function theorem.

### 7.9 Slowly growing contractible blocks: removing the exponential dimension loss (P)

The determinant-relative estimate (7.33) alone loses an exponential in the dimension. We now remove that loss from the **nonlinear remainder** by rotating the local integration contour to the Gaussian contour before estimating it. This yields a compact Wilson result for cubes whose lattice side grows like any fixed power of log β. The boundary is the open contractible cube; the retained-boundary extension of Theorem 7.15 is still only fixed-block here.

Let `C_m={0,…,m}⁴` with its full cubical cell structure and m≥2. Use the original Wilson action and independent frustration sources of §7.8. Write `n_m=(|E_m|−|V_m|+1)dim G`, so `n_m≤C_N m⁴`. All constants below may depend on N, the generator scale τ and a fixed complex-domain margin; none depends on m,β or the source vector.

**Lemma 7.16 (polynomial tree-gauge geometry and analytic bounds).** Choose the spanning tree whose path from 0 to x increases coordinates in the order 1,2,3,4. For every tree-gauge configuration,

`Σ_{e not in tree} ‖U_e−I‖²_HS ≤ C_N m⁶ S_{C_m}(U)`.   (7.46)

In exponential coordinates A near the identity, the action Hessian H_m therefore satisfies

`c_N m⁻⁶ I≤H_m≤C_N I`.   (7.47)

On a sufficiently small **total Euclidean** coordinate ball, the action and each bounded-source combination have third/fourth Taylor remainders bounded by `C‖A‖³` and `C‖A‖⁴`, uniformly in m and `sup|η_e|≤r`. The Haar-coordinate density has

`|log[J_m(A)/J_m(0)]|≤C_N‖A‖²`.   (7.48)

There is a radius `ρ_m=c m⁻⁶` such that on its real coordinate ball `S(A)≥¼AᵀH_mA`, and on the full compact tree-gauge complement of that ball

`S(U)≥c′m⁻¹⁸`.   (7.49)

*Proof.* For a non-tree edge x→x+e_μ, compare the canonical root paths to its endpoints. Move the additional μ-step past the later-coordinate segments, using one elementary plaquette swap per interchange. There are at most `Σ_{ν>μ}x_ν≤3m` swaps. The corresponding tree-loop holonomy is a product of at most 3m conjugated plaquette words or their inverses. For unitary matrices, `‖AB−I‖HS≤‖A−I‖HS+‖B−I‖HS`; conjugation and inversion preserve the norm. Each term is at most `(2S)^{1/2}`, so `‖U_e−I‖²≤C m² S`. Summing over at most C m⁴ edges gives (7.46). This deliberately uses the coarser m⁶ bound and needs no multiplicity assertion about the filling plaquettes.

Linearizing (7.46) gives the lower Hessian bound; bounded plaquette incidence gives the upper one. Each plaquette word and each force-square term depends on a uniformly bounded stencil, and each bond belongs to a uniformly bounded number of such stencils. Finite-dimensional analytic Taylor bounds on one stencil have constants depending only on N. If a_st denotes the Euclidean norm of A on a stencil, `Σ_st a_st²≤C‖A‖²` and `Σ_st a_st^q≤(Σ_st a_st²)^{q/2}` for q≥2. Summing the local cubic/fourth bounds proves the stated total-norm estimates, also for complex bounded sources. The product Haar density has an analytic logarithm near identity with no linear term; summing its quadratic bound proves (7.48).

The cubic remainder is dominated by one quarter of the Hessian quadratic form when `‖A‖≤c m⁻⁶`, proving the local lower bound. If a bond leaves a fixed exponential chart, (7.46) gives an action gap at least c m⁻⁶. If all bonds remain in that chart, `Σ‖A_e‖²≤CΣ‖U_e−I‖²≤C m⁶S`; leaving the radius ρ_m therefore costs at least `c m⁻⁶ρ_m²=c′m⁻¹⁸`. ∎

**Theorem 7.17 (actual-law zero-free source/coupling polydisc on polylogarithmic cubes).** Fix q<∞ and positive θ₁,r such that

`θ:=θ₁+16τr<1/4`.

There are β₀,C<∞ such that for every β≥β₀, every integer `2≤m≤(log β)^q`, and all `|z−1|≤θ₁`, `sup_e|η_e|≤r`, the full compact integral

`I_{β,m}(z,η)=∫exp{−β[zS_{C_m}−Σ_eη_e H_e]}dHaar`

has the representation

`I_{β,m}(z,η)=J_m(0)(2π/β)^{n_m/2}(det H_m)⁻¹/²(det M)⁻¹/²[1+E_{β,m}(z,η)]`,

`M=zI−H_m⁻¹/²(Σ_eη_e K_e)H_m⁻¹/²`,

`sup|E_{β,m}|≤C m⁴⁰/β`.   (7.50)

All matrix branches are continued from z=1,η=0. The representation and remainder are holomorphic on the polydisc's interior, and the integral has no zeros there. For the normalized source integral at z=1,

`|log[I_{β,m}(1,η)/I_{β,m}(1,0)]|≤(n_m/2)[−log(1−16τr)]+C m⁴⁰/β`.   (7.51)

The exponent 40 is a conservative polynomial bound, not an optimal estimate.

*Proof.* Write n=n_m and H=H_m. By (7.44), `M=I+D` with `‖D‖≤θ`. This remains true for the full independent complex source polydisc. Set

`M_s=I+sD`, `T_s=H⁻¹/²M_s⁻¹/²`, `0≤s≤1`,

with square roots defined by their norm-convergent power series. These matrices are invertible; `‖T_s‖≤C m³`. Choose

`R²=D₀(n+log β)`   (7.52)

with D₀ a sufficiently large constant depending only on the fixed margin. Since m≤(log β)^q, for sufficiently large β one has

`β⁻¹/²m⁹R³+β⁻¹m¹²R⁴+β⁻¹m⁶R²=o(1)`,

`βm⁻¹⁸≫n log β+log β`.   (7.53)

These are elementary polynomial-versus-exponential comparisons in log β; their threshold may depend on q. They also imply `β⁻¹/²‖T_s‖R<ρ_m`.

**Original real tails.** Split the real compact integral at the local ellipsoid `A=β⁻¹/²H⁻¹/²b`, |b|≤R. In the remainder of the coordinate ball, (7.39), (7.48) and (7.49) bound its normalized absolute integral by

`exp(Cn−cR²)`.

For example, use `e^{−c|b|²}1_{|b|>R}≤e^{−cR²/2}e^{−c|b|²/2}`; the remaining Gaussian integral and the determinant ratio each cost at most a constant to the n-th power. Outside the coordinate ball, the compact action gap gives the normalized bound

`exp[Cn+(n/2)log β−cβm⁻¹⁸]`.   (7.54)

Indeed `J_m(0)≥exp(−Cn)`, `H≤CI` and `|det M|≤(1+θ)^n` lower-bound the modulus of the leading factor in (7.50) by `exp(−Cn)β⁻n/2`. Equations (7.52)–(7.53) make both tails at most β⁻³, after increasing D₀ and β₀. No normalized Gaussian comparison is used for the actual compact complement; it is controlled by the global Wilson action.

**Contour rotation and its boundary.** Rotate the local ellipsoid through

`A_s(b)=β⁻¹/²T_s b`, `|b|≤R`, `0≤s≤1`.

The integrand times its coordinate volume form is holomorphic throughout the swept region by (7.53). Its quadratic phase on this contour is

`½ bᵀ M M_s⁻¹ b`,

because M_s commutes with M and its square root is symmetric. Since

`‖M M_s⁻¹−I‖≤(1−s)θ/(1−sθ)≤θ/(1−θ)<1/3`,

the real part of this quadratic form is at least `|b|²/3`. Lemma 7.16 and (7.53) make the cubic/higher correction at most `|b|²/12` on the whole swept region. Thus the exponential on its boundary |b|=R is at most `exp(−R²/4)` in modulus, up to the bounded Haar factor.

Stokes' theorem compares the two ellipsoid integrals, with error equal to the swept-boundary integral. There is no hidden inverse-Hessian factor in its relative Jacobian:

`T_s⁻¹ ∂_sT_s=−½M_s⁻¹D`,

whose norm is bounded by `θ/[2(1−θ)]`. Also `|det T_s/det T_1|≤exp(Cn)`. Pulling the holomorphic n-form back to `[0,1]×{|b|=R}` therefore bounds its normalized integral by

`exp(Cn)·R·area(S^{n−1}_R)·(2π)⁻n/2 exp(−R²/4)`.

Using `Vol(B_1^n)≤(C/n)^{n/2}` and maximizing `R^n exp(−R²/8)` shows this is at most `exp(C′n−R²/8)`. The choice (7.52) makes it at most β⁻³. This explicitly controls the contour boundary; oscillation is not bounded by a pointwise phase estimate.

**Endpoint nonlinear error without an exponential dimension loss.** At s=1 the quadratic phase is exactly `|b|²/2`, and its determinant is already the factor in (7.50). Write the complete remaining exponent, including `log[J_m(A_1)/J_m(0)]`, as

`E(b)=−β⁻¹/²P₃(T_1b)+E_rem(b)`,

`|E_rem(b)|≤Cβ⁻¹[m⁶|b|²+m¹²|b|⁴]`.   (7.55)

On |b|≤R its supremum and that of the cubic term are small by (7.53). The cubic polynomial is odd and integrates to zero on the symmetric real ball against the **real** standard Gaussian. The elementary exponential remainder bound then gives an absolute normalized error at most

`Cβ⁻¹[m⁶ E|B|²+m¹² E|B|⁴+m¹⁸ E|B|⁶]+Cβ⁻²m²⁴ E|B|⁸`,   (7.56)

where B is a real standard n-dimensional Gaussian. Its even radial moments are `n(n+2)…(n+2j−2)`. Since n≤C m⁴, (7.56) is at most `C m⁴⁰/β`. The endpoint Gaussian tail is at most β⁻³. Crucially, no factor `exp(Cn)` multiplies (7.56): the determinant was canceled exactly by the contour rotation before the polynomial remainder was estimated. The exponentially small boundaries were the only terms charged such a factor.

Adding the errors proves (7.50). For large enough β, uniformly over the allowed m, its relative error is <1/2, proving nonvanishing. Holomorphy follows from the exact compact integral and the analytic determinant factor. Finally use the matrix logarithm series `log M=Σ_{j≥1}(−1)^{j+1}(M−I)^j/j`: at z=1 its trace has modulus at most `n[−log(1−16τr)]`. The two error logarithms cost `O(m⁴⁰/β)`, proving (7.51). ∎

This result includes all compact fields **inside each such open cube**, and allows arbitrary bounded lattice-scale marks on that cube. It does not decompose the periodic Wilson law into independent cubes. Its unmarked scalar residual has holomorphic size `O(m⁴⁰/β)` on a proportional coupling disc, with geometry frozen while differentiating; Cauchy gives derivative `O(m⁴⁰/β²)`. Polynomial logarithmic losses of this kind are summable along a linear inverse-coupling trajectory, but identification with the actual extracted running coupling and control of inherited effective interactions remain separate problems.

The next boundary extension must keep the constants in Theorem 7.15 polynomial in m and its boundary radius large enough for the actual native data. The zero-boundary proof above does not establish this. In particular a native boundary radius of size g·polylog(g⁻¹) may plausibly fit a polynomially shrinking physical neighborhood, but that requires checking the actual boundary readout, constraints and full inherited interaction, not just comparing two symbolic scales.

### 7.10 Quantitative retained-boundary extension on polylogarithmic cubes (P)

We now make the boundary radius and constants of Theorem 7.15 explicit enough to coexist with slowly growing geometry. The norm below is the Euclidean norm of **all retained physical boundary logarithms**, with the original boundary links fixed throughout the integration. It is not a supremum over an unspecified old readout.

**Theorem 7.18 (growing conditional block, exact boundary scalar retained).** Fix q<∞ and positive θ₁,r such that `θ₁+16τr<1/8`. For the cube C_m, fix its boundary links to `exp(b_e)` and let

`‖b‖₂=(Σ_{e boundary}‖b_e‖²)^{1/2}≤c m⁻²⁴`,   (7.57)

where b may be complex. Gauge the interior vertical forest rooted on the face x₄=0 to I, while keeping every boundary gauge transformation equal to I. Mark interior links with their complete prescribed stencils, using independent coefficients `sup_e|η_e|≤r`. There exist c>0, β₀,C<∞, independent of m and β, such that for β≥β₀ and `2≤m≤(log β)^q` the resulting compact conditional Wilson integral satisfies

`I_{β,m}(b,z,η)=(2π/β)^{n/2} e^{−βΦ_*} J_m(A_*) (det B_*)⁻¹/² [1+E_{β,m}(b,z,η)]`,

`sup|E_{β,m}|≤C m⁴⁰/β`, `|z−1|≤θ₁`.   (7.58)

Here n≤C_Nm⁴ is the actual interior forest-gauge dimension, A_* is the critical point of the **same retained-boundary phase** (7.42), and B_* its interior Hessian. These quantities and E are holomorphic on the interiors of their stated domains, with

`‖A_*‖₂≤C m⁶‖b‖₂`,

`‖H_m⁻¹/² B_* H_m⁻¹/²−I‖≤1/4`,

`|Φ_*|≤C m¹²‖b‖₂²`.   (7.59)

The integral has no zeros on that domain. The exact critical-value scalar is kept; subtracting it and the displayed nonzero determinant/Jacobian factor leaves a logarithm of size `O(m⁴⁰/β)`. No assertion is made that the unsubtracted conditional source logarithm is uniformly bounded for a fixed nonzero physical boundary.

*Proof.* We verify the new geometric and parameter bounds; the remaining contour calculation is then the one proved in Theorem 7.17, with its linear amplitude term retained.

**Forest and zero-boundary geometry.** For each strictly interior transverse coordinate x₁,x₂,x₃, use the vertical bonds from height 0 through height m−1 as a tree rooted on the lower boundary, omitting the last bond from m−1 to the upper boundary. These trees are disjoint and cover all interior vertices. Gauge transformations are identity on their boundary roots, so this fixing leaves the prescribed boundary links unchanged and preserves normalized product Haar measure. At boundary identity, a transverse free link is compared with the corresponding lower-boundary link by a vertical rectangle with at most m plaquettes. A remaining last vertical link is compared with a boundary path running to the side face x₁=0, down that face, and back along the lower boundary; the enclosed rectangle has at most m² plaquettes. The relevant boundary paths have holonomy I. Each rectangle is filled once by its elementary plaquettes; ordering them by successive rows gives its boundary holonomy as a product of conjugated plaquette words. Thus Cauchy–Schwarz gives `‖U_e−I‖²≤C m² S`, and summing at most C m⁴ free bonds yields the same bound (7.46). The Hessian and chart-gap estimates (7.47)–(7.49) follow with uniform constants. Boundary identity has a unique flat forest-gauge configuration.

**A uniform analytic saddle estimate.** Include both A and b among the local coordinate slots in Lemma 7.16. Bounded stencil incidence supplies uniform second-through-fourth total Euclidean derivative bounds for the phase, with the same bound on the independent source polydisc. At b=0 its interior Hessian B₀ obeys `‖H_m⁻¹/²B₀H_m⁻¹/²−I‖≤θ₁+16τr<1/8`; hence `‖B₀⁻¹‖≤Cm⁶`. Write the stationary equation as

`A=−B₀⁻¹[∇_AΦ(0;b)+(∇_AΦ(A;b)−∇_AΦ(0;b)−B₀A)]`.

The first term has norm ≤Cm⁶‖b‖₂; the bracketed nonlinear remainder has derivative bounded by `C(‖A‖₂+‖b‖₂)`. On the ball `‖A‖₂≤C′m⁶‖b‖₂` the right-hand side is a contraction, because its Lipschitz constant is at most `C m¹²‖b‖₂≤C c m⁻¹²`. Choose c so it is <1/4. Uniform contraction gives a unique holomorphic A_* with the first bound in (7.59). The Hessian perturbation relative to H_m has norm at most `Cm⁶(‖A_*‖+‖b‖)≤Cm¹²‖b‖`, giving the second bound with spare margin. The phase has no constant or linear jet at (A,b)=0; its uniform second derivative bound gives the last, conservative bound in (7.59).

**Original compact and translation tails.** On the real compact interior variables, changing the boundary from zero to b changes the complex phase by at most `Cm²‖b‖₂`. Indeed each local term and its boundary derivatives are uniformly bounded on the compact group and a fixed small complex neighborhood of the boundary; only O(m⁴) terms occur, bounded stencil incidence bounds the Euclidean gradient by C m², and integrate that gradient along the boundary segment. At b=0 the compact complement of the coordinate ball of radius `ρ_m=c₁m⁻⁶` has real-part phase gap `c₂m⁻¹⁸`. Equation (7.57) makes the perturbation at most `C c m⁻²²`, and (7.59) makes `|Φ_*|≤C c²m⁻³⁶`. Thus a fixed positive fraction of the gap remains relative to Φ_*.

Translate that local real coordinate ball to A_* plus the same ball. On its swept boundary, the change due to the translation is at most `Cρ_m‖A_*‖+C‖A_*‖²+C‖b‖‖A_*‖≤C‖b‖+C m¹²‖b‖²`. This is smaller than the gap m⁻¹⁸ for the chosen boundary radius. Stokes' theorem therefore bounds the normalized swept-boundary error, as well as the compact-complement error, by

`exp[Cn+(n/2)log β−cβm⁻¹⁸]`.   (7.60)

The local Haar ratio is bounded by (7.48) and `‖A_*‖≪ρ_m`; the surface Jacobian of a translation is bounded by its velocity times the sphere area. The determinant leading factor is bounded below as in (7.54). These facts justify (7.60) without assuming positivity on the translated contour. It is ≤β⁻³ uniformly for polylogarithmic m.

**Rotation at the actual saddle.** In the variable y=A−A_* the Hessian B_* is a complex symmetric accretive perturbation of H_m. Use the contour family of Theorem 7.17 with `M_*=H_m⁻¹/²B_*H_m⁻¹/²` and `R²=D₀(n+log β)`. All local Taylor constants remain uniform because A_* and b lie in the same small coordinate ball. The contour side estimate, its relative Jacobian identity, and its real tail bound are unchanged. At the endpoint the real Gaussian remains exact.

There is now a linear Haar-amplitude term. Its scaled logarithm is

`β⁻¹/² D log J_m(A_*)[T_1v]+O(β⁻¹m⁶|v|²)`.

The derivative is bounded by `C‖A_*‖≤C`; the linear term and the cubic phase correction together form an odd polynomial in v. They integrate to zero on the symmetric Gaussian ball. Their square and the fourth/higher corrections are bounded by the same moments as (7.56), with an additional harmless `Cβ⁻¹m⁶ E|B|²`. The error is therefore ≤Cm⁴⁰/β. This proves (7.58). All leading factors are analytic and nonzero; the relative error is <1/2 for sufficiently large β. ∎

**Exact comparison to native scales, and its limitation.** Suppose a particular retained boundary has at most C m⁴ slots and a proved original-gauge bound `sup_e‖b_e‖≤C β⁻¹/²(log β)^u`, while `m≤(log β)^q`. Then

`‖b‖₂≤C m² β⁻¹/²(log β)^u=o(m⁻²⁴)`.

Hence it eventually satisfies (7.57), with all constants fixed. This is a mathematical implication for an actual verified boundary, not a proof that Balaban's reconstructed, joined or healed boundary has that norm in this forest gauge. The native problem also has block constraints, backgrounds and effective interactions absent from the plain conditional Wilson block. Theorem 7.18 cannot be substituted for it without matching those structures and preserving its original simultaneous source domain.

The proof keeps the boundary reaction rather than discarding it. From the contraction and stationary equation, the exact boundary derivative is `D_bΦ_*=(∂_bΦ)(A_*;b,z,η)` with conservative bound `‖D_bΦ_*‖≤C m⁶‖b‖`. Its exponent contribution is β times this quantity. Uniform control of an old joined multiplier requires the actual augmented constraint inverse and its complete adjoint support; a small scalar block integral does not prove that control.

### 7.11 The original flat-coarse first step: a source class in Balaban's quadratic-growth norm (P/L with native restrictions)

This is a bridge to the original renormalization map, distinct from the open-cube estimates. The background is the flat coarse configuration and the **original small-field selector remains present**. The result is not an estimate for the complete compact measure or for a mixed/healed history.

**Primary-source identification.** CMP109, printed pp.267–268, (2.9)–(2.13), eliminates one selected corridor bond per coarse bond. In its notation the original physical fluctuation logarithm is

`A_g(B)=g C B−hD(gCB)`, `QC=0`, `LQh=I`,

and the independent coordinates B have covariance `C₀=(C* A^(0) C)⁻¹`. The nonlinear D begins in degree two and linearizes the original average. CMP116, Lemma 2, (1.41)–(1.43), admits localized analytic quadratic-growth terms; its estimates (2.18)–(2.25) bound them using a common Gaussian reserve, and Lemma 3, (2.38)–(2.41), produces a convergent logarithmic polymer expansion. In these primary statements the displayed maps are not an ultralocal square-root substitution. Sources: [CMP109](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01215223), [CMP116](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01239022).

Use Balaban's native blocking parameters satisfying those theorems, including his lower bounds on L,M and the chosen locality exponent. This restricted application does not assert that every odd L≥3 allowed in §1.4 already satisfies the native parameter inequalities. Fix the cutoff, geometry, independent variables, gauge factor and Gaussian normalization from the **unsourced** transformation. At its first step with coarse field I, the physical fine field is `exp(iA_g(B))` in the author's Hermitian convention; converting to anti-Hermitian coordinates removes i and changes no norm.

To avoid a normalization ambiguity, let γ=`βg²`, where g here is the scale used in A_g. With the g₀ of §1.4, γ=2N; with Balaban's action `g⁻² Σ(1−Re Tr U_p/N)`, one has `g=g₀/(√2 N)` and γ=1/N. In either case γ is fixed, not cutoff dependent. Let H_b be the force-square frustration polynomial for the unnormalized action of §1.4, so the inserted density is `h_b=βH_b`.

**Lemma 7.19 (actual source factorization, with complete local derivatives).** At flat coarse background there is a fixed radius ε_*>0, depending only on N,L and the native averaging convention, such that on `g‖B‖∞<ε_*`,

`h_b(exp(iA_g(B)))=Σ_{u,v∈Y_b} B_u v^{,b}_{uv}(gB) B_v`,   (7.61)

where Y_b contains the original full plaquette-force stencil and every corridor/block readout needed to evaluate it. Its diameter and coordinate count are bounded in units of the first-step blocking scale, independently of the number of blocks and the cutoff. The functions v are holomorphic on that same fixed physical polydisc. For any smaller fixed physical radius and every fixed multi-index α,

`sup_{u} Σ_{b,u∈Y_b} Σ_{v∈Y_b} e^{κ diam(Y_b)} |∂_B^α v^{,b}_{uv}(gB)| ≤ C_{α,N,L,κ} g^{|α|}`.   (7.62)

The statement includes derivatives of D in A_g; it is not a bound for a bare local polynomial with D omitted.

*Proof.* A coarse average for a bond c uses paths inside its two endpoint blocks and their corridor. Each path crosses that block boundary only in that corridor; among selected bonds b₀(c′) it can use only b₀(c). The linear equation `QB=0` therefore eliminates b₀(c) using coordinates in that fixed neighborhood, with a nonzero coefficient at the flat field. C and h have bounded finite-range matrix norms depending only on L,N. The nonlinear constraint equation for D(c) involves the same neighborhood and its own selected coordinate; its derivative with respect to D at zero is the identity. The finite-dimensional analytic implicit-function theorem gives a common radius and bounded local derivatives, uniformly over translated corridors. Shared ordinary coordinates may occur in neighboring equations; they do not introduce an additional unknown selected coordinate from another corridor. Thus A_g(B)=Ψ(gB) with Ψ local, holomorphic, Ψ(0)=0 and DΨ(0)=C on a common radius.

The exact Wilson force vanishes at the identity. Therefore `H_b∘exp(iΨ)` has zero constant and linear jets. Taylor's formula along a ray gives

`v^{,b}_{uv}(a)=γ∫₀¹(1−s)(D²F_b(sa))_{uv}ds`, `F_b=H_b∘exp(iΨ)`.   (7.63) Since β=γ/g², substituting a=gB proves (7.61) exactly. The full chain rule in D²F_b and all its derivatives retains the derivatives of Ψ, hence of D. Only coordinates in Y_b occur. Local Cauchy estimates on a smaller fixed physical polydisc give a factor g per B derivative. Each coordinate belongs to a bounded number of Y_b, and their diameter and size are bounded; summing gives (7.62). ∎

In particular, the source `Σ_bη_b h_b`, `sup|η_b|≤r`, belongs to a localized analytic quadratic-growth class with coefficient norm at most `C_{N,L,κ}r`. Source anchors are kept as the labels b; the summed estimate is uniform in the number of anchors, not a bound proportional to that number at every coordinate. At B=0 its quadratic matrix is the exact pullback `C* K_η C` of the original Wilson-frustration Hessian, multiplied by the declared fixed normalization. Its constant and linear rows vanish **only because the coarse background is flat**.

**Theorem 7.20 (flat-coarse small-field one-step source polydisc).** Apply the original first small-field transformation at coarse field I, with the above native parameters and its original cutoff. There exist r>0 and g_*>0, independent of the number of blocks and the microscopic cutoff, such that for `0<g≤g_*`, `sup_b|η_b|≤r`, its sourced fluctuation integral has a nonzero holomorphic logarithm and a convergent localized logarithmic expansion. The output activity difference from zero source is bounded in a fixed, slightly weakened rooted polymer norm by `C r`; its first and second source derivatives are the original inserted and connected coefficients, including the generated contact row. The total logarithmic difference has an extensive bound `C r` times the number of first-step blocks.

*Proof and explicit hypothesis check.* The unsourced first-step integral has the form

`I_g(η)=∫dμ_{C₀}(B) χ_g(B) exp[V_g(B)+Σ_bη_b h_b(exp(iA_g(B)))]`.   (7.64)

All the transformation Jacobians, axial gauge terms, cutoff functions and unmarked normalization factors remain exactly those in the original formula. The constraint change is supported on the eliminated bonds, so the real selector on independent bonds is unchanged. At this first flat step no old effective observable is substituted and no large-field R-operation is used.

Lemma 7.19 gives the additional quadratic coefficient on the same physical B-domain, with common spare analyticity after ε₁ is chosen below ε_*/C_{N,L}. Group its bounded carriers Y_b into the original M-polymer grid; finite range and bounded overlap give the quadratic matrix-element bound required in the quadratic part of the localized-action class. The unmarked remainder and its scalar part already satisfy that class by the first-step construction. The new source has no independent scalar remainder that would require a false small sup bound `r(ε₁/g)²`; it is estimated as a quadratic form throughout.

Choose the original Gaussian-reserve parameter α₄ and all other source-free smallness parameters with strict slack. Select r so that `C_{N,L,κ}r` consumes at most half the available quadratic-coefficient slack, and so that its contribution to the resummed quadratic majorant obeys the native condition of the form `(LM)⁴ α₄≤c`. Also require the source coefficient to fit the localized-action prefactor and every extracted Mayer-activity smallness inequality, including CMP116 (2.28) and the final `C₃ε₁` condition in (2.41). All these are finitely many strict inequalities at fixed L,M,κ,ε₁ and fixed carrier size; the added coefficient tends linearly to zero with r, so one positive r satisfies them simultaneously. These choices depend on the fixed native parameters, not on g or volume. Reduce the original g_* if needed for the unchanged failed-cutoff summation. The comparison of all interpolated quadratic forms, determinant quotients, and the auxiliary exterior Gaussian cancellation then uses the same reserve as the unsourced proof; only its quadratic coefficient bound has increased within the chosen slack. The source is holomorphic in η on a larger fixed polydisc and has no dependence on the propagator weakening parameters, so their original Cauchy domains and decoupling factors are unchanged. Every localized source carrier is included before applying the same localization/conditioning procedure.

The convergent connected expansion therefore applies with these uniform bounds. Its exponential equals the original integral (7.64), proving nonvanishing rather than assuming a branch of its logarithm. Uniform convergence gives source holomorphy. To obtain the activity difference bound, use the expansion with the source polydisc twice as large as the stated one (choose the initial slack accordingly): its analytic activity difference vanishes at η=0, and the connected marked-series/Cauchy estimate gives `C sup|η|` in the fixed weaker rooted norm. Differentiating the exact integral or the uniformly convergent connected expansion gives the first two source coefficients and their cross/contact terms. Summing the rooted norm over blocks yields the extensive bound. ∎

**Proof-status boundary.** Theorem 7.20 is a use of the original cluster-expansion theorem for a newly verified finite-range quadratic-growth input; it assumes its precisely stated native parameter conditions, not a new source-free measure. It proves only the original flat-coarse **small-field** first-step integral. The claimed all-history interface, an analytic family on the full original coarse-field domain, and the full compact Wilson source partition function do not follow from it.

At a nonflat coarse field W, exact Taylor expansion of the same admitted source readout is

`h_b(W,B)=c_b(W)+ℓ_b(W)[B]+½BᵀK_b(W)B+R_b(W,B)`.   (7.65)

The constant and linear coefficients need not vanish; the linear row can have size `g⁻¹` times the background force. Treating (7.65) as the flat class (7.61) would therefore fail. One must retain its exact scalar and control the linear row on the common retained background/source domain. Section 7.12 handles bounded canonical backgrounds directly; a source-dependent constrained saddle is a route to the larger native domain. Theorem 7.18 performs this mechanism for literal conditional Wilson blocks, but does not identify the native averaging constraints or inherited interactions with those blocks. That identification, with complete current/anchor derivatives, is the concrete next extension.

### 7.12 A nonflat native first step on bounded canonical backgrounds (P/L with a stated linear-growth extension)

The flat factorization can be extended on a nontrivial retained-field neighborhood without changing the original cutoff or deforming its contour. The neighborhood here is smaller than the full native small-field domain. Its restriction is explicit and cannot be discarded when iterating.

Let W be a coarse configuration in the original first-step domain, with its original source-free constrained minimizing background V₀(W). Work in a regular native chart in which, on every complete source/corridor stencil,

`V₀(W)=exp(i A₀(W))`, `‖A₀(W)‖∞≤gR`,   (7.66)

where R<∞ is fixed independently of g and volume. For complex W use the same complex chart and bound. The unmarked current, covariance, independent coordinates and all cutoffs are those of CMP109/CMP116 and satisfy their original simultaneous restrictions. In particular, (7.66) does not replace their current/regularity hypotheses. It is an additional restriction on the physical background. The conclusion below is uniform over the intersection of these domains.

The constraint-linearizing map is now `A_g(W,B)=Ψ_W(gB)`, where `Ψ_W(0)=0`, `DΨ_W(0)=C_W`, and Ψ_W has the same finite-corridor dependence on B as in §7.11. Its coefficients depend on the original retained external fields. They are used as localized functions of the native extended variables (U,J) before evaluating on their physical graph; the claim is not that V₀(W) is a finite-range function of W. Its general localization is the original minimizer/random-walk localization.

**Lemma 7.21 (exact constant, linear and quadratic source rows).** On a common smaller physical polydisc in gB, the original source has the exact decomposition

`h_b(W,B)=c_b(W)+Σ_u λ_{b,u}(W) B_u+Σ_{u,v}B_u v_{b,uv}(W,gB)B_v`,   (7.67)

with

`c_b=γg⁻² F_{b,W}(0)`, `λ_{b,u}=γg⁻¹ ∂_uF_{b,W}(0)`,

`v_{b,uv}(W,a)=γ∫₀¹(1−s) ∂_u∂_v F_{b,W}(sa)ds`,

where `F_{b,W}(a)=H_b(exp(iΨ_W(a))V₀(W))` and γ=βg² as in §7.11. Uniformly on (7.66), the complete carrier coefficient bounds are

`|c_b|≤C R²`, `Σ_u|λ_{b,u}|≤CR`, `Σ_{u,v}|v_{b,uv}|≤C`.   (7.68)

The corresponding anchored row/column sums obey the same bounds, with fixed native constants; physical B derivatives of v carry g to the derivative order. All functions are holomorphic on the stated common domain.

*Proof.* The complete plaquette-force stencil is finite and the force vanishes when all its links are identity. In a fixed complex chart its force is O(‖A₀‖∞), its force-square H_b is O(‖A₀‖∞²), and its first derivative is O(‖A₀‖∞); its second and higher derivatives are uniformly bounded. These facts follow by differentiating the finite plaquette words and their inverse words, including every factor in the force square. The local analytic map Ψ_W and its derivatives have uniform bounds by the same corridor implicit-function argument as in Lemma 7.19. The chain rule therefore gives `F(0)=O(g²R²)`, `DF(0)=O(gR)`, and bounded D²F. Taylor's formula proves (7.67) and (7.68). Bounded stencil/corridor overlap gives the anchored sums. Cauchy's estimate on a smaller physical polydisc supplies the B-derivative factors. No source-free stationarity is used to suppress DF: it generally does not vanish. ∎

**Lemma 7.22 (the extra linear-growth allowance in the original cluster estimate).** The localized-action input in the first-step CMP116 proof may include, in addition to its analytic quadratic part and bounded scalar remainder, finite-range linear terms `L_Y(B)=Σ_{u∈Y} l_{Y,u}B_u` with bounded-overlap carriers Y and sufficiently small coefficient norm. This allowance preserves convergence and source holomorphy, with constants depending on the fixed carrier geometry and the original parameter slack.

*Proof.* Include each new finite carrier as a term in the original Mayer expansion. All conditioning and propagator weakening are left unchanged, and carrier disjointness gives the same factorization. Write `L_Y=ε_Y L̂_Y`, with `Σ_u|l̂_{Y,u}|≤1`. For any auxiliary complex amplitude |ζ_Y|≤δ and any allocation a>0 to the quadratic reserve,

`|ζ_Y L̂_Y(B)|≤a Σ_{u∈Y}|B_u|²+δ²/(4a)`.   (7.69)

This is Cauchy–Schwarz followed by `xy≤a x²+y²/(4a)`. If the carrier multiplicity is D, choose a≤α₄/(4D). Sum (7.69) over present carriers; it uses at most a fixed fraction of the same quadratic reserve as (2.19)–(2.24). Next choose the fixed δ small enough that δ²/(4a) fits the bounded scalar slack per carrier.

Here is the actual small Mayer factor. The entire function `e^{ζ L̂_Y(B)}−1` vanishes at ζ=0. Cauchy's coefficient formula on |ζ|=δ gives, for |ε_Y|≤δ/2, a bound `2|ε_Y|/δ` times the boundary exponential majorant. For a product of new Mayer factors use independent auxiliary ζ_Y and the summed bound (7.69); the small factor is the product of `2|ε_Y|/δ`. This is precisely the local smallness needed to include the new carrier species in the original connected resummation. Its overlap graph has bounded geometry, and ε_Y can be chosen below all extracted activity thresholds in (2.28) and (2.41). No global volume loss enters the Gaussian comparison. The same argument with the coefficient parameters complex gives uniform holomorphy.

Thus convergence, the identity with the original integral, and its holomorphy conclusion persist. This proves an additional growth estimate; it does not treat a linear function as uniformly bounded on the full g⁻¹-sized fluctuation domain. ∎

**Theorem 7.23 (bounded canonical nonflat first-step source domain).** Fix R. On (7.66) and the original simultaneous first-step domain, there is a source radius r_R>0 independent of volume and g, such that the original small-field fluctuation integral with independent complex sources |η_b|≤r_R has a nonzero holomorphic logarithm for all sufficiently small g. Its exact constant row is retained:

`I_g(W,η)=exp[Σ_bη_b c_b(W)] · I_g^{res}(W,η)`.   (7.70)

The second factor has a convergent localized logarithmic expansion. Its source-dependent difference is O_R(r_R) in a slightly weakened rooted norm. The total log difference from η=0 is bounded by `C_R sup|η|` times the number of native first-step blocks. First and second source derivatives are the exact conditional insertion and covariance rows, with c and λ included.

*Proof.* Extract the constant row in (7.67) exactly; it is an analytic nonzero exponential, however large its extensive sum is. The remaining source quadratic coefficient is O(r_R), and its linear coefficient is O(r_R R), in the localized bounds of Lemma 7.21. Choose r_R small enough for all inequalities of Theorem 7.20 and Lemma 7.22. Their Gaussian reserve, the original cutoff-failure estimates and connected resummation then apply to `I_g^{res}`. The expansion exponentiates to that integral, so it proves nonvanishing. Uniform holomorphic convergence and a source disc with a fixed spare factor give the asserted difference and derivative bounds. Add the exact scalar (7.70); its rooted size is O(r_R R²). At η=0 differentiating the logarithm of the actual integral yields its conditional first moment and covariance, not just the quadratic fluctuation row. ∎

**What this closes, and what it does not.** Nonflatness itself is not an obstruction to the original first-step source expansion: a fixed canonical neighborhood is covered, with explicit constant and linear rows and original cutoffs. The estimates require at least `r_R R` small in the linear-growth argument. If the original physical background is only known to satisfy `‖A₀‖∞≤g p₀(g)` with `p₀(g)→∞`, the radius obtained this way need not stay positive as g→0. Substituting R=p₀(g) therefore does not prove the desired native full-domain interface. Completing the source-dependent constrained square/saddle while retaining its field-dependent critical scalar is the next route on that larger domain. Its contour-face defects must be controlled in the original localized cutoff construction before a full-domain zero-free statement is made.

### 7.13 Absolute anchored source kernels of the actual first-step expansion (P/L)

The one-step analytic logarithm must be controlled coefficientwise, not just after summing the sources. The preceding construction supplies the needed support information because its covariance, selectors and decoupling procedure are source independent.

Write the source-dependent logarithm, after the exact scalar row in (7.70) when applicable, as `Σ_X Φ_X(η)`, with Φ_X(0)=0. Keep each original source anchor b attached to its full finite readout Y_b before performing the Mayer/conditioning expansions. A term contributing to Φ_X can involve η_b only if X contains that readout; enlarge the native localization domain by the fixed readout radius once. Consequently Φ_X depends only on a finite set A_X of source labels, with

`|A_X|≤s₀[1+d_M(X)]`, `tree(A_X)≤t₀[1+d_M(X)]`.   (7.71)

Here d_M is the native connected size; s₀,t₀ depend on the fixed native parameters. The first bound follows from bounded stencil overlap and the native volume/size comparison CMP116 (2.30). The second follows by connecting the native blocks of X and adding the bounded source stencils. It applies to the whole anchor set, hence also to every subset of selected derivative anchors.

With strict slack in the original decay inequalities, the expansion in Theorems 7.20 and 7.23 has a uniform majorant on a spare independent source polydisc |η_b|≤r:

`sup_a Σ_{X:a∈A_X} e^{κ d_M(X)} M_X ≤ E`,

`M_X=sup_{|η|≤r}|Φ_X(η)|`.   (7.72)

This is the rooted polymer estimate from the convergent expansion, with a strictly smaller κ than the decay available before rooted summation.
