Consider the holomorphic line of targets `B_R+ζ B_I/y`, for a fixed 0<y<1/4. Choose c small enough that |ζ|≤1 stays in the original complex chart and its real diameter in the real regular chart. At ζ=iy it gives the specified B. On the real diameter Lemma 7.49 bounds H_b by `Cε²ξ^{4+2α}`. On the upper semicircle use the complex bound just proved. The two-constants theorem on the upper half unit disc gives

`|H_b(U(B))|≤C ε² ξ^{4+s₀}`, `s₀=2α[1−(4/π)arctan y]>0`.   (7.108)

The indicated weight is the harmonic measure of the diameter at iy. It follows by mapping ζ to `(1+ζ)/(1−ζ)`, which sends the half-disc to a quadrant. This interpolation is applied to the gauge-invariant analytic quadratic contraction H_b, so no choice of complex gauge norm enters its conclusion.

*Proof of anchor decay.* To keep the external derivative anchors, use the first two response rows in CMP102 (190). In one-scale coarse units, a single target slot at y produces a relative potential response bounded by `Cσ⁻¹ exp(−δ dist(cell(b),y)/8)` and its first covariant difference by `Cσ⁻²` times the same exponential. Differentiating a plaquette word collects the oriented transported link responses around its four edges. Their first-order sum is a covariant difference. The remaining commutator terms contain one background link of size `O(εξ)` and one response of size `O(ξ)`. Thus the derivative of the plaquette holonomy is bounded by `Cξ²` times the response exponential. This computation may equivalently be made by the analytic variation of `exp(iη𝒜(B))` relative to its real base, using the integral derivative of the exponential. The derivative of the short transport of the opposite plaquette has the same bound. Multiplying by the matching force, whose complex bound is `Cεξ²`, gives

`|D_{B(y)} H_b(U(B))|≤C ε ξ⁴ e^{−δ dist(cell(b),y)/8}`.   (7.109)

All statements are on a smaller common admitted chart and keep a fixed spare physical radius for the following Cauchy estimates. Apply Cauchy to (7.108) in m fixed target slots, obtaining `C_m ε^{2−m}ξ^{4+s₀}`. Alternatively start from (7.109) with any one of those slots held, and take the other m−1 derivatives by Cauchy. This gives `C_m ε^{2−m}ξ⁴ exp(−δ max_i dist(cell(b),y_i)/8)`. The geometric mean of the two bounds retains `s=s₀/2` and a fixed portion of the anchor decay. For m=0 simply use (7.108). For m≥1 the star from the root has length at most m times the maximum distance. Taking c_m small enough leaves an exponential for summation of the m coarse anchors and the polynomial moment. Ordinary one-scale lattice shell counting is uniform on the torus. Each canonical derivative contributes g_k. Finally a coarse cell has at most `C ξ⁻⁴` fine bond roots, cancelling the fourth power of ξ. This proves (7.107). ∎

The estimate is local to the regular cubes in the theorem cited. In a clean periodic geometry a larger periodic lift can be used when the original target and its constrained critical orbit lift within the same regular spaces. To see the stationarity part of this condition, average any tangent variation on the lift over translations by the original periods. The averaged variation obeys the original linearized coarse constraint. Pairing against the periodically lifted action gradient gives the degree of the covering times its pairing with that averaged variation, which vanishes by stationarity. The native uniqueness theorem then identifies the lifted critical orbit wherever its other target and regularity hypotheses hold. A mixed joined wall requires its own admission check.

The next MT36 operation attaches this incoming readout to one distinguished interaction in the same fluctuation integral. The prefactor g_k in that connected attachment, full lower/contact projection and arbitrary stable births require the corresponding localized formation estimate. Equation (7.107) establishes the clean primitive age and its fixed external anchor moments independently of those remaining steps.

### 7.29 A primitive connected attachment at arbitrary clean age

We consider an actual real clean fluctuation integral at flat terminal field and a current-scale interaction. The conditional mean and its moments can first be bounded without estimating the maximum over the whole fluctuation lattice. For an exponentially localized slot estimate one can then use the covariance identity for a strictly convex real fluctuation law. We give the exact spare-chart and Hessian conditions used in this step.

**Lemma 7.51 (local fluctuation envelope from the native response).** Work in the clean one-scale target geometry of Theorem 7.50 and take the base U₀=I in CMP102 Proposition 9. In the current clean integral let `V(B)=exp(iΨ(g_k B))` be the original unit constraint readout at terminal I, with its real original selector. Choose its physical chart small enough for (172). For a current cell x put

`Q_x(B)=1+Σ_y e^{−c dist(x,y)} |B_y|`,   (7.110)

where bounded corridor stencils are included by a fixed enlargement. If b is a fine root in x, then

`|F_{b,i}(U_k(V(B)))|≤C g_k Q_x(B) ξ^{2+α}`,

`|D_{B_y} F_{b,i}(U_k(V(B)))|≤C g_k ξ^{2+α} e^{−c dist(x,y)}`   (7.111)

in the fixed near-identity gauge of Proposition 9. The real clean conditional law μ_k has uniform fixed moments of every Q_x. Consequently, for

`P_x(B)=β₀ Σ_{b∈x} f_b H_b(U_k(V(B)))`,

one has

`‖P_x‖_{L^p(μ_k)}≤C_p ‖f‖∞(g_k/g₀)²ξ^{2α}`,

`‖D_{B_y}P_x‖_{L²(μ_k)}≤C ‖f‖∞(g_k/g₀)²ξ^{2α}e^{−c dist(x,y)}`.   (7.112)

*Proof.* In (190) use the value, covariant first-difference and local Hölder first-difference rows for the response to one original coarse target slot. At base identity the relative field is in a fixed Landau chart and these are ordinary local estimates. Integrate the response along the segment of target logarithms from 0 to the logarithm of V(B). Each component of that logarithm is bounded by `C g_k` times the sum of the absolute B components in its fixed original corridor. Thus the potential, first difference and its Hölder seminorm on the fine stencil have respectively the bounds `C g_k Q_x σ⁻¹`, `C g_k Q_x σ⁻²` and `C g_k Q_x σ⁻²⁻ᵅ`. Their plain uniform chart bounds from (172) and (19) are available at the same time. The Hölder estimate uses the localized cutoff in the third row of (190), equal to one on the stencil with its fixed native collar.

Apply the opposite-plaquette expansion in Lemma 7.49. In products use the uniform small chart bound on all but one field and the weighted bound on the remaining factor. This gives the first line of (7.111). Differentiate the same expansion once. The response to B_y has the same local first-derivative Hölder bound with the factor `C g_k exp(−c dist(x,y))`, by (190) and the derivative of the original finite-corridor map. The differentiated curl difference has the claimed ξ^{2+α} factor. Differentiated commutator and transport terms have a third power of ξ and are bounded by the same expression. This proves the second line. The argument needs no unsupported bound on every second difference of the potential.

To verify the moment assertion, insert a local probe `s|B_y|²` in the original clean fluctuation integral. Its finite carrier fits the quadratic-growth budget for a fixed small positive s at every native step. The same original connected expansion bounds the log difference by a constant independent of volume: only carriers containing that particular probe can contribute. Hence `E_{μ_k}exp(s|B_y|²)≤C` uniformly. Minkowski's inequality and the finite one-scale exponential row sum give all fixed moments of (7.110). Multiply (7.111) by the matching forces for H_b and use the fine-root count `Cξ⁻⁴` in a current cell. This proves (7.112). ∎

**Lemma 7.52 (weighted covariance on the actual product of cutoff balls).** Let the real density on the product `D=∏_i D(P)` be proportional to `exp[−½BᵀHB+V(B)]`. Suppose `H≥mI`, with exponentially bounded kernel rows and columns. Suppose V is a sum of connected analytic activities on a spare physical chart extending to `|B_i|≤2P` and obeying

`|V_X(B)|≤v_X(1+Σ_{i∈X}|B_i|²)`,

`sup_i Σ_{X∋i} e^{κ n(X)} v_X≤ε_s`.   (7.113)

Use a fixed bounded number of coordinate components per native cell and P≥1. For ε_s small enough relative to m and these fixed geometry constants, there is c>0 such that

`|Cov(F,G)|≤C Σ_{i,j} e^{−c dist(i,j)} ‖D_iF‖_{L²} ‖D_jG‖_{L²}`.   (7.114)

The constants are independent of P and volume. This is a real-measure statement. It applies to the native clean steps on which the displayed spare-chart and smallness conditions are verified.

*Proof.* Cauchy's formula on coordinate discs of radius a fixed fraction of P gives a bound `C v_X n(X)` on each second derivative on a smaller chart. Counting the second slot and reducing the spatial weight yields `‖D²V‖_{c,Schur}≤C ε_s`. The same calculation bounds the first derivative by `C P ε_s` per block. These bounds also hold after a smooth sitewise saturation equal to the identity on D, with image in the smaller chart, bounded first derivative and second derivative `O(1/P)`. Extend V by that saturation to the full real space. Its Hessian stays a small perturbation of H. Add smooth convex sitewise penalties tending to infinity outside D and zero inside. Their Hessians are positive and block diagonal. At finite penalty the resulting potential U has Hessian at least m/2 and its off-block kernel has the same exponential Schur bound, independent of penalty strength.

For completeness, let `A=−Δ+∇U·∇` on the normalized real law. Differentiating its scalar resolvent equation gives the one-form operator `A₁=A⊗I+D²U`. Integration by parts then gives

`Cov(F,G)=⟨∇F,A₁⁻¹∇G⟩`.

One may first solve `(A+t)u=G−EG` with t>0, differentiate and use `(A₁+t)∇u=∇G`. In the integration-by-parts identity the term `t⟨F,(A+t)⁻¹(G−EG)⟩` tends to zero by the spectral theorem, since the kernel of A on the connected full space consists of constants. Coercivity of A₁ gives the other limit. The smooth confining approximations and smooth bounded test functions justify these identities by ordinary elliptic regularization, and truncation gives the stated Sobolev test functions. This is the standard Witten-Laplacian covariance identity used, for example, in [Lo's weighted correlation estimates](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0611002).

For a fixed block j conjugate by the weight `D_{ii}=exp(c dist(i,j))`. The scalar operator A commutes with this index weight, as do the sitewise penalty Hessians. The exponential Schur bound makes `‖D A₁D⁻¹−A₁‖≤C c` for small c. Choose it below m/4. The resolvent of the conjugated operator has norm at most 4/m. Its (i,j) block bound for the original inverse gains `exp(−c dist(i,j))`. Insert this into the identity and sum the block gradients to obtain (7.114). Finally take the increasing convex penalties to the sharp selector by dominated convergence, using the sitewise saturation for test functions when needed. This keeps the original cutoff response in the measure and takes no derivative of its indicator. ∎

**Corollary 7.53 (actual real clean primitive and a fresh vertex).** Assume the real clean step at terminal identity obeys the spare-chart conditions (7.113). The original CMP116 quadratic coefficients and bounded scalar terms give (7.113) for clean parameter choices with a larger physical analyticity chart, sufficiently small physical cutoff and fixed spare decay. In applying it one must check the larger chart; the bound on an open chart terminating at the actual selector alone is insufficient. Uniform exponential locality of the augmented unit-lattice precision and its inverse is the native CMP99/CMP116 input. For a current vertex V_Y with

`‖D_{B_i} V_Y‖_{L²(μ_k)}≤C g_k e^{−κ n(Y)}` for i∈Y,

(7.112) and (7.114) imply

`|Cov_{μ_k}(P_x,V_Y)|≤C ‖f‖∞ g_k(g_k/g₀)² ξ^{2α}`

`× exp[−c′ dist(x,Y)−κ′ n(Y)]`.   (7.115)

There is a literal native example: the cubic and higher remainder of the exponential axial-gauge term (CMP109 (2.5)) after the original constraint substitution and its quadratic Gaussian jet have been removed. On each fixed block its physical third derivatives are bounded. The canonical interaction is g_k⁻² times the remainder at g_kB, so its first B derivative is bounded by `C g_k(Σ_{i∈Y}|B_i|)²`. The local probe estimate in Lemma 7.51 supplies the displayed L² bound. Finite fixed carrier weights are absorbed in the constant. More generally (7.115) applies to each original vertex for which this fresh derivative estimate is verified.

*Proof.* Sum (7.114) with the two gradient estimates. The convolution of the two one-scale exponentials is bounded by a slightly weaker exponential in the distance from x to Y. The polynomial slot count in Y is absorbed in the spare carrier decay. All constants are independent of k, ξ and the total number of cells under the uniform hypotheses. ∎

Equation (7.115) has the fresh g_k, the correct canonical coupling ratio, a positive clean age exponent and summable attachment anchors for this actual primitive real connected coefficient. It concerns the flat-terminal real kernel and the stated class of vertices. The full P₆ norm also asks for complex external derivatives, completion of lower and contact rows, and general stable births. Those operations are additional to this covariance estimate.

### 7.30 Uniform control of the actual repeated coarse averages

The age estimate can be applied to the primitive matching force on the genuine Mʲ(U) readout at every regular old scale. A local change of the coarse gauge removes the endpoint terms at linear order. The remaining linear average has norm one, which prevents a constant loss at each repetition.

**Lemma 7.54 (regularity under arbitrarily many original averages, P).** In a local physical cube measure lengths in units σ. Suppose the actual fine links are `U_e=exp(τ A_e)` in anti-Hermitian convention, with initial spacing τ=η/σ and with the dimensionless discrete `C^{1,α}` norm of A at most b. Take b sufficiently small depending on fixed L,N. For `τ_n=Lⁿη/σ≤1`, the original coarse field `Mⁿ(U)` has a local gauge with

`Mⁿ(U)_e=exp(τ_n A_{n,e})`, `‖A_n‖_{C^{1,α}}≤2b`.   (7.116)

Use interior stencils with a collar of width `C_L Σ_{h<n} τ_h`, bounded by a fixed multiple of σ in physical units. The constants are independent of n. A first variation G with a spatial exponential weight to a fixed external anchor obeys the same uniform bound times its initial weighted norm, with a fixed multiplicative constant.

*Proof of the one-step map.* For a coarse center y let U(y,x) be its original averaged contour to a fine site x in its block, CMP109 (0.11). In the local small chart set

`E_y=exp[L⁻ᵈΣ_{x∈B(y)} log U(y,x)]`.

Use as the coarse representative `E_y⁻¹ M(U)(c) E_{y′}` for c=(y,y′). This is a legitimate gauge transformation of the original average and is holomorphic near the small configuration. Formula (0.12) determines its derivative at identity directly. Before the change of frame the derivative is the average of the endpoint contour variations, the straight L-bond segment from x to x′=x+Lτ e_μ, and the reversed endpoint contour variation at y′. The contributions from the closing straight coarse word cancel in (0.12). The first derivative of the new endpoint frames cancels the remaining two endpoint contour terms. Hence the normalized logarithm map is

`A′_μ(y)=T_μ A(y)+τ N_μ(A,τ)(y)`,

`T_μ A(y)=L^{−d−1}Σ_{x∈B(y)}Σ_{h=0}^{L−1} A_μ(x+hτ e_μ)`.   (7.117)

The original contour average and the inverse contour on the second block use the same definition, so this cancellation does not depend on choosing a different averaging rule. Each local group word, logarithm and average is analytic on the fixed small chart, with a finite stencil depending only on L,N. Expanding them in τA shows that N starts in degree two in A. All higher terms have their corresponding additional powers of τ.

*Uniform derivative bounds.* In the dimensionless norm use the supremum, the supremum of the first forward differences divided by mesh spacing, and their α-Hölder seminorm for physical separations at most one. The linear operator T is a convex combination of equal translations of one field component. Its first coarse difference is also a convex combination of first fine differences, since a step of L fine bonds telescopes and is divided by L. Comparing two such coarse differences uses the same translations at both points, so the Hölder seminorm has operator norm at most one as well.

For the nonlinear term, the product estimate in this discrete norm is mesh independent. The first difference of a product is a sum of a translated value times a first difference. Subtracting two such formulas bounds the Hölder seminorm using the Hölder difference of the derivative and the Lipschitz difference of the value. Equivalently first form each translation-equivariant local word on all fine translates and then restrict to coarse centers. The coarse difference is the average of L consecutive fine differences. Summation of the absolutely convergent Taylor series of N therefore gives

`‖N(A,τ)‖_{C^{1,α}}≤C_L ‖A‖²_{C^{1,α}}`,

`‖DN(A,τ)G‖_{C^{1,α}}≤C_L ‖A‖_{C^{1,α}}‖G‖_{C^{1,α}}`

on a common small ball. All translations used at step h have physical length at most `C_L τ_h`. If `b_h=‖A_h‖`, (7.117) gives `b_{h+1}≤b_h+C_L τ_h b_h²`. Since `Σ_{h<n}τ_h≤1/(L−1)`, induction gives `b_h≤2b` for b sufficiently small. The same sum bounds the total collar used. Gauge covariance of each original M ensures that the repeated representative is a gauge transform of the actual Mⁿ(U).

For the weighted variation use `exp(c dist(x,y_ext))` on point values and the smaller of the two distances on Hölder differences. Moving a field slot by `C_L τ_h` costs at most `exp(c C_L τ_h)`. The differentiated map has norm at most `exp(c C_L τ_h)[1+C_L b_h τ_h]`. The product over h is bounded by `exp[C_L(c+2b)Σ_h τ_h]`. Thus there is no loss increasing exponentially in the number of averages. ∎

**Corollary 7.55 (old-scale primitive graph bound).** On the original regular cubes satisfying CMP102 Theorem 1 (7),(9), let the bare fine minimum be U_k(W) and put `V_j=Mʲ(U_k(W))`. Use complete old stencils in the interior specified in Lemma 7.54. For σ the current cell size and old mesh `η_j=Lʲη`, each old matching force satisfies

`|F_{b,i}(V_j)|≤C ε (η_j/σ)^{2+α}`.   (7.118)

After summing old bonds in one current cell, the old primitive frustration has bound `C β_j ε² L^{−2α(k−j)}` in the clean single-scale case. For `ε=Cg_kQ` this is `C Q²(g_k/g_j)² L^{−2α(k−j)}` with the original fixed action normalization included in C.

*Proof.* Normalize A in CMP102 (9) by multiplying by σ. Its dimensionless discrete norm is at most `C_M ε`. Apply Lemma 7.54 to the actual old averages in that local regular frame. Then apply the opposite-plaquette calculation in Lemma 7.49 with the old mesh η_j. Squaring and summing at most `C(σ/η_j)^4` old roots gives the bound. ∎

On the admitted base-identity target chart of CMP102 (172),(190), the value and first local Hölder response of the unaveraged potential have the same spatial exponential to an external target slot. Lemma 7.54 propagates these responses uniformly to A_j. Applying (7.109) and its fixed-order Cauchy argument at the old mesh therefore yields (7.107) with `ξ=L^{j−k}`, β_j in place of β₀, and the old-scale coupling ratio. In a general mixed chart these derivatives are with respect to the **actual B argument of CMP102 (20),(182)**; admission and the full frame/readout chain for a different target variable must be checked separately. In the original clean flat calculation, CMP109 (3.2)–(3.9) and CMP116 (1.1)–(1.5) identify the local physical argument B′ of H_k as `g_k C B−hD(g_kCB)`. Those are the formulas used for the first-step contraction in Lemma 7.51. No finite-support assumption is made for the general joined target map.

This gives an arbitrary-j real graph estimate for the actual **primitive** frustration on Mʲ(U_k), and its external response on the indicated clean chart. The curvature comparison uses the exact averaged contour in (0.12). A stable completed birth with covariant quadratic/cubic subtractions has additional kernels and requires its corresponding old packet and projection estimates.

### 7.31 A dimension-six-normalized stable quartic column

The primitive force estimate (7.107) already includes the old root count ξ⁻⁴. A stable dimension-six comparison in MT39–MT44 also includes ξ⁻². The primitive gain ξ^{2α} in (7.107) alone would then be ξ^{2α−2}. We now keep that additional normalization in a genuine stable example where a positive age gain survives.

For a real or holomorphically continued small plaquette put X_p=log U_p on its fixed branch and

`R_p(U)=s_p(U)+½ Tr X_p²`.   (7.119)

This retains the full gauge-covariant quadratic log-curvature completion separately. Since the continued real trace is `½Tr(e^{X_p}+e^{−X_p})`, the remainder begins at order four in X_p and has bound `C_N‖X_p‖⁴`. Its derivative is bounded by `C_N‖X_p‖³‖δX_p‖`. The actual plaquette and its quadratic completion have thus been separated by an exact analytic identity. The difference has no dimension-four or dimension-six local jet at birth.

**Theorem 7.56 (stable quartic primitive and a real fresh attachment).** Use the real clean flat-terminal kernel of Corollary 7.53 and the repeated original averages of Lemma 7.54. Let `ξ=L^{j−k}` for a primitive old plaquette at scale j and set

`R_{j,x}(B)=A_j g_j^{−d} α_j^{d−4} Σ_{p∈x} f_p R_p(Mʲ U_k(V(B)))`,

where d≤4 is its declared canonical coupling grade, A_j≥0 and α_j its declared positive physical radius. For complete old stencils in the admitted cube and a fresh real vertex satisfying the derivative bound of Corollary 7.53,

`|Cov_{μ_k}(ξ⁻²R_{j,x},V_Y)|`

`≤C A_j ‖f‖∞ g_k ξ² (g_k/g_j)^d (g_k/α_j)^{4−d}`

`× exp[−c dist(x,Y)−κ′ n(Y)]`.   (7.120)

In particular the actual cubic and higher axial-gauge vertex described there supplies this fresh g_k. If α_j is fixed and `g_k≤C α_j`, (7.120) has s=2 and q=d. If `α_j≥c g_j` and the analytic readout is admitted, one may keep q=d and any fixed s<2 by spending a portion of the age decay on the power of g_k/g_j. The statement is a real connected quartic-column estimate; external complex projection and the general stable quadratic/cubic packet are further requirements.

*Proof.* Apply the value and response parts of Lemma 7.54 with the weighted input (7.110)–(7.111). In the current cell the actual old plaquette logarithm satisfies

`‖X_p‖≤C g_k Q_x(B) ξ²`, `‖D_{B_y}X_p‖≤C g_k ξ² e^{−c dist(x,y)}`.   (7.121)

Indeed the discrete curl bound uses the first difference of the old potential; the quadratic commutator uses its ordinary size, and higher products have an extra old mesh factor. For a first variation use the propagated weighted value/first-difference bounds. In nonlinear products all unvaried factors except one may use their fixed small chart bound. This gives (7.121), with a fixed weakening of the exponent for the original collar. The actual old logarithms are on the stated small branch.

Use (7.119), count at most `C ξ⁻⁴` old plaquettes in x, and multiply by ξ⁻². The net power from four curvature factors is `ξ⁸ ξ⁻⁴ ξ⁻²=ξ²`. The coefficient from four canonical factors is

`g_j^{−d} α_j^{d−4} g_k⁴=(g_k/g_j)^d (g_k/α_j)^{4−d}`.

The undifferentiated term uses `Q_x⁴`; its squared moment uses exactly the eighth moment supplied by the single reference law in Lemma 7.51. The first derivative uses `Q_x³` and the exponential to y. Insert these bounds and the fresh-vertex gradient into (7.114) and sum the current anchors. This proves (7.120). Finally the reference flow gives `g_k/g_j≤[1+C(k−j)/x_k]^{1/2}` for `x_k=g_k⁻²` bounded below. Any fixed power of this ratio is paid by `L^{(2−s)(k−j)}`; this is a relative coupling payment and uses no absolute inverse power of g_j. ∎

The same calculation applies to a finite family of complete anchored plaquette-log variables and an analytic function with vanishing jets through degree three and a declared fourth-order majorant. In that case replace the fixed plaquette count by its given absolute carrier norm and include its stated finite moments. For an arbitrary completed birth, such a fourth-order physical majorant must be proved after removing the entire covariant quadratic and cubic completions, including their possible shared cancellation. The explicit remainder (7.119) supplies a checkable quartic part of that program.

### 7.32 First two conditional frustration rows at the nonflat saddle

**Theorem 7.57 (one-loop rows with a rooted error, P/L).** Use the actual first clean integral and all the strict carrier, chart and cutoff margins of Theorem 7.44. Let j(v) denote the product of the analytic physical coordinate and constraint Jacobians in that integral. Retain every v-dependent scalar measure term in j and every action term multiplied by g⁻² in Φ. Set H=Φ₀″(0), C=H⁻¹, H_η=Φ_η″(a_η), γ=g²β. The same normalized integral obeys

`log[I(W,η)/I(W,0)]=−g⁻²[Φ_η(a_η)−Φ₀(0)] + log[j(a_η)/j(0)] − ½Tr log[I+C(H_η−H)] + E(W,η)−E(W,0)`.   (7.122)

On a smaller fixed independent source polydisc the absolute rooted norm of E is bounded by `C[g²p²+exp(−c p²)+P^q exp(−cP²)]`, where p=D log(1/g) and P=ε₁/g. The constant is independent of the number of blocks. For the logarithm and its first two source rows the rooted norm is taken before summing the free space anchor.

*Proof.* At physical g make precisely the fixed-surface translation of Lemma 7.43. Subtract from its connected logarithm the one on undisplaced real balls at the same sourced center and precision. Every surviving term contains a swept-face species. Its majorant in that lemma, with one tagged face designated before summing, gives the last term in the error bound. Reducing the centered balls to |B_b|≤p costs the middle term by the same rare-selector expansion as in §7.14, since the original augmented reference Gaussian and its positive quadratic reserve still apply. These two comparisons involve the original sharp selector.

On the inner balls freeze the physical source and a_η. Replace g in the centered physical argument by ε and divide the centered phase difference by ε². Stationarity gives a removable singularity at ε=0, with value ½ BᵀH_η B. The normalized Jacobian factor is j(a_η+εB)/j(a_η). On |ε|≤c₁/p these centered interactions fit the same scalar and quadratic-growth budgets as (7.102d), after reserving the small fixed quadratic perturbation H_η−H. The carrier log on the inner cutoff is consequently uniformly bounded on that disk. The difference of its value at g and zero is O(g²p²): the exact change B↦−B on the balls makes the entire logarithm even in ε, and the inner ratio starts at one. For an individual carrier one may take the even part of its analytic coefficient, since their sum is even. This argument controls the absolute rooted norm of the resulting representation. At ε=0 enlarge the centered Gaussian balls to their full spaces, with the same rare-selector cost. The convergent trace series for log[I+C(H_η−H)] is localized by closing a chain of kernels in (7.102b). The contraction bound in (7.102c) gives `‖C(H_η−H)‖<1/2` after reducing r, so the trace series has a rooted sum independent of volume. The analytic normalized Gaussian determinant gives precisely the third term of (7.122). The deformation, inner cutoff and Gaussian comparisons all use fixed source discs, so Cauchy or the absolute source-coefficient estimate of §7.13 controls their differentiated errors. ∎

Write H_b and its derivatives below at (W,0); write Φ₀ derivatives at zero. Define the tangent and mixed tangent of the stationary point by

`u_b=γ C ∇H_b`, `u_bc=C[γH_b″u_c+γH_c″u_b−Φ₀‴[u_b,u_c]]`.

Set `K_b=Φ₀‴[u_b]−γH_b″` and
`K_bc=Φ₀⁗[u_b,u_c]+Φ₀‴[u_bc]−γ(H_b‴[u_c]+H_c‴[u_b])`. These equal the first and second derivatives of H_η. Then the genuine first-step conditional mean and covariance of h_b=βH_b are

`E_W h_b=βH_b + Dlogj[u_b]−½Tr(CK_b)+e_b`,   (7.123)

`Cov_W(h_b,h_c)=βγ DH_b C (DH_c)ᵀ + D²logj[u_b,u_c]+Dlogj[u_bc] +½Tr(CK_b CK_c)−½Tr(CK_bc)+e_bc`.   (7.124)

The errors obey the fixed-order rooted bounds of (7.122) with the appropriate two source Cauchy factors. Indeed the critical derivative is −γH_b(a_η), by stationarity; its mixed derivative is −γ DH_b u_c. Differentiating the determinant and Jacobian gives the displayed terms exactly. At flat background u_b=0, and the determinant terms reduce to the familiar Gaussian trace and connected trace cycle. At a nonflat background there is also the classical conditional tilt covariance of order β. Extracting the marginal action coefficient from (7.123) requires the external-field projection of the entire right side. In particular a trace at one background does not identify that coefficient.

### 7.33 The flat constrained quadratic sector at arbitrary age

Here the birth is an even translation-invariant curvature bilinear, with its dimension-four and dimension-six moments removed. We can prove a positive gain *after* its dimension-six normalization, uniformly in the number of original averages. The proof uses the transverse jump of the adjoint of the original averaging map. This jump limits the fractional regularity available without further cancellations.

**Theorem 7.58 (stable Gaussian principal sector, P).** Work on a periodic torus in units of the terminal spacing. Write η=L⁻ᵏ for the finest spacing, τ=L^{j−k} for the old spacing and 1 for the terminal spacing. Use the quadratic Wilson action at identity with its original repeated contour averages, quotienting discrete gradients. Let B=g_k z prescribe the terminal linear constraint and let A minimize the fine curvature energy ½‖d_η A‖² at this constraint. Write F_j for the linear curvature of the actual j-times averaged A. All lattice norms below use the physical cell measure. Let K(h) be a matrix on plaquette components satisfying K(h)=K(−h)=K(h)ᵀ and

`Σ_h K(h)=0,` `Σ_h h_μ h_ν K(h)=0` for all μ,ν, `M=Σ_h (1+|h|)^{2+s} ‖K(h)‖<∞`

with 0<s<1. Then the integrated quadratic packet satisfies

`|τ⁻² g_j⁻² Σ_h ⟨F_j,K(h)F_j(·+τ h)⟩|≤C_s M (g_k/g_j)² τ^s ‖z‖²₂`.   (7.125)

Uniformity includes coarse torus size, j and k. The physical inner product includes the old root count exactly. The breadth of the kernel class in (7.125) is fixed by the stated moment cancellations and translation symmetry. It is an integrated Gaussian bound. External-field projection of a local nonconstant coefficient has further commutators.

*Original linear constraint.* Compose (7.117) at the identity. Base-L expansion of its block offset and its independent segment offset gives the single map from mesh η to mesh t=mη,

`(T_{η,t}A)_μ(y)=m⁻⁵ Σ_{x∈B_m(y)} Σ_{l=0}^{m−1} A_μ(x+lη e_μ)`.

The gauge changes in (7.117) add only gradients. Thus the actual contour constraint and T specify the same curvature minimization modulo coarse gradients. More explicitly T sends a fine gradient to the coarse gradient of its block scalar average, as a telescoping sum shows; every coarse scalar has a block-constant extension. Conversely, an actual fine gauge transformation induces the coarse transformation at the coarse sites, so gradient differences at the terminal target can be matched. Hence one may minimize with TA=B modulo gradients. Choose representatives with TA=B. Variations of this linear constrained minimum give
`d_η*F₀=T_{η,1}*λ` and `d_η F₀=0`; the coarse multiplier λ annihilates gradients. Possible flat fine directions leave F₀ unique.

There is a right inverse of T from terminal ℓ² into fine first-difference energy with uniform norm. In each terminal Fourier cell use only its representative p in the coarse Brillouin zone. On that component μ the Fourier multiplier is a phase times the product of four normalized box Dirichlet factors and one additional segment factor in direction μ. For |p_i|≤π each has modulus `|sin(p_i/2)/(m sin(p_i/(2m)))|≥2/π`, with continuous value one at zero. Divide each coefficient by this product. Its fine first differences have bounded multipliers on that zone. The extension has both ℓ² norm and curvature norm ≤C‖B‖₂. This proves `‖F₀‖₂≤C‖B‖₂`. Testing the multiplier equation against the same right inverse applied to an arbitrary coarse vector gives `‖λ‖₂≤C‖B‖₂`. At self-conjugate boundary frequencies a complex extension suffices, or average with its complex conjugate to preserve reality for real data.

*Fractional adjoint estimate.* At terminal spacing one, T*λ is piecewise constant transverse to its link direction and a linear interpolation between two neighboring coarse values in the link direction. This follows by counting the convolution of the two one-dimensional length-m box kernels along μ, and the single box in each transverse direction. In particular for a fine shift of length t=lη in one direction,

`‖(S_{lν}−I)T*λ‖²₂≤C min(1,t) ‖λ‖²₂`.   (7.126)

For t≤1 in a transverse direction only the t-neighborhood of the coarse faces changes. The value there is bounded in squared ℓ² by the adjacent coarse values, with overlap at most a fixed constant. In the longitudinal direction the difference across t has ℓ² norm at most Ct‖λ‖₂ by interpolation. For t≥1 the contraction of T* in ℓ² gives the other bound (T itself is a convex composition of averages on translates). This proves (7.126), including t=η and periodic cells.

For 0<v<1 the discrete fractional seminorm of a directional Fourier mode is uniformly comparable to the mesh sum `Σ_{l≥1}η(lη)^{−1−2v}|exp(ilp_νη)−1|²`. The upper bound follows by splitting at `lη=1/|p_ν|` and using min(2,lη|p_ν|). For a lower bound when |p_ν|η is small, sum l in a band with `lη|p_ν|∈[1,2]`; when |p_ν|η is bounded away from zero the first term suffices. Thus the Fourier weight is comparable to `|2η⁻¹sin(p_νη/2)|^{2v}`. Combining with (7.126) gives `‖T*λ‖_{H^v}≤C_v‖λ‖₂` whenever v<½. The torus periods do not affect this argument.

For lattice differential forms the Fourier symbols of d and d* are exterior and interior products with the forward-difference vector and its conjugate, with the form placement phases chosen consistently. Their anticommutator is the scalar lattice Laplacian. Therefore `‖F₀‖_{H^{1+v}}≤C_v(‖F₀‖₂+‖T*λ‖_{H^v})≤C_v‖B‖₂`. Fix v=s/2<½.

*Old curvatures and canceled moments.* At mesh τ the linearized coarse curvature equals the block average and the two segment averages in its two plaquette directions applied to F₀. This is the curl of the linear T: telescope the coarse difference in its direction into fine differences and commute all translation averages. The resulting area map from η to τ is a contraction on ℓ² by Jensen applied to a block average and to the two fine segment averages. It is also bounded on H^{1+v} with a mesh-independent constant. To see this, decompose fine Fourier modes by their coarse alias class. On a class the map is a single row of multipliers of ℓ² norm ≤1 by the preceding contraction. For each alias the coarse lattice differential symbol in each direction has modulus at most its fine modulus, by `|sin(mθ)|≤m|sin θ|`. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz now proves the assertion class by class. In particular `‖F_j‖_{H^{1+s/2}}≤C_s‖B‖₂`.

By evenness and both moment cancellations the symbol of K is bounded by `C_s M |θ|^{2+s}` on the old Brillouin zone: apply `|cos t−1+t²/2|≤C_s|t|^{2+s}` to each h·θ. Here |θ|≤Cτ times the old physical lattice-difference symbol. Fourier multiplication, followed by the H^{1+s/2} bound for F_j, proves (7.125). ∎

This proof exhibits a specific source of regularity beyond the pointwise C^{1,α} bound of (7.118). It also shows why a statement for every separately anchored old summand is stronger. The cancellations in (7.125) occur in the sum over h and use the quadratic form's reverse symmetry. The moment-subtracted operator, its age factor and the coupling ratio are all retained in the displayed estimate.

### 7.34 A nonlinear real quadratic sector on a common periodic chart

The next estimate concerns a real regular minimizing configuration with one common small potential chart on the entire clean periodic lattice. CMP102 (9) in general supplies separate gauges on regular cubes. The common-chart condition here is an extra restriction that avoids joining these gauges in a multiplier equation.

**Lemma 7.59 (fractional curvature on the nonlinear constrained minimum).** In terminal unit coordinates suppose U=exp(ηA) is an actual original Wilson minimum at a prescribed Mᵏ(U) modulo site gauges, `‖A‖_{C^{1,α}}≤ε`, and its physical Wilson current has supremum at most Cε as in CMP102 (2),(8). Take ε sufficiently small depending on the fixed L,N,α. For 0<v<min(α,1/2) and every 0≤j≤k the actual old plaquette logarithms, based at their lower corner in the gauged averages (7.117), satisfy

`F_j=τ_j⁻² log[Mʲ(U)(∂p)],     V⁻¹ᐟ² ‖F_j‖_{H^{1+v}}≤C_v ε,`   (7.127)

where τ_j=L^{j−k} and V is the terminal physical volume. Constants are uniform in V,j,k.

*The multiplier.* Write Φ for the full gauge-adjusted logarithmic constraint obtained by composing (7.117). The derivative J_l of one step is `T_l+τ_l E_l`, where E_l is a finite translation stencil with entries bounded by C_L ε by (7.116)–(7.117). Between the physical ℓ² spaces both E_l and its adjoint have norm ≤C_L ε, and the same holds in ℓ∞. For the adjoint, the factor L⁴ converting physical cell volumes is fixed at a single step and is included in C_L. The positive linear averages T_l and their adjoints are ℓ² and ℓ∞ contractions. In particular T_l* sends the constant one to one in each component. The product J obeys `‖J*−T_{η,1}*‖_{∞→∞}≤Cε`, and likewise in ℓ², by expanding one deviation at a time and using Σ_l τ_l≤1/(L−1).

At terminal spacing one, T T* has only displacements −e_μ,0,e_μ on the μ component. Counting the two hat overlaps gives diagonal `(2m²+1)/(3m²)` and each off-diagonal `(m²−1)/(6m²)`, m=η⁻¹. Hence `‖(TT*)⁻¹‖_{∞→∞}≤3` by diagonal dominance, including coincident periodic neighbors. The ℓ² bound follows as well. Therefore T J* is invertible with both inverse norms bounded uniformly for small ε; in particular J is surjective.

Any variation in ker J is tangent to a local level set of Φ by surjectivity. Along this level set the actual ungauged coarse field differs by a coarse site gauge, by construction of the representatives in Lemma 7.54. This gauge can be lifted to a fine site gauge, and Wilson action is invariant. Hence its physical gradient P_A in the logarithmic coordinates annihilates ker J and equals J*λ for a coarse vector λ. The group-coordinate Wilson current in (2) and the uniformly bounded exponential-coordinate differential give `‖P_A‖∞≤C ε` (lengths here have terminal unit one). Applying T gives `‖λ‖∞≤C ε` by the inverse bound for T J*.

To obtain the fractional norm, expand
`J*λ=T_{η,1}*λ + Σ_{l<k} T_{η,τ_l}* τ_l E_l* (J_{l+1:k})*λ`.
By rescaling (7.126), `‖T_{η,t}*f‖_{H^v}≤C_v t⁻ᵛ‖f‖₂` for η<t≤1. For t=η this follows from the ordinary inverse inequality on the fine mesh. Also `‖(J_{l+1:k})*‖_{2→2}≤exp(CεΣ τ_l)`. The geometric sum of τ_l^{1−v} is bounded. Thus `V⁻¹ᐟ²‖P_A‖_{H^v}≤C_v ε`.

*Fine Hodge estimate.* Direct local logarithmic expansion of the four plaquette links gives `‖F₀‖_{C^α}≤Cε`. In the covariant divergence formula for the Wilson gradient, the bounded invertible logarithmic differential relating P_A to the group-coordinate current is a smooth function of ηA. Its reciprocal has uniformly bounded C^α norm. Such multipliers are bounded on H^v for v<α: in each directional difference expand the product, use the L∞ bound for the field factor and `min(1,t^α)` for its increment, then sum the fractional squares. This proves the H^v bound for the covariant divergence of the Wilson projected curvature. In physical units the projected curvature is `η⁻² Π Im exp(η²F₀)`; up to the fixed Lie-algebra convention its difference from F₀ is O(η⁴ε³). Applying a first difference and H^v costs at most Cη^{-1−v} in ℓ². Replacing a parallel-transported difference by an ordinary difference costs a bounded local product of A and F₀, of C^α size Cε². We obtain `V⁻¹ᐟ²‖d*F₀‖_{H^v}≤C_v ε`.

For dF₀ use the elementary cube identity. The ordered product of its six oriented face holonomies, each brought to one corner along edges of the cube, equals one: cancel successive shared edges along a cut-open boundary surface, leaving its empty boundary. Equivalently fill one face by the other five using their common-edge paths. The linear terms of its logarithm pair opposite faces with precisely the signs and shifts in the exterior difference. The connector adjoints differ from identity by η times bounded analytic functions of nearby A. The nonlinear products of two face logarithms start at η⁴. Dividing the identity by η³ expresses dF₀ as finite convergent local products of A,F₀ of order O(ε²), including the order O(ηε²) two-face terms. These products have the same uniform C^α bound, so `V⁻¹ᐟ²‖dF₀‖_{H^v}≤C_v ε²`. Apply the exact flat lattice Hodge identity in Theorem 7.58 to F₀. This proves (7.127) at j=0.

*Coarse Hodge regularity.* At any mesh t the four-link expansion also gives
`F=d_t A + [A_μ,A_ν] + t R_t`, up to a fixed sign convention on the Lie bracket, with `‖R_t‖_{C^α}≤C ε²`. Indeed the plaquette word's degree-one contribution is exactly its discrete curl; in its quadratic BCH coefficient replace each translated A by A at the lower corner plus t times its bounded first difference. Higher terms contain another t. All these products obey the uniform C^α bound. Choose v<v₀<α. The commutator is bounded in C^{1,α}, hence in H^{1+v} with bound C_v ε²V¹ᐟ². For R_t use the inverse inequality `t‖R_t‖_{H^{1+v}}≤C t^{v₀−v}‖R_t‖_{H^{v₀}}`. It follows that the initial ordinary curl d_ηA belongs to H^{1+v} with the required size.

Now take the curl of (7.117). Its linear term is the area average in Theorem 7.58. The nonlinear term is `τ_l d_{τ_{l+1}}N_l`, with the latter difference of C^α size Cε² by the C^{1,α} bound on N_l. The same inverse inequality gives an H^{1+v} error `C_v τ_l^{v₀−v} ε² V¹ᐟ²`. In the telescoping iteration, each remaining *product* of linear area maps is one combined box and its two segment averages by the base-L digit formula. Its ℓ² and H^{1+v} bounds follow with a single mesh-independent constant as in Theorem 7.58. Summing τ_l^{v₀−v} over l thus gives `V⁻¹ᐟ²‖d_{τ_j} A_j‖_{H^{1+v}}≤C_v ε`. Add the old bracket and τ_j R_{τ_j} by the same estimates to obtain (7.127). ∎

**Theorem 7.60 (reversible covariant quadratic packet on this chart).** Under Lemma 7.59, take a real even scalar kernel K(h) with its zeroth and second moments zero as in Theorem 7.58. For each displacement h choose a translation-covariant old path P_h with length ≤C|h|₁ and net displacement h. Use its real unitary adjoint transport to compare plaquette curvatures at their lower corners. Write T_h F for the translated field transported back along P_h. Then
`|τ_j⁻² g_j⁻² Σ_h K(h) ⟨F_j,T_h F_j⟩| ≤ C_v g_j⁻² ε² V τ_j^v Σ_h |K(h)|(1+|h|)^{2+v}.`   (7.128)

The bound applies componentwise or after any fixed symmetric contraction of the plaquette components commuting with the color transport. At ε≤C g_k it has coupling grade (g_k/g_j)² and a positive real age gain. A larger canonical envelope enters through its square in ε².

*Proof.* Each T_h is a real isometry in the integrated ℓ² norm. Thus `⟨F,T_hF⟩=‖F‖²−½‖(T_h−I)F‖²`. For a fixed symmetric component tensor use polarization; the four bilinear cross terms combine in its quadratic-form identity. Put `D_μ F=τ_j⁻¹(T_{e_μ}−I)F` using a positive single edge. Ordinary increments and multiplication by A_j in (7.127) give `‖D_μ F‖_{H^v}≤C ε V¹ᐟ²`. In fact the link correction is a smooth bounded multiplier times a translated F, with C^α multiplier bounds. For a negative edge its increment equals minus the translated and transported positive increment. Along a path of length l with t=τ_j and tl≤1, telescoping therefore gives
`‖(T_h−I)F−tΣ h_μ D_μ F‖₂≤C ε V¹ᐟ² (tl)^{1+v}`.
To see this, each transported derivative differs from the derivative at the initial base by at most `C ε V¹ᐟ²[(tl)^v+tl]`. The first term is the H^v shift estimate, the second is the product transport difference from identity, bounded by the sum of the lengths times the uniform potential bound. Add the l increments of size t. This proof covers negative/backtracking segments as well. For tl≥1 use `‖(T_h−I)F‖₂≤2‖F‖₂` and `‖tΣh_μD_μ F‖₂≤C ε V¹ᐟ²tl`. In both regimes the difference of the two squared norms is bounded by `C ε²V(tl)^{2+v}`.

The constant term vanishes by the zeroth moment. The leading squared norm has coefficients `t² h_μ h_ν ⟨D_μF,D_νF⟩`, whose weighted sum vanishes by the second moments. Divide the remainder by t² and include the displayed grade to get (7.128). ∎

Theorem 7.60 supplies an actual nonlinear arbitrary-age bound for a reversible quadratic sector on a common real chart. It uses an integrated curvature form; orientation-odd tensors, generic area-dependent cubic completions, spatially varying source anchors and independently gauged patches need their own cancellations. Those conditions matter for the complete birth packet.

### 7.35 Local gauges and a smooth source anchor

We can also remove the common periodic gauge and the volume factor in a pure clean hierarchy. This uses the adjoint of the *original* coarse constraint on divergence-free coarse multipliers. Gauge-dependent changes of its endpoint frames disappear from precisely that adjoint.

**Theorem 7.61 (local multiplier and curvature on a clean regular covering).** Assume the periodic system has only the terminal-scale prescribed averages Mᵏ(U), with unit terminal spacing. Around every terminal cell assume the actual regular cubes of CMP102 (2),(8)–(9) contain a collar of fixed width D_L sufficient for all combined stencils of (7.117), twice their radius, and a fixed unit localization cutoff. In their possibly different real gauges the actual minimum has `‖A‖_{C^{1,α}}≤ε` and its physical Wilson current has sup norm ≤Cε. These are the terminal-scale local hypotheses in Lemma 7.59. For any fixed smaller terminal patch, all old actual logarithmic curvatures in its propagated local frame obey `‖F_j‖_{H^{1+v}(patch)}≤C_v ε` at the old mesh, uniformly in j,k and total volume. The local norm means the norm after multiplication by a fixed smooth cutoff supported inside that patch. The collar constant may depend on the fixed cutoff.

*Multipliers without a global gauge choice.* Let M denote the derivative of the actual repeated group-valued constraint, in left tangent coordinates with the physical cell volumes. It is gauge covariant. It maps tangent variations of fine site gauges onto all coarse site-gauge tangents, since an arbitrary coarse site generator extends to the fine sites. Consequently an element of ker M* annihilates all coarse gauge tangents. We first bound the full norm of any such horizontal dual λ by the sup norm of M*λ, also for λ outside the kernel provided it annihilates the coarse gauge tangents.

Let c attain its largest link norm m_λ. Use one regular patch containing c and the combined stencils used below. Transform all its fine links by the fixed real gauge of that patch. Compute the gauge-adjusted representative Φ of the repeated averages from (7.117). It differs from the original coarse group field by site frames depending on the fine input. When its derivative is paired with λ in the corresponding transformed frame, differentiating these site frames gives a coarse infinitesimal gauge transformation. The pairing with λ is exactly zero. This holds locally for compactly supported fine variations by extending the frame choices outside their stencil; gauge generators with this support also extend to the periodic lattice. In coarse logarithmic coordinates the dual λ′ is obtained by the orthogonal endpoint frame change and the transpose logarithmic-exponential differential. Since the terminal potential has norm ≤2ε by (7.116), `(1−Cε)|λ_e|≤|λ′_e|≤(1+Cε)|λ_e|` throughout the patch. The input differential at ηA is likewise uniformly bounded. It follows that, on the fine slots used by T at c,
`J*λ′=Dexp(ηA)^* (M*λ)^{frame}`,
where the physical normalization of the tangent differential is understood (divide dexp(ηA)[ηδA] by η). In particular the right side has sup norm ≤C‖M*λ‖∞.

The entire product stencil is contained in a physical collar of radius `C_L Σ τ_l≤C_L/(L−1)`. The local row bound for J*−T*, proved in Lemma 7.59, costs at most Cε m_λ on these slots, since every intermediate value is evaluated inside that collar. Apply T and evaluate at c. The exact three-point formula for TT* gives
`|(TT*λ′)_c|≥(2/3)(1−Cε)m_λ−(1/3)(1+Cε)m_λ`.
Hence `m_λ≤C‖M*λ‖∞`, uniformly on the clean periodic covering. This argument needs only the patch at the maximizing c. It also works for a wrapped neighbor, by the same reversed triangle inequality.

For any dual in ker M* horizontality follows as above, so the estimate proves it is zero. In finite dimensions M is therefore surjective. The smooth real constraint is a local submersion at this configuration, and stationarity of the actual minimum gives `P_U=M*λ` for its physical group-coordinate action gradient. Fine gauge invariance of the action and surjectivity on coarse gauge tangents imply that this particular λ is horizontal. Applying the estimate proves `‖λ‖∞≤C ε`. Existence and the physical meaning of this multiplier follow from the actual constraint, without differentiating a gauge-fixing penalty.

*Local Hodge estimate.* Apply the J* Duhamel expansion of Lemma 7.59 in a patch of the stated collar size. For its value on the inner patch, λ′ may be set to zero beyond the neighboring terminal collars because the total stencil radius is bounded. Its resulting ℓ² norm is O(ε) independently of total volume. Intermediate linear/nonlinear coefficients may be extended with the same entry bounds outside the collars, since every term used on the inner patch agrees with its original value. In particular E_l may be extended by zero wherever needed for the ℓ² estimates. By the rescaled (7.126), each term of that expansion has the same global H^v norm bound as its extended expression. Multiplication by an inner smooth cutoff is bounded on H^v. Thus `‖χ P_A‖_{H^v}≤C_v ε` for each such inner χ. The local cube and divergence formulas in Lemma 7.59 give the same bound for the cutoff derivatives d(χF₀), d*(χF₀). Terms from differencing χ use the local C^α curvature bound and smooth cutoff increments. Apply the global Fourier Hodge identity to χF₀ to obtain its H^{1+v} bound.

For propagation choose a smooth real cutoff equal to one on all the backward stencils of the desired old patch, and supported inside the larger region just estimated. Replace A there by its cutoff extension, zero outside. Its ordinary fine curl has H^{1+v} norm O(ε) by the localized fine F₀ bound, the bracket expansion in Lemma 7.59, and the cutoff product rule (dχ times A is C^{1,α}, including its shifted versions). Its C^{1,α} norm and every fixed C^α error norm have constants independent of total volume, by compact support. Apply the last propagation argument in Lemma 7.59 to this field. Its j-times gauged readout agrees with the original within the desired patch, since all required fine stencils are unchanged. This proves the asserted local bound. ∎

**Corollary 7.62 (actual anchored reversible packet).** Under Theorem 7.61, let f be a smooth terminal-unit test supported in a fixed inner cell patch, with its derivatives through order two bounded. Let a real even K and paths satisfy Theorem 7.60 and require P_{−h} to be the reversed translated path of P_h. Then

`|τ_j⁻² g_j⁻² Σ_h K(h) ⟨f F_j,T_h F_j⟩|≤C_{v,f} g_j⁻² ε² τ_j^v Σ_h |K(h)|(1+|h|)^{2+v}.`   (7.129)

The bound is independent of total volume, j and k. It allows a signed f. For a partition by translates of fixed terminal bumps the same constant works for every anchor.

*Proof.* First let f=ζ², ζ real and compactly supported. The symmetry in h and reversal of the paired paths replace the coefficient ζ_x² inside the trace by `(ζ_x²+ζ_{x+th}²)/2`, t=τ_j. This equals `ζ_xζ_{x+th}+½(ζ_{x+th}−ζ_x)²`. The first part is exactly the reversible quadratic form of ζF. Its local H^{1+v} bound from Theorem 7.61 and the telescoping derivative argument of Theorem 7.60 give an O(ε²t^{2+v}) moment sum. On displacements t|h|≤a small fixed collar radius the entire path is in the chosen local chart when either endpoint lies in the support. On longer paths one uses only the actual real unitary transport, C^α potential on a bounded neighborhood for the subtracted first derivative, and the pointwise curvature bound. The bound by a constant times (t|h|)^{2+v} on the longer paths absorbs all these terms.

For the second part subtract `t²(h·∇ζ_x)² ⟨F_x,F_x⟩` in each old summand. Its sum in h vanishes by the second moments. For short displacements Taylor's formula bounds the square-increment error by `C(t|h|)^3`; its spatial support has bounded physical volume. Replacing transported F_{x+th} by F_x costs `C ε t|h|` in local ℓ² on this support, by the unitary telescoping argument and the local H¹ bound. Thus this part has the same O(ε²t^{2+v}) moment bound. For the longer displacements use the two translated bounded-volume supports and the uniform pointwise curvature; their actual distance contributes no volume loss. This proves (7.129) for ζ². Finally choose a smooth bump ψ equal to one on supp f, supported inside the patch. Then `f=[(ψ+f)²−(ψ−f)²]/4`. Applying the square result proves the signed case. ∎

Equation (7.129) gives the arbitrary-age factor at the level of an actual real spatially anchored quadratic family. The smoothness is measured in terminal physical coordinates. A fine oscillatory source has different commutators; evenness, kernel sum rules and path reversal used above need to hold on the completed physical row before this estimate can be applied.

### 7.36 Ordered path expansion and the combined cubic center

The real quadratic sector extends to oriented paths and tensor coefficients. Its oriented path area supplies a definite cubic curvature term. This is the term that has to cancel with the cubic completion of the same stable packet.

**Lemma 7.63 (weak expansion of an old path).** On the real locally gauged clean covering of Theorem 7.61 write t=τ_j. Let T_{±μ} be translation by one old bond with adjoint parallel transport to the initial vertex, so `T_{−μ}=T_{+μ}*`. Write `D_μ=(T_{+μ}−I)/t`, `D_μ^0=(T_{+μ}−T_{−μ})/(2t)`. For a word P of signed unit vectors s₁,…,s_l set `h=Σs_i` and its oriented area relative to the straight chord
`A_{μν}(P)=½Σ_{r<i}(s_{r,μ}s_{i,ν}−s_{r,ν}s_{i,μ})` (μ<ν).
Let X=f F_a, Y=F_b for a smooth bounded test supported on one terminal patch and two old curvature components. Then, with all inner products integrated on the old mesh,

`⟨X,T_PY⟩=⟨X,Y⟩ + tΣ_μ h_μ⟨X,D_μ^0Y⟩ − ½t²Σ_{μν}h_μ h_ν⟨D_μX,D_νY⟩`
`+ t²Σ_{μ<ν} A_{μν}(P)⟨X,[F_{μν},Y]⟩ + E_P,`
`|E_P|≤C_f ε² [t(1+l)]^{2+v}.`   (7.130)

For the sign in (7.130) the plaquette is oriented so that `T_{+μ}T_{+ν}=Ad(U_{μν})T_{+ν}T_{+μ}`. A change in the convention changes the sign of the associated area center consistently.

*Proof.* Let `δ_i=T_{s_i}−I`. Two telescoping identities give the exact operator formula
`T_P−I=Σ_i δ_i + Σ_{r<i} δ_r T_{s_{r+1}}⋯T_{s_{i−1}} δ_i`.
For the singles use `δ_{±μ}=±tD_μ^0−½t² D_μ*D_μ`. For a pair move δ_r to the left by its adjoint. If tl is below a fixed collar width, the H^{1+v} and H^v derivative estimates in Theorems 7.60–7.61 give
`⟨δ_r*X,T_{s_{r+1}}⋯T_{s_{i−1}}δ_iY⟩=−t²Σ_{μν}s_{r,μ}s_{i,ν}⟨D_μX,D_νY⟩+O_f(ε² t²[t(1+l)]^v)`.
For example `δ_{−μ}Y=−t T_{−μ}D_μY`; replacing its translated derivative by D_μY costs O(ε t^{1+v}) on the relevant bounded collar. The middle word produces error O(ε[t(1+l)]^v) in the derivative by the shift and transport estimate of Theorem 7.60. The left X factor is compactly supported and may be extended by zero across the larger collar. Summing all pairs costs at most C l² of these errors.

Put `I_{μν}=⟨D_μX,D_νY⟩`. The symmetric part of the ordered count plus the singles gives `−½t²Σ h_μh_ν I_{μν}` exactly, since each single contributes its diagonal squared signed step. The residual antisymmetric part is `−t²Σ_{μ<ν}A_{μν}(I_{μν}−I_{νμ})`. In weak form,
`I_{μν}−I_{νμ}=−⟨X,[D_μ,D_ν]Y⟩+O_f(ε² t^v)`.
Indeed D_μ*X equals −T_{−μ}D_μX and differs from −D_μX in local ℓ² by O(εt^v). Apply this to each term after moving the outer difference in the commutator to X. Finally,
`[D_μ,D_ν]Y=t⁻²(Ad(U_{μν})−I)T_{+ν}T_{+μ}Y`.
The old real plaquette is exp(t²F_{μν}). Replacing its scaled adjoint difference by ad(F_{μν}) costs O(t²ε²); replacing the transported Y by Y costs O(εt) in local ℓ². Pairing with X gives the claimed area term with an error bounded by O_f(ε² t^v) before the area factor, since ε≤1, v<1. For tl above the fixed collar width one may bound each displayed term directly. The actual transport is unitary, the actual curvature is pointwise O(ε), all other terms involve at most bounded terminal volume, and their coefficients grow at most quadratically in tl. These estimates imply (7.130) in that regime as well. ∎

**Theorem 7.64 (real quadratic–cubic packet with one total center).** Retain all hypotheses of Theorem 7.61. Take the quadratic packet `t⁻² Σ_{abP}K_{abP} ⟨f F_a,T_P F_b⟩` and a cubic packet `Σ_{abc,P,Q} D_{abc,P,Q} ∫ f·𝒯_{abc}(F_a,T_P F_b,T_Q F_c)`, where 𝒯 are fixed bounded invariant trilinear tensors. The coefficients may carry their actual coupling grades. Suppose the quadratic translation moments `Σ_P K_{abP}`, `Σ_P h_μ K_{abP}`, `Σ_P h_μ h_ν K_{abP}` vanish for each indicated component. It suffices that the corresponding *paired* forms in the first line of (7.130) vanish identically on these test families. Assume also that the following single local cubic polynomial vanishes identically in the curvature variables:
`Σ_{abP,μ<ν}K_{abP} A_{μν}(P)⟨F_a,[F_{μν},F_b]⟩ + Σ_{abc,P,Q}D_{abc,P,Q} 𝒯_{abc}(F_a,F_b,F_c)=0.`   (7.131)

Then their combined, actual real anchored readout satisfies
`|R_{j→k}(f)|≤C_f t^v[ε² Σ_{abP}(1+|P|)^{2+v}|K_{abP}| + ε³ Σ_{abc,P,Q}(1+|P|+|Q|)^v |D_{abc,P,Q}|].`   (7.132)

*Proof.* Apply (7.130) and retain its explicit area term until after adding the cubic local center. To replace either transported cubic slot by its value at the base, use the local H¹ shift estimate at distance tl and the uniform L∞ bounds for the other two curvatures. This gives O_f(ε³ min(1,tl)) on short paths, and O_f(ε³) on long paths by unitarity. Hence each costs at most C_f ε³[t(1+l)]^v. Now (7.131) kills the remaining complete cubic polynomial on the physical graph. Taking absolute values of the two *remainders* proves (7.132). ∎

For example if `‖K‖_{2+v}≤A_j g_j⁻²`, `‖D‖_v≤A_j g_j⁻³` and ε≤C g_k q, (7.132) has the respective weights `C A_j t^v (g_k/g_j)² q²` and `C A_j t^v(g_k/g_j)³q³`. The area center itself has size `C A_j g_k(g_k/g_j)²q³` before cancellation. Thus the cubic coming from the quadratic path has precisely its distinct coupling grade, as in MT45. A birth for which the moment identities hold only after phase/translation pairing must supply that actual pairing; a single polymer from an arbitrary wall decomposition need not have these moments. The test and current descendants are explicit in D_μ(fF_a) on the first line of (7.130).

### 7.37 Attachment of the completed quadratic and cubic row on a clean kernel

It is possible to pass from (7.132) to a normalized real connected attachment while keeping the current coupling factor. This requires an absolute carrier moment and the actual original regular target. We state the external chart and grade conditions because they are stronger than real cancellation of a single scalar.

**Theorem 7.65 (arbitrary clean age, an actual real fresh attachment).** Use the base-identity clean target map of Lemma 7.51 and its locally gauged regular covering as in Theorem 7.61. Let `z_y=g_k B_y` be the current physical independent fluctuations. Take the original near-identity target map through its unit local corridors, CMP109 (3.2)–(3.9), CMP116 (1.1)–(1.5), on a fixed physical complex polydisc of radius δ sufficiently small for the CMP102 (172),(190) chart. The original real cutoff must lie inside the smaller fixed polydisc specified below, and the real law μ_k must satisfy (7.113). All these restrictions are on the displayed pure clean family.

At one fixed terminal test anchor x₀ take the actual joint quadratic–cubic readout of Theorem 7.64 with its completed moment identities and exponential path moment norms `M₂=Σ_{abP}e^{a|P|}|K_{abP}|`, `M₃=Σ_{abc,P,Q}e^{a(|P|+|Q|)}|D_{abc,P,Q}|`, a>0. Include the actual coupling coefficients in M₂,M₃. For a real fresh vertex V_Y satisfying the derivative bound in Corollary 7.53, there is s>0 independent of j,k such that

`|Cov_{μ_k}(R_{j→k}(f),V_Y)|≤C_f g_k t^s (M₂ g_k² + M₃ g_k³) e^{−c dist(x₀,Y)−κ′ n(Y)}.`   (7.133)

In particular `M_p≤A_j g_j^{-p}` gives the two weights from MT36 with q=2,3 and one fresh g_k. The distinct physical-core caps of MT41 may also be kept in the respective M_p. The conclusion is a real connected coefficient at the stated clean terminal field. Formation of its complete complex projected offspring through all walls is a separate operation.

*Complex value and absolute fixed jets.* First subtract the known local area polynomial from the quadratic row to get R₂, and subtract the trilinear local center from the cubic row to get R₃. Equation (7.131) gives the exact equality R=R₂+R₃. This identifies the cancellation on the actual physical graph before taking separate norms. Each R_p now has field valuation at least p and obeys the respective real bound `C_f M_p δ^p t^v` on the real target disc. This follows separately for the two *remainders* in (7.130)–(7.132), at input regularity O(δ). Real CMP102 (9) applies on the real near-identity target disc through the indicated original map.

On the native complex disc about zero, the physical fine curvature and the first difference of the fine potential satisfy the uniform bounds used in the proof of (7.108)–(7.109). At base identity this follows directly in the fixed relative Landau coordinates of (172),(190), by integrating the value/first-difference response along the segment from zero. The composition of original averages in (7.117) is analytic on this small chart. Its first variation has the uniform exponential weight from Lemma 7.54. In particular `‖F_j‖∞≤Cδ` and `|D_{z_y}F_j(x)|≤C e^{−c dist(x,y)}`; multiply the four analytic old link factors, as in the proof of (7.121), before dividing by t². The coarse-link products along a path of l steps have complex norm at most `e^{Cδtl}`; the derivative of the product costs at most `C t l e^{Cδtl+c t l}e^{−c dist(x,y)}`. Here one may reduce c. The bound follows by differentiating one link at a time, using the physical link factor t and the distance from the root x to every slot of the path. Choose δ,c sufficiently small relative to a so the path moments pay these factors with a fixed margin. The physical inner product in one terminal test patch has O(1) volume at every old mesh. Thus, for both p,
`|R_p|≤C_f M_p δ^p t^{-2},` `|D_{z_y}R_p|≤C_f M_p δ^{p−1} t^{-2} e^{−c dist(x₀,y)}`.
The common t⁻² is a safe upper bound here; the cubic sector needs no such factor.

Apply the upper-half-disc argument of (7.108) to the holomorphic line through each small complex target. It can equally be applied in the independent physical z variables because their finite-corridor map is holomorphic, real on the real line, and has uniformly bounded derivatives. If the point has imaginary parameter iy, the diameter weight is `ω=1−(4/π) arctan y`. Choose fixed y so small that `s₀=vω−2(1−ω)>0`. Then on a sufficiently small but fixed concentric physical polydisc `|R_p|≤C_f M_p δ^p t^{s₀}`. The real selector must fit in a strictly smaller fraction of this disc; this is an explicit clean cutoff margin and may be imposed by choosing the original fixed physical cutoff parameter sufficiently small. It is not a conclusion for a differently prescribed mixed record.

For m fixed, Cauchy on that spare disc gives `|D_{y₁}⋯D_{y_m} R_p|≤C_{m,f}M_p δ^{p−m} t^{s₀}` there. Alternatively use the complex first derivative for any one of the m slots and Cauchy for the others, to get the same bound with `t^{-2} exp(−c max_i dist(x₀,y_i))` in place of `t^{s₀}`. A geometric interpolation with sufficiently small positive weight on this second bound retains an exponent s>0 and an exponential to all m external slots:
`|D_{y₁}⋯D_{y_m} R_p|≤C_{m,f}M_p δ^{p−m} t^s exp[−c_m Σ_i dist(x₀,y_i)]`.   (7.134)
In particular the fixed-order absolute anchor sums allow all spatial polynomial weights at a strictly smaller exponential rate. The constants may depend on δ,a and m, uniformly in j,k. No high-order analytic common disc for exponential polynomials is being invoked.

*Canonical moments and normalized attachment.* At z=0 the physical target, minimizer and old curvatures are identity or zero; R_p and its derivatives of orders <p vanish there. For the first derivative at z=g_kB, Taylor's formula along the segment integrates the p-th derivative against p−1 copies of z. Use (7.134) with m=p. Taking the derivative with respect to B_y supplies one more g_k, giving
`|D_{B_y}R_p(g_kB)|≤C_f M_p t^s g_k^p e^{−c_p dist(x₀,y)} Q_{x₀}(B)^{p−1}`,
with the exponent of (7.110) decreased if needed. Taylor at order p for the undifferentiated term gives the same bound with Q^p and without the fixed external exponential. The real expectation of these polynomials, and their squared norms for the derivative estimate, use the one original measure in Lemma 7.51. Apply the weighted real covariance identity (7.114) to R_p and the distinguished V_Y, and sum the exponentially decaying kernel rows. This gives (7.133) and retains the full normalization of the clean conditional law. ∎

The argument handles the actual regular physical readout of the completed quadratic–cubic family under its stated moment, path and chart conditions. It also identifies the distinction between a fixed complex *external-field* Cauchy disc used for finitely many field derivatives and a common analytic *source* disc for arbitrary polynomial insertions. Theorem 7.41 excludes the latter in unrestricted degree.

### 7.38 The inherited unmarked vertex and gauge covariance of source carriers

**Corollary 7.66 (attachment to the original inherited difference).** On the actual clean family of Theorem 7.65, suppose the real selector has fixed physical slack δ_B inside the domain of CMP116 (1.34). Then (7.133) holds for the complete unmarked inherited term localized at Y in CMP116 Lemma 1 (1.33), with the factor from its bound (1.36). The sum over all ages in that vertex is already included.

*Proof.* Before localization the original term is the difference of E_k evaluated at its perturbed and unperturbed minimizing configurations. Lemma 1 constructs its local V′_k(Y,U,J,B) as a function on (1.34), with sup norm at most `C_{M,κ} E₀ exp[−(1−2δ)κ d_k(Y)]` there; retain the fixed native prefactors in C_{M,κ}. The old X,j sums and the factor Lʲη controlling the age sum are given immediately before (1.33). On the real selector, for a single B_i inside Y there is an analytic coordinate circle of radius δ_B/g_k (or a smaller fixed fraction in each color component). Cauchy thus gives
`|D_{B_i} V′_k(Y,U,J,B)|≤C_{M,κ} E₀ g_k δ_B⁻¹ exp[−(1−2δ)κ d_k(Y)]`; the derivative at any slot outside Y vanishes. Here U,J are the original fixed external data, so this is the actual canonical fluctuation derivative. No separate assertion about the size of V′_k at zero is needed for this derivative. On the regular unit-scale connected geometry the native length bounds a fixed multiple of the number of cubes up to an additive constant. Use this in (7.114), retaining fixed native size slack, to obtain (7.133) for this full inherited vertex and its sum over current supports. At printed pp. 8–11 the source explicitly separates this inherited (1.36) term from the quadratic-growth part of Lemma 2. Applying the same scalar sup bound to that quadratic-growth part would give the wrong estimate. [Balaban, CMP116, Lemmas 1–2](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01239022). ∎

**Proposition 7.67 (gauge invariance of the localized first-step scalar carriers).** For the original independent sources multiplying the color-contracted matched plaquette force squares in Theorem 7.44, its centered scalar log L, and the one-loop split in Theorem 7.57, admit carrier decompositions invariant under simultaneous real site gauge transformations on their orbit domains. The bounds from those theorems hold on the native intersections and on their real gauge saturation.

*Proof.* CMP116 Lemma 2 states simultaneous invariance of both pieces of (1.42) under the rule CMP109 (3.29). The closing paragraph following (2.41) proves that the localized integrated expressions (2.14) have that same invariance, by covariance of their Gaussian operators and determinant factors. We check the added operations explicitly. The actual force components of a complete tagged bond transform by one adjoint orthogonal color rotation at that bond. Its contraction H_b is invariant for each fixed source η_b. Pulling the force through the original gauge-covariant fluctuation and constraint map preserves this identity on each source stencil. The original physical fluctuation transforms by its real adjoint block rotation in (3.29). Taylor contractions, scalar weakening parameters and individual walk products use the covariant operators and preserve that transformation on their own carrier; all internal edges of a product have matched endpoint rotations. The unique small critical point in (7.102c) transforms covariantly by uniqueness of the stationary equation, also termwise in its convergent iterative carrier expansion. It follows that the extracted critical scalar, j(a_η), and each localized cyclic trace term of log[I+C(H_η−H)] are invariant. In the actual marked face species of Lemma 7.43 the sphere, Lebesgue surface measure, outward normal and signed contraction −P u_b·n transform under the same real orthogonal rotation. Thus the exact integral on a fixed set of tagged faces is invariant; no arbitrary displacement variable needs to stay fixed under a gauge transformation. Taylor substitution of the covariant displacement preserves this identity after recollecting all color components for a carrier. Connected resummation and subtracting source-free terms preserve it as well.

The analytic continuations are consequently constant on intersections of complex orbits with the common native domain, first in a neighborhood of real transformations by holomorphy along gauge parameters, as in the final paragraph of CMP116. One may extend constantly along the real gauge orbits without changing the support or norm. In particular a local tree gauge may be used to estimate a complete scalar carrier when its actual field and own current can be placed in its admissible chart. This argument concerns the genuine source scalars just constructed, and does not assume that a general saved marked current is a function only of the field. ∎

### 7.39 Quartic tails on complete clean physical carriers

The following result replaces the single plaquette in Theorem 7.56 by an analytic family with its actual old support and physical-core norm. Its domain requirement is explicit; it cannot be used on an unreleased history core.

**Theorem 7.68 (quartic analytic family with path and volume counting).** Use the original near-identity clean target and smaller real selector of Theorem 7.65. At old spacing t=τ_j let E_X be a gauge-invariant physical scalar rooted at one old site, on a connected carrier X of n old cubes of fixed native size. Include a fixed stencil collar in n. Write d≤4 for its declared grade, α_j≤α_* for its physical old-core radius and A_X for its carrier norm, with `sup_root Σ_{X at root} e^{a n} A_X≤A_j`, a>0. Assume the following two physical domain properties.

1. On the old physical logarithmic coordinate ball `max|b_e|<α_j` of its support and collar, the *whole physical pullback after its lower, quadratic and cubic completions have been removed* is holomorphic, bounded by `A_X(α_j/g_j)^d`, and its jets through order three vanish at the trivial field. If it uses an own-current argument, that current must be substituted in this composition. For the dimensionless Wilson current `Σ_{p∋e}X_e s_p` on the actual old links, this local substitution is a finite analytic function of the plaquette stencil and maps a sufficiently reduced link ball into its current ball by the ordinary product estimate.
2. On the actual admitted complex target graph of Theorem 7.65, including long carriers, `|E_X|≤A_X(α_j/g_j)^d` with a spare holomorphic neighborhood in its old physical slots for differentiation. More precisely it suffices that first variations on the actual local old readout cost at most `C α_j⁻¹ A_X(α_j/g_j)^d` per varied slot there. In this theorem take a fixed clean lower bound α_j≥α_min>0. A shrinking live core requires a separate admission and expense.

Sum these actual E_X over their roots in a bounded current test patch with bounded f and multiply by t⁻². The resulting R₄ obeys on the indicated real clean kernel, for some s₄>0,

`|Cov_{μ_k}(R₄,V_Y)|≤C_f A_j g_k α_j^{d−4} g_j^{-d} g_k⁴ t^{s₄} e^{−c dist(x₀,Y)−κ′n(Y)}.`   (7.135)

One may take any s₄<2 by making the physical source-independent selector a sufficiently small fixed fraction of its complex chart, retaining sufficient path decay for the external anchor. For the undifferentiated real graph at physical size ε on a bounded clean chart, the quartic radial estimate has the full t² age factor on short carriers.

*Old real tree coordinates.* On a contractible short carrier nt≤c_L, include it in an old box of side Cn and use the rooted coordinate-order spanning tree as in §7.9. Each non-tree edge holonomy in tree gauge is a product of conjugated plaquettes over the elementary path commutations. At most Cn² elementary swaps suffice (the comb proof in §7.9 gives Cn for its rectangular box). By (7.116) each old plaquette has distance at most Cε t² from identity in the real gauge. Unitarity of every transporting product bounds each non-tree edge by `b_X=C ε n² t²`. Choose the tree gauge on the complete support and collar before restricting the field in E_X. If b_X≤α_j/2, the elementary radial Schwarz estimate in its actual physical ball yields `|E_X|≤C A_X α_j^{d−4}g_j^{-d} b_X^4`. If b_X>α_j/2 one may instead use the bound on the actual admitted graph from item 2, with precisely the same right side after increasing C. This does not invoke a radial continuation outside its domain.

If nt≤c_L and the box wraps, take c_L smaller than a fixed fraction of the shortest terminal period (at least one); then such a short box lifts without wrapping. For nt>c_L, including all possibly winding carriers, the bound on the actual graph suffices. The tail in the exponential carrier sum is ≤`C A_j exp[−a c_L/(2t)]`. For fixed δ,α_* this is bounded by `C_{δ,α_*} A_j δ⁴ t⁸ α_j^{-4}` on 0<t≤1. This last estimate uses the fixed target radius ε=Cδ for the complex-interpolation argument, rather than a uniform fourth-order bound for arbitrarily small ε on wrapping sectors. Every subsequent canonical g_k factor will be obtained by vanishing at the actual physical identity and holomorphic differentiation. Summing n⁸ from the near carriers against their exponential weights gives the same order. With at most C t⁻⁴ old roots in the current patch, and the separate t⁻² normalization, the full real bound on the fixed real target disc is
`C_{δ,f} A_j α_j^{d−4}g_j^{-d} δ⁴ t²`.

*Complex tube and attachment.* The crude complex graph sum is at most `C A_j(α_j/g_j)^d t⁻⁶`. Its single-slot derivative also has exponential decay to the terminal anchor with this crude t⁻⁶ factor. Indeed each old link and its finite-stencil own current has an exponentially decaying response as in Lemma 7.54. Item 2 pays the old derivative at each varied slot; summing the old slots costs at most Cn with a fixed number of bonds per old cube. Transport from x₀ to those slots costs `exp(c nt)` against the source carrier exponential e^{−an}; take c sufficiently small. The fixed parameters δ,α_min,α_* allow the common prefactor in the real estimate above. Apply the interpolation and Cauchy proof of (7.134) with real exponent 2 and crude exponent −6. The diameter weight can be arbitrarily close to one on a sufficiently small fixed inner disc; the subsequent interpolation against external anchor decay also has arbitrarily small weight. This gives s₄<2 with a correspondingly small positive anchor exponent. The exact physical composite R₄ has no jets through order three at z=0 by item 1 and because its old physical inputs vanish there. Using its fourth derivative in the segment argument of Theorem 7.65 gives derivative bound `C_f A_j α_j^{d−4}g_j^{-d} t^{s₄}g_k⁴ Q_{x₀}³ e^{−c dist(x₀,y)}`. The normalized covariance identity gives (7.135). The same proof applies to the inherited vertex of Corollary 7.66. ∎

In particular the three incoming rows (7.133),(7.135) can now be attached simultaneously on their shared real clean law. Their respective square bounds use fourth, sixth and eighth local moments from that one law. The result concerns the stated actual old physical family. The corresponding independent-current carrier may be used only if its own-current substitution and its physical domain satisfy the two listed conditions.

### 7.40 A sharp seam in the actual constrained Gaussian model

For the smooth root test in (7.129), Taylor expansion of the test commutator is legitimate. At a sharp indicator it can fail even for the actual flat constrained Wilson minimizer and an exactly moment-subtracted kernel.

**Proposition 7.69 (nonzero flux from a sharp assignment, P).** There is a periodic clean constrained Gaussian Wilson minimum and a real even finite-range two-curvature kernel with vanishing zeroth, first and second moments such that, restricting its roots to one coarse slab, its t⁻²-normalized quadratic form stays bounded away from zero as the fine mesh t tends to zero. The full periodic form has a positive age gain. Each component of the configuration may be multiplied by any fixed small constant.

*Proof.* Work in a fixed Cartan direction of the linearized SU(N) theory, terminal transverse period 4, fine t=1/m, m=Lᵏ. Use field component A_μ(n) depending only on transverse position n in a distinct direction ν. Its forward curvature F_n is chosen so
`F_n−F_{n−1}=t λ_n`, where λ_n has successive constant values 1,−1,0,0 on the four coarse slabs of m sites each, starting with n=0. Give F mean zero. With periodic indexing, `F_{−1}=−1/4`, `F_0=−1/4+t`, `F_{m−1}=3/4` and `F_{m−2}=3/4−t`. Indeed F rises linearly by one across the first slab, falls by one across the second, and stays constant across the last two. Since F has mean zero it is the forward difference of a periodic A_μ. Take all other components zero. A shift of the origin puts the transverse boxes of the original average at the listed slabs.

The multiplier with only coarse μ-component λ is independent of the μ-coordinate. Thus the linear original T* exactly gives the transverse piecewise-constant λ_n; the longitudinal hat factor preserves a longitudinal constant. Its coarse divergence is zero. The actual fine equation `d*F=T*λ′` holds with λ′ equal to λ or −λ according to the curvature sign. By convexity the constructed field minimizes the quadratic action for its prescribed coarse target TA modulo gradients. As in Theorem 7.58 this is the same curvature as for the original contour-average constraint. The coarse T A stays bounded independently of m.
