### 7.109 What remains in the constant tensor and in the volume-normalized observable

On the complete homogeneous physical graph the initial operator-valued marginal for the unamplified H starts quantum mechanically. For a constant commuting compatible curvature, the two staples in a given plane give, in the link frame, the sum of the forward and backward plaquette matrices `2 cos F_i`. This is Hermitian and has zero tangent projection. Thus H_b and its first derivative vanish at that background. On the actual first regular physical chart, (7.123) reduces there to its Gaussian derivative trace, with the rooted error stated in that equation: the recentering term u_b vanishes because DH_b=0. Its F² coefficient depends on the curvature dependence of both the constrained covariance and the H Hessian. It may have different electric and magnetic components. The absence of the classical marginal does not assert that this trace vanishes. The constrained lattice covariance, orientations and normalization make it a specific finite first-birth coefficient.

At a later homogeneous step for a *constant traceless tensor* M in the compact plaquette representative, consider the linear harmonic coefficient of the return matrix. At a complete compatible stationary Abelian affine background the classical directional force vanishes for each full orientation sum separately, because opposite transported curvatures coincide. The one-loop coefficient of the linear tensor return in this evaluation is
`L_{αM,t}= (1/2) P_{4,α} Tr[C_t(U) D² S_M(U)]`   (7.239)
in the canonical tangent normalization, multiplied by β_t⁻¹ in the mean. C_t is the actual stationary constrained Gaussian covariance with its gauge contribution retained. This identity is for the assembled homogeneous Gaussian evaluation; the true nonlinear correction and departures from the compatible background have their own terms as in (7.231),(7.235). For M equal to the complete physical scalar representative (7.237) eliminates the field-dependent trace, and hypercubic symmetry eliminates the linear traceless-to-scalar matrix entry when all homes and orientations are combined. A traceless-to-traceless eigenvalue is not fixed by the scalar running equation. Its potentially harmonic constant-profile piece has to be estimated as a coupled transport, or canceled/normalized by a verified anisotropic coupling or stress-tensor identity. It is not eligible for (7.234) without subtracting and accounting for its actual row sum. For the operator-valued second contact a pair of these constant traceless representatives can project to a scalar. Its leading affine classical Gram term cancels by (7.232); the Gaussian trace with two insertions is of order β_t⁻². At a mismatched wall there is instead the explicit signed boundary Gram/completion of (7.230),(7.232), as well as the defect (7.236). No surviving physical harmonic divergence is proved by the absolute bound on these separate pieces.

For the full susceptibility the norm is per **fine** site. If a filed marginal coefficient per t-site has size m_t, the extensive Gaussian scalar covariance of two complete action scores at that stage contributes at scale `L^{-4t} O(m_t² β_t⁻²)` per fine site, with the actual physical dimension in (7.237). Operator-valued contacts and outer means are accounted for through (7.229),(7.230); they are not that Gaussian scalar. In particular uniform unweighted control of m_t down to the final stop is stronger than what this scalar sum alone requires.

**Lemma 7.169 (volume-weighted marginal growth).** Suppose that for the actual one-step source norms one has verified
`A_{t+1}≤(1+C/β_t)A_t+u_t`,
`Q_{t+1}≤(1+C/β_t)Q_t+(C/β_t)A_t²+v_t`,
where A,Q are the amplitudes of the first and operator/contact jets and the forcing terms, uniformly in cutoff, grow at most as fixed polynomials in 1+t. Then both amplitudes grow at most as fixed polynomials in 1+t, uniformly in K. In particular `Σ_t L^{-4t}(A_t²+Q_t)` is uniformly bounded, even if the unweighted constant-profile transfer matrix has a bounded nonzero harmonic coefficient. This algebraic implication requires the stated actual norm inequalities before being applied to incoming mixed source generations.

*Proof.* The admitted trajectory has β_t≥c(1+K−t) at a fixed weak stop. On any interval of h stages `Σ β_t⁻¹≤C log(2+h)` by monotonic comparison with the final interval of h stages. Hence every product of the linear factors on that interval is bounded by a fixed power of 2+h. The first recurrence now gives a polynomial bound by one variation-of-constants sum. Substitute it into the second and repeat. The final geometric sum converges. ∎

For the displayed regular stationary and Q_{a+1} subfamilies (7.237),(7.238) supply concrete summable parts of these inequalities. What still lacks a full signed bound is the replacement boundary kernel, including the compact-to-S_cl representative change on unrestricted genuinely mixed charts, the constant anisotropic return (7.239) with its later interactions, and subsequent generations of the mixed lower/contact rows. Equations (7.230),(7.235),(7.239) identify their precise partners. The uniform trajectory bound for the complete unamplified H jet, and the fixed bare physical polydisc excluded by Proposition 7.86, have consequently not been inferred from this calculation.

### 7.110 The real rough contribution of a direct action or H cell

The physical susceptibility does not ask for a uniform complex marginal coefficient on every exterior. The following estimate treats a direct real constituent even in the early part of the tower. It uses the global physical intermediate minimizing graph, not an arbitrary analytic old-wall extension. Normalize volumes in original fine-site units.

**Lemma 7.170 (physical Wilson action per current cell).** Let Q be one t-cell, with a fixed native enlargement if its incident stars are included. Evaluate on the actual physical graph at t, with the same real regular-layer hypotheses as (7.220). Assign a microscopic plaquette its actual local layer n≤t, taking the minimum on its complete star if it meets a layer interface. Use the native physical curvature bound `||∂U−I||≤C L^{-2n}` on the matched positive layers, and the compact group bound on a genuinely retained depth-zero part. Then for any fixed finite r≥1,
`||Σ_{p∈Q} s_p(U_t)||_{L^r} ≤ C_r B̄_stop^{1/r}`.   (7.240)
This covers full cells on the original real graph wherever these are the genuine layer ceilings; on a different joined operator take only the part whose actual readout has those ceilings. A zero-depth assigned part must have a real continuous rough predecessor since that layer. One may not label an arbitrary artificial exterior as depth zero and then claim its age cost. The bound also applies to sums with original membership restrictions and deterministic coefficients bounded by one. For a direct unamplified H cell its right side is multiplied by Cβ₀, since `0≤h_b≤Cβ₀ Σ_{p∋b}s_p` on the compact group.

*Proof.* Root first at a fixed microscopic p. For a true layer n the Wilson defect is ≤C L^{-4n}, using the quadratic trace at identity; n=0 is covered by compactness. If the minimum on its finite star is n, at least one star location is in that layer, so Lemma 7.153 gives probability ≤C B̄_stop L^{-A(t−n−1)} for n<t, with fixed star multiplicity. If the field evaluation is missing on an unadmitted piece do not include it. With A>4r the resulting geometric sum gives `||s_p(U_t)||_r ≤ C_r B̄_stop^{1/r} L^{-4t}`; the same estimate follows directly from the pointwise vacuum-subtracted plaquette on the physical layers in (3.49),(3.68). Sum by Minkowski over at most C L^{4t} such p, retaining their true layer indicators. The positivity used for H is the complete compact force bound; no sign is assigned to subsequently generated polymer coefficients. ∎

**Proposition 7.171 (an early mixed susceptibility row at current-home resolution).** On the ordinary mixed physical conditionals of Proposition 7.159 and their admitted real changes (7.228), consider the *direct* action or H input at a fixed original scale, summed over fine roots in each current cell Q_x. Take the original finite stencils on the genuine graph of Lemma 7.170, and require their ordinary localized substitution used in Proposition 7.159. Write F_x for that real sum. Consider the contribution to the fresh covariance on the exterior event E_x that the home x is within a fixed number, or O(R_t), of the actual current rough components. The rough components must be those of the joint history, not boundaries imposed on a new independent theory. For the bare h readout, uniformly in mesh at fixed reference volume,
`Σ_t L^{-4t} sup_x Σ_{y at scale t} E_out [1_D 1_{E_x} |κ_T(F_x,F_y)|] < C(T*,g_*).`   (7.241)
The same bound holds with the event at y, or with both, and for the compact Wilson action input. Formation of an already declared second jet remains a separate term of (7.229). This is a signed-normalized actual mixed contribution, not a claim for every representation of an emitted low operator.

*Proof.* Lemma 7.170, conditional Cauchy–Schwarz and Hölder bound the indicated expectation at any pair by `C B̄_stop^C β₀² Pr(E_x)^{1/2}`, using fourth moments of the real cells and the actual disintegration. Apply the one-component consequence of (7.226) as in Corollary 7.167; a fixed collar polynomial can be absorbed by reducing a. This gives `C B̄_stop^C β₀² exp(−a p_t²)`. The pointwise rough spatial estimate of Proposition 7.159, summed over both fine stars in Q_x,Q_y, gives the other bound `C β₀^{D₁} exp[C₁(1+t)] exp[−c dist_t(x,y)]` on D. Here the numbers of microscopic roots, native cover counts and finite old Cauchy factors are all explicit finite scale or fixed powers; the initial h has coefficient O(β₀) on its finite physical plaquette chart. Dropping E_x preserves this upper bound. Now interpolate with weight `θ_t=1/(2+t)` on the spatial bound. The apparent exp(Ct) costs only a fixed constant; the remaining spatial exponential has decay `c/(2+t)`. On a four-dimensional periodic grid its y-sum is ≤C(2+t)^4, independently of the side. On the resulting estimate replace β₀ by `C(β_t+t)` on the admitted weak trajectory. The factor `exp(−a' p_t²)` absorbs every fixed power of β_t; powers of 1+t and the four-dimensional row count sum against L^{-4t}. For the compact scalar one may drop the β₀ in its real cell bound. This proves (7.241), with both homes and the original conditional denominator still present. Incidence information was used solely after verifying the direct spatial kernel on D. Unlike a Cauchy bound with fixed positive interpolation weight, this estimate allows polynomial loss in the current-home row to avoid an exponential loss in elapsed age.

The event bound extends to any explicitly listed portion of these source cells whose rooted physical moments and ordinary two-home kernel satisfy the same inequalities. It does not prove the corresponding rough spatial inequality for nonscalar all-wall histories, or for the covariance of two unknown previously emitted conditional means. The unresolved earliest entries of the recurring matrix remain (7.230),(7.236),(7.239), with the ordinary subset and specific proper returns treated above. ∎

### 7.111 The scalar test for the surviving constant anisotropy

**Lemma 7.172 (constant comb symmetry and the counterterm test).** In a complete homogeneous regular filing the reflection-even constant quadratic tensor allowed by the spatially cubic temporal comb has just the two coefficients on `Σ_i tr F_{0i}²` and `Σ_{i<j}tr F_{ij}²`. Its scalar part and its electric-minus-magnetic part do not mix under the linear hypercubic step on the full constants. In particular the constant-profile part of (7.239) on the second subspace is a *single real number* λ_t rather than an unconstrained matrix on all plaquette components. This statement concerns the complete constant part, with the other periodic comb components carried as profiles, and does not assert these symmetries after fixing a mixed history.

*Proof.* An independent sign reversal of any coordinate changes the sign of a cross term between two different unoriented planes having an index of odd multiplicity. It thereby excludes every such quadratic term from the reflection-even constant expansion. A spatial permutation identifies the three electric coefficients and the three magnetic ones separately. Equivalently the anisotropic vector on unordered pairs is `d_{μν}=b_μ+b_ν` with b₀=3/2 and b_i=−1/2 for the three spatial indices; it is +1 for an electric plane and −1 for a magnetic plane. The permutation representation on all six two-subsets has the constant subspace, the three-dimensional subspace of such pair sums with Σb=0, and its two-dimensional complement. To see directly that a linear S₄-equivariant kernel preserves the pair-sum subspace as a scalar, its entries can depend only on whether input and output pairs are identical, share exactly one coordinate, or are complementary. The sum over the four neighboring pair-sums at a fixed pair is zero for Σb=0, and the complementary pair-sum is its negative. Thus the eigenvalue is the identical-pair coefficient minus the complementary-pair coefficient. The scalar eigenvalue is their sum plus four times the neighboring-pair coefficient. The first row of (7.237) controls the latter for the stationary scalar representative with its separate compact-representative difference; it does not compute the former. ∎

Normalize d as above and extract the assembled regular constant coefficient by the fixed physical directional projection. At Gaussian order λ_t is the d-output of `(1/2)Tr[C_t(U)D² S_d(U)]` in (7.239), or the equal-plane minus complementary-plane response using that same normalization. The coefficient of this one-loop term in the upper-scale inverse-action parameter is λ_t/β_t. If a controlled nonlinear extension gives an actual return `v_{t+1}=(1+λ_t/β_t+ε_t)v_t+a_t` with `Σ|ε_t|<∞` and bounded λ_t, the fundamental solution is uniformly bounded over all time intervals precisely when
`sup_{j<k} Σ_{t=j}^{k−1} λ_t/β_t <∞`   (7.242)
under a sufficiently weak positive-factor margin. Indeed the log of the product differs from this sum by a bounded amount, because `Σ β_t⁻²<∞` and the errors are absolutely summable. If an actual stress-tensor normalization is needed, its homogeneous multiplicative factor is the product of these very coefficients along the trajectory. A convention change moves it between the tensor representative and its source coefficient; it does not prove (7.242) in the original normalization. No nonzero value or sign of λ_t is claimed here. The nonlinear mixed contributions and the complete sign of their R replacements still enter (7.230). A bound inferred solely by replacing λ_t by |λ_t| would implement a different test and cannot decide the original uniform coefficient. On the other hand, for the physical extensive Gaussian scalar contribution the weaker volume-weighted Lemma 7.169 is insensitive to the sign of this bounded harmonic term.

### 7.112 A window test for the one-loop tensor coefficient

Use a stationary classical tracer for the anisotropic tensor: deform the original classical Wilson action by its constant electric-minus-magnetic metric coefficient σ, then minimize with the same physical data and the original constraints. Take its σ derivative at zero. This is an alternative exact representative of the same F² tensor on a compatible affine field. Its difference from the compact current-plaquette representative of (7.239) must be kept among the remaining rows. The following identity concerns the one-loop physical Hessian and this consistently propagated representative, not the complete interacting effective action.

**Lemma 7.173 (the constrained determinant over a scale window).** At an admissible compatible stationary affine background with the physical axial/gauge slice and its pin data fixed, let H_σ be the positive physical Wilson fluctuation Hessian at a given input scale, with the old physical gauge directions removed. For j<k let V_{j,k} be the space of free variations whose last k-scale linearized constraints vanish. In a consistently nested physical Gaussian calculation with the same native averaging differentials and fixed external/coordinate Jacobians, the sum of the induced one-loop tensor coefficients on [j,k) is
`(1/2) P_d ∂_σ log det(H_σ restricted to V_{j,k})|_{σ=0}`   (7.243)
per final cell, with the same tensor normalization as its incoming curvature. If j>0, H_σ here is the actual incoming *Schur complement* from the earlier constrained Gaussian steps. If a compact representative is reinserted instead at each intermediate scale, also include the sum of its differences from the induced representative. On a finite periodic torus regard the constant-curvature Taylor coefficient as the bulk local kernel with its winding part identified, or use affine Dirichlet boundary data and state the separate boundary contribution. Nonquantized periodic flux is not an external variable of this proof.

*Proof.* At a compatible constant commuting plaquette field the action is stationary against each free variation, also for the constant anisotropic weighting (opposite oriented force sums cancel). Thus the constrained physical Gaussian Hessian is obtained by restriction and ordinary finite-dimensional completion of the square at every stage. Split the variables into one-step free directions and the remaining constrained directions. The determinant of the positive block matrix is the determinant of its first block times the determinant of its Schur complement. Apply the same identity to the latter, using the actual linearized determining rows. The Jacobian of a fixed physical splitting may depend on background and geometry, but not on σ, since the compatible stationary field is unchanged. Removing or separately integrating based gauge coordinates has the same consequence on the stationary charts where this splitting is verified. Thus the log of the physical window determinant is the exact sum of the logs of the successive induced determinants. Differentiate in σ, take the same curvature jet of this assembled identity and normalize by final volume. At each finer stage the old flux is `L^{-2(k−t)}` times a final curvature, whose square is exactly compensated by its number of sites per final cell. This proves (7.243). No loop expansion of the remaining nonlinear law was used. ∎

A useful sufficient upper estimate is `Σ_{t=j}^{k−1} λ_t ≤ C(1+k−j)^γ` for all windows and some γ<1; a negative linear slope with bounded error is stronger. Indeed β_t⁻¹ is increasing up to the native running constants (or impose the actual increment bound and monotonicity for this implication), with `0≤β_{t+1}⁻¹−β_t⁻¹≤C/(1+K−t)²`. Abel summation written in terms of suffix sums on [t,k) bounds (7.242) by a fixed multiple of `1+Σ_{h≥1} h^γ/(1+h)²`. One does not need a sign for each individual one-step determinant.

**Proposition 7.174 (the colors commuting with the background).** For a constant Cartan curvature F on compatible affine data, the contribution of colors commuting with its generator to (7.243) is bounded in absolute value per k-cell uniformly in j,k. This holds also on a finite regular affine Dirichlet window with the fixed physical constraints. In particular this part obeys the preceding window summation test.

*Proof.* Work in a gauge with the affine background in this same Cartan direction. On its centralizer the covariant transports are identity in the adjoint. The differential of each original contour average reduces on this color space to its flat one: its constituent background path transports commute with the variation, and the logarithm of a small relative Cartan holonomy has the ordinary differential on commuting directions. Consequently the neutral restricted tangent space and the gauge-slice splittings can be chosen independent of F and σ. If the centralizer contains a nonabelian block, the second variation coming from path commutators has zero color trace against any function of the Cartan generator, which is scalar on that block. The physical quadratic form is therefore `Σ_p c_p(σ) tr[ cos(F_p H) (d a)_p²]` up to the common positive trace normalization, with `c_p(σ)=1+σ d_p` at the required derivative. It follows on every fixed neutral physical subspace V that its Hessian at flux F and its flat Hessian differ, relatively in the latter form norm, by at most `C L^{-4k}|F|²` when F denotes the final curvature. This is uniform also on a small complex σ-disc: first whiten with the positive isotropic flat quadratic form, then use a Neumann inverse for its bounded anisotropy deformation. Hence the relative log determinant is bounded by `C rank(V) L^{-4k}|F|²`, by its convergent trace-log series. Cauchy in σ and the field parameter gives the same coefficient bound. Both the total [0,k) and the shorter earlier fine [0,j) determinants have rank ≤C n₀⁴ and the *same* microscopic flux when taking their difference for the j→k Schur complement in this background. Division by n_k⁴ and `n₀⁴L^{-4k}=n_k⁴` prove the bound. In the earlier determinant the compatible affine j-target is fixed for its integration; this dependence on the physical flux is retained before differentiation. On a box replace the two site counts by the corresponding fine and coarse volume bounds at fixed shape. ∎

### 7.113 The orbital contribution in a charged proper-time comparison

One component of the remaining comparison can be evaluated without passing to a continuum cut-off. Let the scalar magnetic lattice Laplacian act on Z⁴ by nearest-neighbor covariant hops with positive rates a_i and their inverses, in a constant plaquette phase B in the μν plane. For metric anisotropy take `a_i=exp(σ b_i)`, Σ b_i=0, where b_i is as in Lemma 7.172. These rates are for a scalar magnetic comparator, not an assertion that the full native Yang–Mills precision is this scalar.

**Lemma 7.175 (exact charged orbital heat coefficient on the fine lattice).** If K_B(s) is its diagonal heat kernel per site, then
`K_B(s)/K₀(s) = 1−(B²/6) m(a_μ s)m(a_ν s)+O_s(B⁴)`,
`m(u)=u I₁(2u)/I₀(2u),    K₀(s)=Π_i e^{-2a_i s} I₀(2a_i s).`   (7.244)
Consequently for s≥1 and σ near zero the B² coefficient is `−(4π)⁻² a_μ a_ν/6 + O(s⁻¹)` at determinant-one metric. The error and its first σ derivative have the same integrable ds/s bound. This controls every proper-time window [L^{2j},L^{2k}] for this orbital coefficient.

*Proof.* The covariant hopping series is the continuous-time nearest-neighbor random-walk kernel with the product of phases along its path. At a return to the starting site, that product in Landau gauge is `exp(iB A)` with oriented area `A=∫ X_{u-} dY_u` in the selected plane; the other two coordinates factor. In each coordinate the numbers of positive and negative Poisson jumps conditioned on a return are equal. Conditional on that common number n, both sets of n times are independent uniform samples on [0,s]. The mean n is `a s I₁(2as)/I₀(2as)` by differentiating the elementary return series `Σ_n (as)^{2n}/(n!)²`. Conditional on X and on m positive/negative Y jumps, the area is the difference of sums of m independent samples of X, so its conditional variance is `2m[s⁻¹∫ X²−(s⁻¹∫ X)²]`. Conditional on n in the X coordinate, its bridge covariance is `2n[min(u,v)/s−uv/s²]`. The two time integrals of this covariance give respectively n/3 and n/6; their difference is n/6. Thus `E[A²|n,m]=mn/3`. Independence of the two coordinate bridges and symmetry under B→−B give (7.244), with finite higher moments at fixed s. For large u, the Laplace expansion in `I_j(2u)=(2π)⁻¹∫ e^{2u cos q} cos(jq)dq` gives `e^{-2u}I_j(2u)=(4πu)^{-1/2}[1+O(u⁻¹)]` and its differentiated expansion uniformly on a small positive-rate neighborhood. Splitting at |q|=u^{-2/5} bounds the complement exponentially and Taylor expansion on the inner region gives successive powers of u⁻¹; it also justifies σ differentiation of the `O(s⁻¹)` coefficient. In determinant-one metric the four leading heat diagonals multiply to `(4πs)⁻²`. This proves the stated window error. ∎

For comparison, in the charged continuum background-covariant vector Laplacian with its physical spin term the spin trace in that single plane is `2+2 cosh(2u)`, with `u=B s √(a_μ a_ν)`. The scalar return factor is `u/sinh u`, obtained by the harmonic-oscillator Landau levels (their transverse degeneracy is |B|/(2π), the other directions are free). The vector-minus-ghost trace of the quadratic operator at half vector weight is therefore `(4πs)⁻² [1+(11/6)u²+O(u⁴)]`: the spin contribution is 2u² and the orbital contribution is −u²/6. Because log det has the negative heat-integral sign, its anisotropic metric derivative in this finite window gives a negative coefficient proportional to `(b_μ+b_ν)log(L^{2(k−j)})`. This statement uses only the quadratic Taylor coefficient in a finite window, not a large-field or infrared vacuum stability assertion. The lattice calculation (7.244) already has the correct orbital coefficient with bounded window error. The full native charged Wilson spin Hessian, the original Q constraints and the difference between their finite determinant cut-off (7.243) and a proper-time window have not been identified by that scalar computation. Establishing a sublinear *upper* window error for these actual operators would suffice in (7.242); substituting the continuum sign before the comparison would not. [Schwinger, constant-field proper-time method](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.82.664), [Savvidy, one-loop Yang–Mills background calculation](https://inspirehep.net/literature/119942).

### 7.114 The charged fine Wilson Hessian in the proper-time window

**Proposition 7.176 (the charged lattice spin term has the same window slope).** Take the Wilson plaquette Hessian on the infinite *fine* lattice at a constant commuting flux B in a single μν plane. Fix the usual covariant nearest-neighbor background-divergence gauge in this quadratic computation, with its covariant scalar ghost. Use a single charged color pair, writing B for its charged plaquette phase, and diagonal metric rates a_i of determinant one as above. With the usual common normalization in which the flat physical Hessian is the lattice Laplacian, the B² coefficient per lattice site of the half-vector-minus-ghost heat trace is
`(4π)⁻² (11/6) a_μ a_ν + O(s^{-1/2})`   (7.245)
for proper time s≥1. The error bound applies also to the first metric derivative at σ=0. The term is counted per charged mode with the same real/complex color multiplicities as its scalar heat trace. Thus its negative log-determinant heat integral over `[L^{2j},L^{2k}]` has the predicted negative traceless metric derivative with an O(1) window error. This is the unconstrained fine Wilson Hessian with the stated gauge/ghost and proper-time cutoff. It is not yet (7.243) for the original nonlinear averages.

*Wilson quadratic operator.* Write T_i for the forward unitary covariant shift on the charged subspace, D_i=T_i−1. They obey `T_μ T_ν=e^{iB}T_ν T_μ` in the flux plane; conjugation reverses B in the opposite root. For a positively oriented i,j plaquette write its background holonomy as P. After left link variation, its four first-order Lie increments transported to the starting site are `a_i,T_i a_j,−Ad(P)T_j a_i,−Ad(P)a_j`. Expanding the ordered product through degree two gives its covariant curl squared, with the real symmetric trace metric from `(P+P^{-1})/2`, and the sum of commutators of the four transported increments paired with `(P−P^{-1})/2`. This follows by multiplying the four exponentials, or from their logarithm `Σ b_l + (1/2)Σ_{l<m}[b_l,b_m]+O(a³)`. The difference of the symmetric trace metric from the flat one is O(B²). The sum of the four increments is `D_i a_j−D_j a_i−(Ad(P)−1)(T_j a_i+a_j)`. Cross terms with this last bracket have a first power of B times a finite hop combination whose ordinary zero-momentum symbol vanishes, as one curl difference remains. The term quadratic in the bracket is a bounded O(B²) finite hop.

For the flat-form curl-square plus background-divergence square, its off-diagonal Hodge commutator in the μν plane is `[D_ν,D_μ^*]=[T_ν,T_μ^*]=(e^{iB}−1)T_μ^*T_ν`, up to the transpose orientation. The remaining diagonal is the scalar magnetic Laplacian. In the explicit plaquette commutator term evaluate its first-B coefficient at zero ordinary momentum: the increments there are `a_μ,a_ν,−a_μ,−a_ν`, whose pair-commutator sum is `2[a_μ,a_ν]`. The resulting Hessian term has the same sign as the Hodge commutator, as follows from `(F,[a_μ,a_ν])=([F,a_μ],a_ν)` with the invariant positive Lie inner product. These two terms give spin eigenvalues `±2B` in this plane and zero in the other two directions. For the diagonal metric, use plaquette weights a_i a_j, gauge divergence `Σ a_i D_i^* a_i^{field}` and canonical link coordinates `√a_i a_i^{field}`. The scalar Laplacian has rates a_i and the spin eigenvalues become `±2B √(a_μ a_ν)`. The remaining bounded finite-hop coefficients and their σ derivatives are uniform for σ near zero.

More precisely, modulo this scalar magnetic Laplacian and constant spin matrix, the operator has to second order a term `B D₁(B)+B² D₂(B)`, where D₁ is a fixed finite combination of magnetic hops with flat symbol vanishing at p=0, and D₂ has bounded finite coefficients. This follows directly from the preceding plaquette expansion: all paths have bounded length, their differing short orderings can be fixed once with the extra bounded plaquette phases put in D₂. Rates, Taylor coefficients and metric derivatives are uniformly bounded. No assertion that the full coarse Δ_t is finite-range is made.

*Heat trace estimate.* Duhamel expansion at B=0 is sufficient since only the second curvature coefficient is required. Insertions of D₂(0) cost `C s K₀(s)=O(s⁻¹)`. In terms with two first-order spin/D₁ insertions at zero flux, their flat Fourier symbols commute with the scalar heat kernel. If one is D₁(0), its symbol has norm ≤C|p| near zero, so those terms cost at most `C s² ∫ |p| exp(−cs|p|²) d⁴p=O(s^{-1/2})` on the Brillouin zone, with exponentially small complement. The two constant spins give the previously computed 2u² coefficient at half-vector weight. One remaining term differentiates the magnetic heat trace with a single D₁(B) insertion. For each of its bounded hops γ of displacement z, the per-site trace of `T_γ(B)exp(−s L_B)` is the free walk return weight from z to the origin times the closed-loop phase of γ followed by this bridge. In the bridge with fixed endpoint the conditional mean coordinate is the linear interpolation between its endpoints, by exchangeability of the jump times (also after summing the counts). Its two plane coordinates are independent when their endpoints are fixed. Therefore the mean oriented area of this closed path is bounded in absolute value by C_γ independently of s: the expected bridge integral equals the integral of these two linear means, and γ has fixed area. Differentiation at B=0 thus gives a bound `C_γ K₀(s;z,0)=O(s⁻²)`, costing O(s⁻¹) after the single time integral. Differences in a short phase convention have the same bound. The estimates apply to the rate derivative as well: the bounded-endpoint heat diagonal and its derivative are O(s⁻²), and differentiating a flat heat multiplier supplies at most C s|p|² in the Fourier integral. All fixed-time differentiations are justified by the finite jump moments of the path expansion or finite Duhamel series for its coefficient. Finally the scalar orbital coefficient is (7.244); use four vector directions at half weight minus one ghost. This proves (7.245). ∎

A remaining determinant comparison is now very specific. The native restrictions are linearizations of the original averaging/gauge rows at the chosen physical background, while (7.245) uses the complete fine heat trace. One possible finite-box comparison is `det(H|ker Q)=det H det(QH⁻¹Q*)/det(QQ*)` for a positive H with Dirichlet data and a full row rank Q in the chosen Euclidean coordinates. The missing estimates would bound the metric/curvature derivative of that finite coarse Schur determinant per final cell, treat the actual gauge and constraint Jacobian and compare the physical finite-box determinant to the infinite-lattice heat window, including boundary effects. Only the neutral sector has been given this native window bound here. In particular (7.245) cannot be used as the sign of (7.239) in an unrestricted mixed recursion without those operator and representative matches.

### 7.115 Coarse Gaussian conditioning in a fixed box

**Lemma 7.177 (the coarse Gaussian correction on the physical quotient).** At a compatible stationary background, take a finite Dirichlet physical box with based fine and coarse gauge maps d,d_c, linearized native averages Q,Q′, `Qd=d_c Q′`, and onto Q′ on the gauge coordinates under consideration. Remove any genuine stabilizer or use based data making these maps injective. Assume the physical Hessian H is positive on the fine gauge quotient. These qualifications matter, in particular for torons. Let P_c be orthogonal projection onto a fixed physical coarse slice complementary to im d_c, and set `Q̄=P_c Q` in coarse slice coordinates. The σ-dependent log determinant of the native constrained physical Hessian at this background equals the corresponding *unconditioned* fine physical determinant plus the finite-dimensional correction `log det(Q̄ C_{F,σ} Q̄*)`, up to σ-independent determinants of coarea or frame coordinates. Here C_{F,σ} is the inverse in any complete fine Gaussian gauge, with its accompanying Faddeev–Popov determinant included in the unconditioned physical partition. Determinants in the effective action carry the usual half weight.

*Proof.* Q̄d=0. A fine configuration with Q̄a=0 has Qa in the coarse gauge image; choose λ with prescribed Q′λ to subtract this coarse gradient. It now satisfies the full hard constraint Qa=0. The choices differ by the permitted based kernel of Q′, up to any previously removed coarse stabilizer. Thus the physical condition is exactly Q̄a=0 on the fine quotient. Use a single σ-independent Euclidean physical slice for this argument. Passing between this quotient and a full gauge-fixed integral changes the mass of its pure gauge Gaussian and the corresponding gauge Jacobian, but the marginal of the gauge-invariant linear observable Q̄a is the same physical Gaussian in either representation. Its normalized zero-density equals `const · det(Q̄ C_{F,σ} Q̄*)^{-1/2}`. The Euclidean coarea Jacobians for the fixed Q and coarse frame can depend on the chosen curvature, but are independent of σ for the compatible unchanged affine classical field. Taking the physical negative log proves the formula. This uses equivalence of Gaussian gauge slices only at the stationary level, not an inverse estimate for the nonGaussian mixed-frame equation (106). ∎

**Proposition 7.178 (uniform finite-rank bound at matched homogeneous rows).** Let a fine mesh be h=L⁻ᵏ in coarse units and take a fixed Dirichlet box of R coarse cells per side, using complete interior coarse bond constraints with their complete averaging stencils. Use the homogeneous centered physical Q on its common real and complex transported weak chart, including its original endpoint gauge corrections. Then at flat and small compatible Cartan curvature q, the contribution of the preceding coarse Schur determinant to the σ derivative of the q² coefficient is O(C_R r), uniformly in fine mesh, where r is the number of physical coarse rows. This statement is for these matched rows; constraints cut by the wall with a different stencil or gauge frame require their actual boundary dictionary.

*Flat norm and right inverse.* Modulo an endpoint coarse gradient the flat physical one-step Q is the straight box/parallel-segment average. Its composition on k levels is the straight average over the whole k-block: the independent digits of the starting offset and of the longitudinal traversal sum give precisely the offsets `[0,L^k)` and traversal lengths `[0,L^k)`. A coarse gradient from a prior endpoint change remains a gradient by `Qd=d_cQ′`. In physical vector-potential units the full straight map S has nonnegative kernels of total row mass one and the corresponding bounded column masses in the fine h⁴ and coarse unit measures. Its ℓ² norm is bounded. For clarity here is a coercivity construction which does not assume that the flat average is point evaluation. For the coarse μ-bond of a block y take a μ-only smooth field bump supported in the interior of that block in the transverse coordinates and within a distance δ on both sides of its forward μ-face. Normalize its transverse and longitudinal discrete integrals. The longitudinal kernel of the double (offset and segment) sum of S is triangular; in δ of the central face it differs from its maximum by O(δ+h). Consequently the intended link receives a coefficient bounded away from zero, and the sum of the leakages to the two neighbor links is O(δ+h). No transverse neighboring block or different component receives any contribution. Normalize by the central coefficient. For fixed small δ and h≪δ, the resulting full coarse matrix is I+E with row and column norm of E less than 1/2. The bumps have bounded fine physical H¹ norm as a map from coarse ℓ², by bounded overlap and fixed δ. Multiplication by the inverse coarse matrix therefore constructs an H¹-bounded right inverse. For the finitely many remaining values of k one can use the exact pure face lift of §7.96 on the full native coarse cells; its finite mesh norm is bounded in this finite range. The construction supplies a right inverse also after projecting to the physical coarse slice, and vanishes on the fixed outer boundary when the stipulated stencils are interior. 

*Perturbation and Schur estimate.* On an R-box in a single affine gauge the fine link angle is O_R(h|q|) and the plaquette angle O(h²|q|). Dirichlet Poincaré in these units bounds the norm of a fine potential by C_R times its gradient norm. Expanding the covariant difference, spin term and the finite hop corrections of §7.114 gives a relative quadratic-form perturbation of the flat Feynman Hessian of norm `≤C_R(|q|+|σ|)` on the common complex disc. The charged ghost obeys the same assertion. At zero the fine inverse is consequently bounded on physical ℓ² uniformly in h. The centered homogeneous variation of Q on these charts has bounded physical ℓ² norm and is O_R(|q|) from its flat value on the matched quotient (T2 §4.21,(4.53),(4.54); CMP99 (3.78)–(3.81)). More explicitly each normalized native step in this chart is its straight averaging derivative plus a finite-stencil error of norm `C_L σ_n O_R(|q|)` at physical scale σ_n. Summing the single-step telescoping errors uses `Σ σ_n≤C_L` and the flat row/column bounds. The compensated endpoint changes are coarse gauges; an unresolved raw mixed endpoint map is not included. At this fixed R the coarse Dirichlet gauge projection and its chosen nearby frame vary analytically by O_R(|q|), using the finite coarse based gauge gap.

For the flat operator the coarse matrix `Q̄ C_{F,0} Q̄*` has a uniform upper bound by the ℓ² bounds above and a uniform positive lower bound by the constructed H¹ right inverse: the inverse coarse quadratic form is the minimum fine Feynman energy with its physical coarse datum, and the trial lift has energy ≤C_R||b||². The relative Hessian and Q perturbations show that the scaled coarse covariance stays in a fixed complex invertibility disc about this positive matrix, on smaller |q|,|σ| depending on R only. All stars in this argument mean analytic continuations of the real adjoints. The change of its log determinant is bounded by C_R r there, by the finite-rank trace-log series. Cauchy in σ,q proves the claimed derivative bound, with no factor involving h⁻¹. The same result follows on a native Dirichlet geometry when the actual (3.132),(3.156) estimates supply the corresponding bounded coarse inverse and the specified scaled variation bounds hold there. [CMP99, (3.78)–(3.81),(3.124),(3.132),(3.156)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01240355), T2, §4.21. ∎

The last assertion uses the original homogeneous *physical* quotient on a matched gauge chart. This is why it does not resolve the bound for a true arbitrary mixed joining frame. A periodic global massless Feynman determinant with zero modes cannot substitute for the finite-box relative determinant used here.

### 7.116 A Dirichlet-window calculation and its boundary condition

**Lemma 7.179 (finite fine box versus proper time).** Consider the charged fine Wilson Feynman and ghost Hessians of §7.114 on a Dirichlet box of side m=R L^k fine units, by principal restriction of the vector and scalar stencils, with any fixed-width difference of their edge/site boxes retained. Keep R fixed and take compatible physical curvature q, so the fine plaquette phase is `B=L^{-2k}q` times its charge. In the assembled fine unconditioned determinants the metric derivative of the q² coefficient per final cell differs from its infinite-lattice proper-time integral over `[1,L^{2k}]` by at most C_R, uniformly in k. This is the finite box with fixed affine boundary, not an assertion that all native boundary constraints have this form.

*Proof.* First keep a scalar walk and fixed displacement z of bounded size, including returns with up to two bounded inserted hops. For s≥1 the unrestricted transition probability to z is comparable to `s⁻²`; the upper bound for any endpoint is Cs⁻². A bridge with this bounded endpoint hits a wall at distance D from its diagonal point with probability ≤`C exp[−c min(D²/s,D)]`, allowing a fixed collar for the inserted hops. Indeed stop at s/2, bound the remaining transition probability by Cs⁻², and use the exponential moment martingale of the coordinate Poisson walk for its first-half maximum. Reverse time for the second half. The area has conditional fourth moment ≤Cs⁴: splitting into the two halves with the same transition supremum reduces to an unrestricted walk integral `∫X dY`. Conditional on X its fourth moment is `2∫X⁴+3(2∫X²)²` at unit rates, bounded by Cs⁴ for s≥1 by the ordinary Poisson coordinate moments. Other positive bounded rates give fixed constants. Reversing the second half changes the origin only by the bounded endpoint, and bounded hops add at most a fixed multiple of the coordinate maximum. This proves the stated conditional order also for these paths. By Cauchy–Schwarz, restriction to hit paths gives an exponential tail with a reduced exponent for the area and area-squared weights.

At zero flux the free heat factors in every second coefficient of §7.114 are independent of spin/component. For the Dirichlet error discard only paths which hit the relevant boundary (or start/end in its fixed collar). The scalar orbital part has two area factors, a first finite-hop insertion one area factor times its one time integral, and two ordinary first-order spin/hop insertions two time integrals without area. Their diagonal sizes are all bounded by `Cs² s⁻²` times the preceding boundary tail; a direct B² hop costs less. The same argument applies to derivatives of the finite coefficients. For the metric derivative of the free walk factors one may also work on a smaller fixed complex rate disc by analytic continuation of individual killed paths; a naïve absolute-value bound of all such paths there can cost exp(Cs). To avoid that loss, differentiate the real centered rate semigroup. Equivalently use the product of the one-dimensional killed heat kernels and reflection images on the coordinate box for each free segment. The derivative of a rate kernel is the corresponding time derivative times its scaled time. Its images satisfy the same Gaussian/Poisson displacement estimates with a fixed polynomial factor in displacement divided by √s, absorbed in a smaller tail. A direct justification of this rate bound, including for weighted magnetic areas, is given next. Thus averaging diagonal locations costs at most `C min(1,(1+√s)/m)`. Integrating ds/s from 1 to L^{2k} and dividing by final volume (the fine q² coefficient conversion is L⁻⁴ᵏ) gives O(1/R) at fixed R. For 0<s<1 the finite-hop series bounds the curvature coefficient by Cs at each initial site, so its integral costs O(1).

For precision about the metric differentiation, one can avoid differentiating a conditioned hit bound altogether in this Dirichlet comparison. For the q² term at real rates a_i use the abelian Landau gauge `A_ν=B X_μ` (up to a constant phase shift of origin). Along any diagonal loop based at x₀ replace X_μ by X_μ−x_{0,μ}. Two magnetic derivatives insert at most two factors of this displacement with the two oriented ν jumps. In the Duhamel formula at zero B these jumps are the centered-difference kernel in ν and the diagonal quadratic hopping term, with derivatives of signs as in expansion of the covariant lattice Laplacian. On a rectangular Dirichlet box the free 1D kernels are image sums of the unrestricted Fourier kernel. For a free time segment u a fixed order of centered spatial differences r and time derivatives l contributes `C(1+u)^{-r/2-l}` relative to the Gaussian displacement majorant for u≥1; for 0≤u≤1 use bounded finite-hop norms. The bound with a fixed power of the standardized displacement follows by Fourier differentiation or shifting the Fourier contour by `min(c,|z|/(C(1+u)))`; the real part of `2(1−cos p)` controls p² on the real contour and the displaced real part is ≥c p²−Cθ². A rate derivative on that segment is `u ∂_u` of its 1D factor and so costs only a fixed constant in the integrated estimates. For an image reflected in a face, the displacement entering that segment's bound is its reflected length. If a centered difference differentiates an image across its boundary, take the image formula before differentiating, which yields the same bound. Each path through the selected segments carrying at least one reflection has total displacement to the boundary at least D up to the fixed hops. Summing intermediate points by convolution leaves the same reduced boundary tail. On the A′² term one uses two first differences and the factors `|X_μ−x_{0,μ}|`: their typical products cost ≤Cs from the Gaussian displacement moments and the two inverse square-root segment factors are integrable on the time simplex. More explicitly use cyclicity of the trace to place the two velocity insertions separately adjacent to their two successive free segments and sum the basepoint afterwards; in the chosen constant magnetic gauge X_μ commutes with the ν difference away from the Dirichlet endpoint, with the identical Dirichlet image bound there. Fixed spin hops between the two insertions appear only at higher than second curvature order. The quadratic hopping term costs `C s·s·s⁻²` per location. For one velocity and one fixed spin/hop there is only one inverse square-root segment and one displacement factor; for two plain hops there are neither. The time integrals give at most `Cs² s⁻²` in each case, with the same hit/reflection tail. Extra metric derivatives on explicit magnetic hops have the same derivative order. This proves the metric estimate without a growing complex-rate path weight. Equivalent gauges for different basepoints give the same diagonal kernel, so the shifted coordinate costs no whole-box R factor in the short-time comparison.

For s≥L^{2k}, use a single affine gauge on this fixed R box. At small complex q and σ the numerical real part of each fine Hessian is bounded below by a fixed multiple of its flat Dirichlet Laplacian in form sense. The proof is as in Proposition 7.178: the link change is O_R(L⁻ᵏ |q|), its spin is O(L⁻²ᵏ |q|), and Dirichlet Poincaré pays these perturbations. In finite dimension the trace norm of `exp(−sH)` is ≤`Tr exp(−s Re H)` by the Lie product formula and Schatten Hölder (unitary factors from the skew-adjoint part). The Dirichlet sine sum then bounds this by `C m⁴ s⁻² exp(−c_R s L⁻²ᵏ)` for s≥1. Cauchy on fixed smaller q,σ discs bounds the corresponding q² metric derivative, and integrating ds/s from L^{2k} gives at most C_R m⁴ L⁻⁴ᵏ, namely O_R(1) per final cell. This establishes the stated finite-window comparison. ∎

Combining (7.245) with Lemmas 7.177–7.179 gives a negative term proportional to k, with bounded error, in the induced traceless one-loop determinant of the matched homogeneous Dirichlet prototype. The fine orbital/spin calculation and this coarse normalized comparison make no assertion about a native outer rough component. To pass to (7.242) for the original infinite-periodic bulk sequence it suffices to verify uniform prefix comparison with these fixed-R boxes at every k: the local coefficients of all actual boundary, coarse-constraint and measure determinations have to agree for carriers missing the boundary, with a summable boundary deficit. If such locality holds with ordinary exponential tails at each t, its missing fraction of t-homes is at most `C_R L^{t−k}` and their sum over t<k is O_R(1). One may then compare two separately calculated prefixes to obtain the needed windows; using the same physically large box for the earlier prefix without controlling its boundary constants would not prove this. The actual all-carrier dictionary for the induced (as opposed to the chosen compact) tensor, the boundary-dependent coarse/axial rows and their return to the nonlinear recursion have not been established here. Thus this prototype supplies a tested sign and cutoff comparison on its specified domains, while the unqualified T1 interface remains open.

### 7.117 Periodic winding and the comparison on the common interior

Use the actual homogeneous periodic averaging/constraint operators at scale t in (7.239). Keep the compact current plaquette representative. We take its local curvature Taylor coefficient on the lifted regular graph, identifying the winding part as in §§7.48–7.53. One must not manufacture continuous periodic flux states by changing an integer flux at fixed finite torus.

**Lemma 7.180 (winding costs over the whole window).** With the native exponential walk margin and shortened regular physical curvature chart, the difference between the t-step compact Gaussian coefficient on a periodic torus of n_t sites per side and its nonwinding lifted coefficient is bounded by `C exp(−c n_{t+1}/M)` per current cell when the side exceeds the fixed construction collars. The sum of these differences in absolute value over *any* window before the fixed physical stop is bounded by a fixed constant. The same conclusion holds for supported physical insertions at any single entrance mesh whose actual rooted norm is uniform.

*Proof.* At the stationary Gaussian, the compact Wilson derivative is the trace of the actual constrained covariance with the local Wilson Hessian at the current coarse links, (7.239). The derivative of the nonlinearly constrained arguments is their true tangent inclusion; second derivatives of that inclusion paired with the complete uniform compact first force vanish on the compatible affine graph. CMP99 (3.107),(3.132),(3.153)–(3.158) expands the covariance and the required interpolation into localized walks; the CMP116 weakening contours give the same anchored bounds for a finite field derivative. In particular the normalized compact source Hessian is bounded on the fixed current stencils and the coarse gauge orbit/pivot factors used in this formula remain those of the physical covariance. These are localized kernels, not a claim that Δ_t has finite range. A contractible walk family of total support diameter less than a fixed fraction of n_{t+1} can be lifted without identifying distinct local sites. Its terms and their local derivative agree on the periodic and infinite constructions: all local inverses in that walk are computed only on their stated lifted localization domains. A term not matched in this way has a path spanning at least `c n_{t+1}/M` native steps or an equivalent large localization support. The finite curvature derivatives cost only support moments: use one local affine gauge on that carrier and the spare exponential as in the physical F² extraction. Summation gives the stated rate. This argument uses the established physical localized representation; it does not compare two unrelated vacuum scalars. Since `n_{t+1}=n_K L^{K−t−1}`, the exponential series is bounded independently of the number of steps. When n_{t+1} is smaller than the fixed collars, only a fixed number of final scales need use their admitted bounded finite-torus estimates. ∎

**Lemma 7.181 (actual tapered Dirichlet hierarchies, common part).** Fix R sufficiently large in terminal units. In a fine Dirichlet box of side R L^k choose the original nested domains Ω_t with layers of thickness comparable to `b L^{t−k}` in final units, b a sufficiently large fixed multiple of RM in CMP96 (2.1)–(2.4). Use aligned native partitions and preserve all starred boundary rows required at those layers. Such domains can be chosen by eroding the preceding domain by whole blocks at the next mesh, rounding with a bounded extra block; the sum of all widths through t is O(`b L^{t−k}`), so the final domain is nonempty when R≫b. At the t-th Gaussian trace for the compact tensor, the difference of its *common interior* density from the periodic homogeneous density, summed over the window and measured per final cell with the same affine normalization, is bounded by C_R. This includes omission of homogeneous sites from the tapered layer and local changes to their constrained operator on the overlap. It does not yet include the genuinely different determinant of the fine retained boundary data outside that common intersection.

*Proof.* Use the actual domain-comparison theorem CMP99 Theorem 3.14, (3.154), not a finite-range ansatz. For two admissible hierarchies its resolvents, constrained Green functions, interpolation and inverse coarse kernels differ by their original bounds times `exp(−δ d(y,y′,Ω))`; common local walks cancel. For the covariance trace one can equivalently apply the resolvent identity before joining the two source ends; a changed row is necessarily visited by at least one walk. The compact one-step derivative has the same local current readout at the common affine background. Thus a coefficient rooted at a top t-home x gains an additional `C exp(−c dist_t(x,Ω_t^c))`. The fixed curvature derivatives can be made on the common shortened local chart, absorbing the polynomial support moments as in Lemma 7.180. Traverse only the common graphs when using this estimate. In t units the boundary shell has O_R(`L^{3(k−t)}`) sites; its native inside exponential tail has at most the same total count. The excluded layer of the full square has t-volume at most C_R times this count as well, since its thickness from the outside is O(`b L^{t−k}`). The squared t-flux is `L^{-4(k−t)}` times the squared final curvature. Hence the expense at step t is at most `C_R L^{t−k}` per final volume, summable in t. The figure does not rely on absolute smallness of a trace difference throughout the same physical R-box; it uses its localized change on the true common graph. [CMP99, printed pp.426–429, (3.154)–(3.158)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01240355), [CMP96, (2.1)–(2.4)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01240221). ∎

### 7.118 A genuine representative difference which accumulates

An absolute O(1) comparison of the raw compact one-step tensor with the stationary induced one, repeated independently at each t, is in fact false. This can already be seen in the periodic neutral colors. It is a statement about a particular summand of the proposed comparison and its sign; it is not a counterexample to (7.242).

**Proposition 7.182 (negative neutral compact contribution).** At a homogeneous physical flat target take a regular Cartan generator H, a neutral color T commuting with it, and the traceless diagonal plane tensor d of Lemma 7.172. For the constant affine F² evaluation in plane α, the repeatedly inserted compact Wilson representative gives in neutral colors
`λ^{c,neu}_{t} = −c_t + O(L^{-4t}),      0<c₀≤c_t≤C,`   (7.246)
on the completed full cells, with the bounded winding qualification of Lemma 7.180. In contrast the consistently induced neutral window has bounded prefixes by Proposition 7.174. Thus the sum of the compact-minus-induced *raw one-step trace* differences has a negative term of order k−j. It aids an upper bound but cannot be dropped as an absolutely bounded representative discrepancy.

*Proof.* In the background with final plane flux qH, write c for the neutral physical incoming one-step covariance at q=0 on ker Q (or its physical inclusion). The neutral fine Wilson stiffness at scale zero has weight `cos(L^{-2(t+1)} qH)` at the plaquettes of that plane. Its relative change is `O(L^{-4(t+1)}q²)` in the flat positive quadratic-form norm. Restriction to a finer constraint and taking its Schur complement preserve the two-sided form comparison: minimize the inequalities with the same imposed coarse data. The coarse constraints on neutral colors are the flat ones because all background path transports commute on these variations. The same comparison passes to the inverse on the current physical free slice. The neutral gauge factors have fixed rank. These facts apply also as analytic variation at q=0, or by polarizing the real second derivative. **Lemma 7.183 (what is counted once after reinsertion).** On the homogeneous compatible classical graph let L_t be the actual pullback of a first source row to the next constrained minimum, and L_{s,t} its composition. ### 7.119 The entrance mismatch after retaining its signed partners

**Proposition 7.184 (age of the transported compact-minus-induced classical row).** On the complete homogeneous physical regular chart of Lemmas 7.50,7.54,7.79, take the source home sum of a constant plane tensor d. Fine and j meshes give the same total physical volume per coarsening cell. *The trace and the external coefficient.* For separately differentiated graph values the exp-decay in current target anchors is the actual CMP102 (190) response with the first differences and the physical-current substitution on the homogeneous chart, as used in (7.107),(7.125). Thus each of the two quadratures, without cancellation, has its derivative at a target slot u bounded by `C exp(−c dist_t(Q,u))`: use the normalized plaquette derivative O(1) after division by its squared mesh, and sum fourth mesh powers over the fine sites of Q. Other fixed derivatives are obtained on the spare same chart by Cauchy. Independently the Cauchy bound for any prescribed fixed derivatives of D_Q carries the full `C τ^α`. Taking a geometric mean gives `C τ^{α/2} exp[−c′ max dist_t(Q,u_i)]` for two internal and two external slots (and the corresponding lower orders). All four slots and their finite moments sum against this remaining exponential. Contract the two internal slots with that covariance and take the external F² moment. Derivatives landing on C or on D_Q have the same positive τ power; fixed curvature/path moments cost only a further fixed spare rate. At a compatible constant affine physical field the first variations of both complete S_d functionals vanish, so that source-induced motion of the classical saddle adds no first-order term to this assembled one-loop trace. ### 7.120 A periodic probe for the same curvature coefficient

Take constant periodic links `V_ρ=exp(h A_ρ)` at fine spacing h=L⁻ᵏ in terminal units, where two of the small Lie algebra matrices fail to commute. Give them independent amplitudes s,t. The plaquette holonomy is `I+h²st[X,Y]+O((|s|+|t|)³)` in that plane. Indeed contractible loops expanded about a pure gauge have no constant-connection fluctuation at first order; their leading Lie curvature is the same oriented area times this commutator. Two curvature factors give degree four, higher curvature products cannot contribute, and derivatives of the constant connection curvature bring extra powers of s or t. One may equivalently use the localized axial-tree curvature expansion in §7.48. Winding loops have their separate estimate (Lemma 7.180). This test really is periodic at all real s,t.

**Lemma 7.185 (the current partner on localized carriers).** On homogeneous regular graphs the Wilson background current of this constant link family begins at degree three in s,t. An analytic locally covariant adjoint coefficient has zero constant term at identity and zero term linear in a spatially constant infinitesimal connection on a contractible carrier. Consequently its pairing with this current has zero s²t² coefficient on these carriers.

*Proof.* Each current is the covariant difference of opposite plaquette forces. The order-st curvature is constant and transports are identity to zeroth order, so it cancels in the difference; the remaining current has degree at least three. An adjoint value at the identity invariant under all constant color rotations is zero in su(N). To first order a constant connection is a gauge change of identity on a contractible patch (take the linear site potential `Σ x_ρ A_ρ`). By covariance the corresponding variation is a commutator with that zero value, hence zero. Summing a local expression linear in a freely placed adjoint J with its common endpoint frames therefore gives no quartic term. This includes the properly assembled *localized* multiplier terms containing J in CMP99 (3.117)–(3.120),(3.135)–(3.137),(3.156) after their native Gaussian contraction on the regular graph. It is not permissible to drop J before taking a gauge-covariant combined contraction, or in a nonlocal full inverse with zero modes before estimating its winding part. ∎

The true critical graph for the final targets obtained from these constant links agrees with the constant-link field through degree three at a fixed finite cutoff on its admissible constrained physical slice. At identity the linearized average is straight averaging plus a coarse gradient. The spatially constant degree-three fine current is in the range of its adjoint on the complete periodic sum: constant coarse colors in a bond orientation pull back to constant fine colors since the straight kernel has constant weighted column sum, while the endpoint-gradient part has zero pairing with this constant coarse test. The fine field satisfies the imposed target by construction. Thus through cubic order the Lagrange equations hold with a degree-three coarse multiplier, and solving the regular restricted critical equation alters the field first at degree four. This uses a regular slice or the equivalent orbit statement; a different color representative may include a gauge change. A variation of the regular source-free determinant or measure through a degree-four change of the stationary field pairs with its *linear* field jet at identity, which is zero for the invariant scalar. This argument compares jets; it does not turn the displayed constant field into an everywhere stationary solution at nonzero s,t.

**Proposition 7.186 (charged fine periodic determinant and its sign).** On the completely periodic fine torus of side `n=R/h`, R fixed, take the Wilson Hessian and covariant background-divergence gauge with its scalar ghost as in §7.114, now in the above constant periodic link field. Give their flat constant Fourier modes a positive reference mass comparable to h². This specifies a fine Gaussian comparator, not a silent removal of a true toron. In the s²t² response per terminal cell its traceless metric derivative has negative logarithmic slope, with O_R(1) error uniformly in k. This proof uses no boundary rows or nonquantized magnetic flux.

*Proof.* All symbols are translation invariant. In a color representation let `P_i=−i ad A_i` be Hermitian and use anisotropy rates a_i=e^{σ b_i}, Σb_i=0. In fine units the ordinary covariant shift is `e^{ip_i} exp(ihP_i)` up to the common sign convention. For momenta 0<|p|≤c the fine Wilson Feynman symbol agrees to order two in `(p,hA)` with the continuum background-gauge kinetic symbol: its scalar part is `Σ_i a_i(p_i+hP_i)²`, and its vector curvature spin is the matrix `±2h²[√a_i P_i,√a_j P_j]` with consistent Hermitian vector action. This follows by expanding the four plaquette increments and the gauge square as in §7.114, now for the constant full matrices; the explicit plaquette commutator and curl-divergence commutator have the same spin sign. Errors are analytic of order at least three in the small momenta and link potentials. The ghost has the corresponding scalar symbol. For a complex-amplitude polydisc `|hA|≤c₁|p|`, both reference inverses have norm ≤C|p|⁻². Therefore the difference of their log determinants is O(|p|) at fixed σ, and its fourth link derivative costs at most C|p|⁻³. This bound and its σ derivative are integrable at the origin in four dimensions. Away from the soft momentum ball the same derivatives are uniformly bounded, yielding only O_R(1) in the fine sum after the h⁴ from the four physical fields is restored. The p=0 block has fixed rank; after division by h² it is analytic and invertible on a fixed small amplitude disc because of the declared constant-mode stabilization. Its fourth response costs O_R(1).

For the logarithmic coefficient rescale p_i by √a_i and P_i likewise; determinant-one metric has Jacobian one. The coefficient of the logarithmic radial integral is independent of the smooth cutoff shape, as follows by integrating the homogeneous term of degree −4. For a unit direction n on S³ let `D=2Σ n_i P_i`, `E=Σ P_i²`. The quartic coefficient of the scalar log determinant, before its radial factor, is `Tr[−E²/2+D²E−D⁴/4]`. Spherical averaging uses `⟨n_i n_j⟩=δ_ij/4` and `⟨n_i n_j n_l n_m⟩=(δ_ijδ_lm+δ_ilδ_jm+δ_imδ_jl)/24`, giving `+(1/12)Σ_{ij}||[P_i,P_j]||²_HS`. In the half-vector-minus-ghost combination this scalar contribution has net multiplicity one. Terms linear in the vector spin have zero vector trace, and its square adds `−Σ_{ij}||[P_i,P_j]||²_HS`. Thus the total angular coefficient is `−(11/12)Σ_{ij}a_i a_j ||[P_i,P_j]||²_HS` in the original P conventions, with the common positive momentum-shell measure. The finite periodic Riemann sum for the degree −4 term differs from the annular integral by O_R(1): on each cell outside the first few momentum cells the gradient is O(|p|⁻⁵), so the mesh times its radial integral down to the mesh is bounded. The finitely many innermost nonzero cells also cost O(1). Taking the metric derivative gives the required negative coefficient on the electric-minus-magnetic test, because the spin pairs which survive have weight `b_i+b_j=d_{ij}` and the d-output contracts it again with d_{ij}. This verifies the order and sign of the positive-source marginal return convention: the derivative is that of the *positive* effective action `+½ logdet H_vec−logdet H_ghost`, with β_t⁻¹ multiplying the resulting coefficient in the source mean. Abel summation must use increasing inverse β_t and suffix, not prefix, sums as after (7.243). ∎

The soft p=0 stabilization and the omission of the nonlinear hard Q multiplier are explicit features of Proposition 7.186. A finite-rank toron contribution cannot be discarded in the actual native constrained integral on the strength of this calculation. The first rank bound on the physical quotient (Lemma 7.177) used exact stationarity; Lemma 7.185 disposes of the *localized* degree-four current term, but not yet the entire finite-volume gauge/conditioning difference. These are distinct from the already controlled winding and entrance differences of Lemmas 7.180–7.183 and Proposition 7.184.

### 7.121 Quantized periodic curvature and finite-rank normalization

For the periodic comparison choose once an integer R divisible by the native block partitions and sufficiently large for the weak chart. **Lemma 7.187 (extracting prefix sums with a fixed flux measurement).** Let δ_t^J denote the induced constant anisotropy one-loop response on this homogeneous physical Gaussian, and use the d-output normalization of Lemma 7.172. The curl-square term per fine plaquette is O(L⁻⁴ᵗ), as is the background-commutator term with two link variations. The L⁴ᵗ fine roots per t-cell spend exactly these four powers. The exponential response factors to the external and internal homes remain, giving the uniform rooted trace bound and fixed curvature moments on the native chart. A local affine gauge on a carrier of diameter D needs at most fixed polynomial D factors to differentiate the small real flux; use a radius reduced by that polynomial at each real point of the intervening interval. The spare carrier exponential controls the finite third derivative. The nonwinding terms consequently have Taylor error `C |q_t|³` per t-cell after their quadratic contribution is separated. Multiplication by the number of t-sites per final cell converts q_t² exactly to q_R², and the third-order remainders sum `C Σ_{t<k}|q_t|≤C_R`. This proves (7.248). The comparison uses a different physical torus for each prefix but the same lifted local coefficients, not a comparison of their absolute bare vacuum constants. ∎

**Lemma 7.188 (hard constraints versus the periodic stabilized physical Gaussian).** At each of the two real fluxes in (7.248), the σ derivative of the hard determinant differs from the σ derivative of a stabilized unconditioned fine physical Gaussian determinant by O_R(1). Its divided contribution to (7.248) is uniformly bounded. Stabilization can be chosen of rank O_R(1) and size O_R(h²), independent of σ in the original physical coordinates. *Proof.* Use the fine physical quotient with its σ-independent orthogonal slice V at this stationary point. Any stabilizers can be removed before taking the respective Gaussian integrals; their dimensions are bounded by the group dimension, and are σ independent at a fixed background. Coarea, Haar-at-saddle and gauge-section constants independent of σ do not affect this comparison. The rank of the imposed constraint is at most the number of coarse link components, C R⁴ irrespective of k.

Here are the uniform form bounds. The physical hard quadratic Hessian on its native based slice has a fixed positive gap in final units at the regular background, hence in fine link units `H₀|hard ≥c h²`. This is the fine constrained Green estimate of CMP99 (3.143)–(3.153), or the corresponding hard variational estimate with (3.42)–(3.47), rather than a one-step bound asserted for an unrelated space. In V the background-gauge form bound from §7.114 gives `H₀≥c L_B−C|q_R|h²` as a quadratic form, where L_B is the scalar covariant kinetic form on link components. The anisotropic Wilson derivative has bound `|H′₀[a,a]|≤C(L_B[a,a]+|q_R|h²||a||²)` there by the same plaquette expansion. Thus on the hard subspace it is bounded relative to the true positive H₀. The bounds apply at zero flux with the usual removal of gauge directions. [CMP99, §§C,D, (3.143)–(3.158)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01240355).

On the unconditioned quotient stabilize the physical spectral subspace of H₀ below c₁h², by adding a fixed positive multiple of h² times its orthogonal projection. That projection has rank O_R(1). Indeed the magnetic scalar return trace at s=h⁻² is at most the ordinary periodic return trace O_R(1), by the unit modulus of each real path phase, and the preceding form bound gives the vector eigenvalue count by the min–max principle. The stabilized physical Hessian H_s is positive with lower bound c_R h² and controls its anisotropic derivative relatively. On restriction to the hard subspace the stabilizer is still positive of rank O_R(1). For a positive Gaussian with covariance C, conditioning by r independent linear constraints changes the covariance by `C^{1/2} P C^{1/2}` with P an orthogonal projection of rank r. Hence the change of its logdet derivative costs at most `r ||C^{1/2}H′ C^{1/2}||`. Removing the stabilizer **on the already positive hard space** also changes the derivative by O_R(rank): the corresponding positive covariance difference is, relative to the unstabilized covariance, a positive contraction of that rank. These two comparisons prove the claim for metric-independent stabilizers; on canonical rescaling a derivative of the resulting finite-rank mass costs the same bound by its O_R(h²) size. Notice that no inverse of a possibly small stand-alone old return mass has been divided out. ∎

At each stationary field the stabilized physical determinant can be evaluated in the covariant vector Feynman gauge and its scalar ghost. Add the physical stabilizer to H only on the quotient; it annihilates gauge directions. With `Γ_σ=d* diag(a_i)` and ghost `Γ_σ d`, the Gaussian change of variables along the fine gauge orbit shows that the metric dependence equals `½ logdet(H_σ+B_s+Γ_σ*Γ_σ)−logdet′(Γ_σ d)` up to σ-independent coarea factors, just as in Lemma 7.177.
